---
title: Introduction
description: Get started with Data Engineering Questions
---

Welcome to the Data Engineering Questions guide. This is your resource for mastering common interview topics and questions in data engineering.

## What You'll Find Here

- Common data engineering interview questions
- Best practices and patterns
- Real-world scenarios and solutions

Let's get started!

## Data Structures: Interview Questions

**Data structures are inherently coding-problem territory — understanding them well means writing efficient data processing code and choosing the right organization for a given problem.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Data structures matter to a data engineer for three reasons: writing efficient processing code, optimizing memory usage in pipelines, and choosing the right organization for a given problem. Arrays offer fast, indexed access but are expensive to resize; linked lists trade that random access for cheap insertion and deletion by chaining nodes with pointers; stacks and queues layer LIFO/FIFO ordering on top of either; and more complex structures (hash tables, trees, graphs) each trade off differently on lookup, insert, and memory cost. A recurring interview thread is memory management — how allocation, free pools, and garbage collection reclaim space, and what happens when code mismanages a pointer after freeing it. Understanding these trade-offs is less about memorizing de

finitions and more about being able to justify why a particular structure fits a particular pipeline problem.

---

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Data Structures" storagePrefix="data-structure">

<QuestionCard id="ds-01" number={1} question="What is a data structure?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A way of organizing data that considers not only the items stored, but also their relationship to each other. Knowing that relationship in advance allows designing efficient algorithms for manipulating the data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-02" number={2} question="What are the goals of a data structure?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
It must be rich enough in structure to reflect the actual relationships of data in the real world, while staying simple enough for efficient processing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-03" number={3} question="What doe

s abstract data type mean?" difficulty="medium" topic="ADTs">
A data type is a collection of values plus a set of operations on those values. An abstract data type (ADT) is the mathematical concept defining a data type's logical properties, independent of implementation. An ADT has two parts: a **value definition** (e.g. the ADT `RATIONAL` consists of two integers, the second non-zero) and an **operation definition** (creation, addition, multiplication, equality test).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-04" number={4} question="What is the difference between a stack and an array?" difficulty="medium" topic="Stacks & Arrays">
**Stack:** an ordered collection whose size changes dynamically as items are pushed/popped, may hold mixed types conceptually, and is typically implemented as

a structure containing an array plus an integer tracking the current top.

**Array:** an ordered, static collection — size is fixed at declaration, and it holds a single data type. An array can back a stack's implementation (declared large enough for the stack's maximum size).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-05" number={5} question="What do you mean by recursive definition?" difficulty="easy" topic="Recursion">
A definition that defines an object in terms of simpler cases of itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-06" number={6} question="What is sequential search?" difficulty="easy" topic="Searching">
Comparing each item in the array (or linked list) against the target until a match is found.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-07" number={7} question="What acti

ons are performed when a function is called?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
Arguments are passed, local variables are allocated and initialized, and control transfers to the function.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-08" number={8} question="What actions are performed when a function returns?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
The return address is retrieved, the function's data area is freed, and execution branches back to the return address.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-09" number={9} question="What is a linked list?" difficulty="easy" topic="Linked Lists">
A linear collection of nodes where order is given by pointers rather than physical placement. Each node stores the element's data plus the address of the next node.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCar

d id="ds-10" number={10} question="What are the advantages of a linked list over an array?" difficulty="medium" topic="Linked Lists">
Arrays are expensive to insert into or delete from, and can't be resized without reallocating a new memory block. In a linked list, each element carries a pointer to the next, so successive elements need not occupy adjacent memory — insertion and deletion just rewire pointers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-11" number={11} question="Why can't you apply binary search to a sorted linked list?" difficulty="medium" topic="Linked Lists">
Binary search needs random access to the middle element by index; a linked list has no way to index directly to the middle, so binary search isn't applicable — a key drawback of using linked lists.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-12" number={12} question="What do you mean by a free pool?" difficulty="medium" topic="Memory Management">
A list of unused memory cells, maintained with its own pointer, from which new nodes are allocated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-13" number={13} question="What do you mean by garbage collection?" difficulty="medium" topic="Memory Management">
An operating system technique that periodically reclaims deleted space back onto the free storage list — triggered when free space runs low or the CPU is idle. The alternative, immediately reinserting freed space into the list, is more time-consuming.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-14" number={14} question="What do you mean by overflow and underflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
**Overflo

w:** inserting into a data structure when no space is available (the free storage list is empty).

**Underflow:** attempting to delete from a data structure that is already empty.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-15" number={15} question="What are the disadvantages of an array implementation of a linked list?" difficulty="medium" topic="Linked Lists">
The number of nodes needed can't be predicted at compile time, and the declared nodes remain allocated for the program's entire execution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-16" number={16} question="What is a queue?" difficulty="easy" topic="Queues">
An ordered collection where items are inserted at the rear and removed from the front — FIFO (first in, first out) — with no inherent limit on the number of elements.
</Questi

onCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-17" number={17} question="What is a priority queue?" difficulty="medium" topic="Queues">
A data structure where the intrinsic ordering of elements determines removal order rather than insertion order.

**Ascending priority queue:** smallest item is removed first. **Descending priority queue:** largest item is removed first.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-18" number={18} question="What are the disadvantages of sequential storage?" difficulty="medium" topic="Arrays">
A fixed amount of storage stays allocated even when the structure holds fewer elements, and once that fixed allocation is exhausted, overflow occurs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-19" number={19} question="What are the disadvantages of representing a stack or queue with a

linked list?" difficulty="medium" topic="Linked Lists">
Each node's info + next-pointer fields occupy more storage than the equivalent array element, and extra time is spent managing the available-node list.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-20" number={20} question="What is a dangling pointer, and how do you avoid it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Memory Management">
After `free(p)`, a subsequent reference to `*p` is illegal — the storage is freed but `p`'s address value is unchanged, so it may still be dereferenced (with no way to detect the illegality). This is a dangling pointer. Avoid it by setting `p` to `NULL` immediately after `free(p)`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-21" number={21} question="What are the disadvantages of a linear list?" difficulty="medium" topic="L

inked Lists">
You can't reach nodes preceding a given node `p`, and to traverse the list again, an external pointer to its head must be preserved.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-22" number={22} question="What is a circular list?" difficulty="medium" topic="Linked Lists">
A linear list where the last node's next field, instead of holding a null pointer, points back to the first node. Advantage: from any point in the list, every other point is reachable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-23" number={23} question="What are the disadvantages of a circular list?" difficulty="medium" topic="Linked Lists">
You can't traverse it backward, and given only a pointer to a node, you can't delete that node (you'd need the predecessor).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ds-24" num

ber={24} question="What is a doubly linked list?" difficulty="easy" topic="Linked Lists">
A collection of nodes where each node has three parts: an info field holding the data, a left pointer to the previous node, and a right pointer to the next node.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Implement a queue using two stacks."** A classic coding prompt that tests whether you understand the amortized cost of shuffling elements between the two structures.
- **"You need O(1) lookups but also need to preserve insertion order — what do you reach for?"** Tests whether the candidate knows the trade-offs behind ordered hash structures (e.g. Python's `dict`).
- **"A pipeline job keeps running out of memory while reversing a huge linked list in place — how would you debug it?"** Probes understanding of pointer manipulation, free pools, and garbage collection under memory pressure.
- **"Walk through what happens in memory when a recursive function calls itself too many times."** Tests understanding of stack frames and why deep recursion causes a

stack overflow, tying back to what happens when a function is called.

---

## Further Reading

- [SQL Interview Questions](/level-1-foundations/sql/) — the query-writing counterpart to these coding-structure problems
- [Python Practice](/level-1-foundations/python/practice/) — coding exercises that build on these data structures
- [Data Engineering Roadmap](/roadmaps/data-engineering/) — where data structures fit into the broader curriculum

## Language Fundamentals in Practice

Why Python shows up everywhere in data platforms, and how its concurrency model plays out in real pipelines.

<QuestionList topic="Language Fundamentals in Practice" storagePrefix="py-prac-fundamentals">

<QuestionCard

  question="Why is Python widely used in data engineering?"
  difficulty="easy"
  topic="Fundamentals"
>
Python is popular because it's productive, readable, and has a strong ecosystem for data processing, orchestration, and integration.

- **Glue code** — connecting APIs, databases, and file systems with minimal boilerplate
- **Rich libraries** — pandas, PyArrow, SQLAlchemy, boto3 cover most pipeline needs out of the box
- **Orchestration native** — Airflow, Dagster, and Prefect are all P

ython-first
- **Interop layer** — even when heavy compute runs on Spark or a warehouse engine, Python is the language stitching the pipeline together

It's rarely the fastest language for raw compute, but it's usually the fastest to build and maintain a correct pipeline in.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard
  id="py-prac-02"
  number={42}
  question="How do iterators and generators help with large data processing?"
  difficulty="medium"
  topic="Fundamentals"
>
Iterators and generators let you stream data instead of loading everything into memory — processing row-by-row or batch-by-batch keeps memory flat regardless of input size.


This pattern — pull, don't load — is what lets a single job process files far larger than available RAM.

<QuestionCard

  question="What is the difference between threads, multiprocessing, and async IO in Python?"
  difficulty="medium"
  topic="Concurrency"
>
| Approach | Good for | Limited by |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| `threading` | I/O-bound work (network, disk) | GIL — no CPU parallelism |
| `multiprocessing` |

CPU-bound work (parsing, transforms) | Process spawn/IPC overhead |
| `asyncio` | Many concurrent I/O waits (API calls) | Single-threaded event loop |

**Rule of thumb:** if the job spends most of its time *waiting* (network, disk), reach for threads or `asyncio`. If it spends its time *computing*, reach for `multiprocessing` or push the work to a native/distributed engine.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

  question="What is the GIL and why does it matter for a data pipeline you're building?"
  difficulty="medium"
  topic="Concurrency"
>
The **Global Interpreter Lock** allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time in CPython, even on a multi-core machine.

In practice, most data engineering jobs are I/O-bound (waiting on S3, a da

tabase, or an API), so the GIL rarely matters — threads still help because the GIL is released during I/O. It only becomes a bottleneck when a job is CPU-bound (row-by-row transforms in pure Python), at which point `multiprocessing` or vectorized libraries (pandas/NumPy, which release the GIL in their C internals) are the fix.
</QuestionCard>

Practical patterns for reading, writing, and moving data reliably in production pipelines.

<QuestionCard

`pyarrow` is the standard choice — it supports columnar reads, predicate pushdown, and explicit schema control.

<QuestionCard

  difficulty="easy"

Pin dependencies with a lockfile (`poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`, or `requirements.txt` with hashes), and isolate environments per project with a virtualenv or container.

Profile before optimizing — guessing at bottlenecks wastes time:

```python

```

Common fixes, in order of how often they apply:
1. **Vectorize** — replace `iterrows()`/Python loops with pandas/NumPy operations
2. **Reduce copies** — avoid chained `.loc`/`.copy()` calls that duplicate large frames
3. **Offload CPU work** — `multiprocessing`, or push to a native/distributed engine
4. **Cache repeated I/O** — `functools.lru_cache`, or batch reads instead of per-row

## Serialization & Data Formats in Practice

Handling the messy realities of real-world ingested data — mixed formats, encodings, and partial failures.

<QuestionList topic="Serialization & Data Formats in Practice" storagePrefix="py-prac-fmt">

<QuestionCard
  id="py-prac-fmt-01"
  number={58}
  question="How do you choose between JSON, Avro, and Protobuf for a data pipeline?"
  difficulty="medium"
  topic="Serialization"
>
**JSON** — human-readable, no schema enforcement, widest tooling support; good for APIs and low-volume/debugging-friendly paths. **Avro** — compact binary format with an embedded schema, strong support for schema evolution, common in Kafka pipelines. **Protobuf** — compact binary, schema defined separately and compiled, very fast, common for service-to-ser

title: Read only the columns you need, filtered at the file level
content:
vice RPC (gRPC).

In practice: JSON when human-readability and flexibility matter more than size/speed, Avro when you need schema evolution inside a streaming pipeline, Protobuf when you need a fast, strongly-typed contract between services.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard
  id="py-prac-fmt-02"
  number={59}
  question="How do you handle inconsistent date formats coming from multiple upstream sources?"
  difficulty="medium"
  topic="Datetime"
>
```python
from dateutil import parser

def parse_flexible_date(value: str):
    try:
        return parser.parse(value)   # handles many formats automatically
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        logger.warning("Unparseable date: %r", value)
        return None
```

`dateutil.parser` handles a wide range of formats witho

```python
from collections import deque

class RollingDeduplicator:
    def __init__(self, window_size=10_000):

        if len(self.order) == self.order.maxlen:
```

```python
from functools import lru_cache
```

  question="What is the difference between a mutable and an immutable object? Give examples of each."
  difficulty="easy"
  topic="Fundamentals"
>
**Mutable** objects can be changed after creation:
- `list` — `my_list.append(4)` modifies in place
- `dict` — `my_dict["key"] = "value"` modifies in place
- `set` — `my_set.add(5)` modifies in place

**Immutable** objects cannot be changed:
- `int`, `float`, `bool` — reassignment creates a new object
- `str` — `"hello" + "!"` returns a new string
- `tuple` — elements cannot be added, removed, or changed
- `frozenset` — immutable version of set

**Why it matters for data engineering:** immutable objects are safe as dict keys or set members; sharing mutable objects across threads causes subtle bugs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

  question="Explain the difference between == and is in Python."
  difficulty="easy"
  topic="Fundamentals"
>
| Operator | Checks | Example |
|----------|--------|---------|
| `==` | **Value equality** — same value? | `[1,2] == [1,2]` → `True` |
| `is` | **Identity** — same object in memory? | `[1,2] is [1,2]` → `False` |

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a           # same reference
c = [1, 2, 3]   # new object, same value

print(a == c)   # True  — same value
print(a is b)   # True  — same object
print(a is c)   # False — different objects
```

> Use `is` only for singleton checks (`if x is None`). Use `==` for all value comparisons.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

  question="How does m

title: ❌ Loads all 1M rows into memory at once
content:
emory management and garbage collection work in Python?"
  difficulty="medium"
  topic="Fundamentals"
>
Python uses two mechanisms:

**1. Reference Counting**
Every object tracks how many references point to it. When the count hits 0 the memory is freed immediately.

```python
import sys
a = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # 2 (a + getrefcount arg itself)
del a  # refcount → 0, memory freed
```

**2. Cyclic Garbage Collector**
Reference counting cannot handle circular references (A → B → A). Python's `gc` module runs periodically to detect and clean these cycles.

```python
import gc
gc.collect()  # manually trigger GC
```

**Memory pools:** CPython uses `pymalloc`, a private heap for small objects (≤ 512 bytes), reducing `malloc` overhead.

**For data engine

title: ❌ Loads all 1M rows into memory at once
content:
ering:** use `del df` + `gc.collect()` after processing large DataFrames, or prefer chunked processing to avoid OOM.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard
  id="py-fund-05"
  number={5}
  question="What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and how does it affect data engineering workloads?"
  difficulty="hard"
  topic="Concurrency"
>
The **GIL** is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, even on multi-core machines.

**Impact by workload type:**

| Workload | GIL Impact | Solution |
|----------|-----------|---------|
| I/O-bound (network, disk) | Minimal — GIL released during I/O | `threading` or `asyncio` |
| CPU-bound (parsing, transforms) | Full — only one core used | `multiprocessing` |
| NumPy / pandas ops | Minimal — C extension

```python
from multiprocessing import Pool

def process_partition(chunk):
    return chunk.apply(some_transform)

with Pool(processes=4) as pool:
    results = pool.map(process_partition, chunks)
```

> Python 3.13 introduced an experimental **no-GIL** build (PEP 703). This will change concurrent Python data pipeline design.

| `threading` | I/O-bound (HTTP, DB queries) | Yes | Low |

```python
# asyncio — ideal for many concurrent API calls
import asyncio, httpx

async def fetch(url, client):
    r = await client.get(url)
    return r.json()

async def fetch_all(urls):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        return await asyncio.gather(*[fetch(u, client) for u in urls])

results = asyncio.run(fetch_all(["https://api.example.com/data"] * 100))
```

**Rule of thumb for data engineering:**
- Reading 100 S3 files in parallel → `asyncio` or `ThreadPoolExecutor`
- Transforming 10 million rows → `multiprocessing.Pool`
- Single background task → `threading.Thread`

## Comprehensions & Functional Patterns

Concise, idiomatic ways to transform data without writing explicit loops.

<QuestionList topic="Comprehensions & Functional Patterns" storagePrefix="py-comp">

<QuestionCard
  id="py-comp-01"
  number={15}
  question="What are list, dict, and set comprehensions, and why prefer them over loops?"
  difficulty="easy"
  topic="Comprehensions"
>
Comprehensions build a collection in a single expression instead of an explicit loop with `.append()`/assignment:

```python
squares = [n ** 2 for n in range(10)]                       # list
by_id   = {row["id"]: row for row in records}               # dict
unique  = {row["user_id"] for row in records}                # set
```

They're preferred because they're usually faster (the loop runs

title: ❌ Loads all 1M rows into memory at once
content:
in C, not Python bytecode), more concise, and signal intent clearly — "this builds a new collection" — rather than mixing that intent with manual accumulator bookkeeping.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard
  id="py-comp-02"
  number={16}
  question="What's the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?"
  difficulty="easy"
  topic="Comprehensions"
>
```python
squares_list = [n ** 2 for n in range(1_000_000)]   # built eagerly, all in memory
squares_gen  = (n ** 2 for n in range(1_000_000))   # lazy, one value at a time
```

The only syntax difference is `[]` vs `()`, but the memory behavior is completely different — a list comprehension materializes the entire result immediately, while a generator expression produces values on demand. Use a generator exp

title: ❌ Loads all 1M rows into memory at once
content:
ression when you're piping the result into something that consumes it once (`sum(...)`, another loop) and don't need it as an indexable collection.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard
  id="py-comp-03"
  number={17}
  question="How do map(), filter(), and functools.reduce() work, and when would you prefer a comprehension instead?"

  difficulty="medium"

```python
to_cents = make_multiplier(100)
to_cents(19.99)  # 1999.0
```

```python
class ManagedConnection:
    def __enter__(self):

        return self.conn
```

  question="What's the difference between a list and a deque, and when does it matter for pipeline code?"
  difficulty="medium"

A `list` has O(1) appends/pops at the **end** but O(n) at the **start** (every remaining element shifts). A `deque` (double-ended queue) has O(1) at **both** ends.

```python
from collections import deque

recent_events = deque(maxlen=1000)   # fixed-size rolling window, oldest drops automatically
recent_events.append(new_event)
```

It matters for any rolling-window or queue-like pipeline pattern — a sliding window of recent events, a work queue being consumed from the front while new items arrive at the back — where a plain list would silently become a performance problem as it grows.
</QuestionCard>

## Aggregate Queries: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX

**Aggregate functions collapse many rows into a single summary value — a count, a total, an average, a smallest or largest — and the one detail that separates a correct aggregate query from a subtly wrong one is almost always how each function treats NULL.**

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
## Key Concepts

Aggregate functions compute one value across a set of rows — either the whole table, or per group when paired with `GROUP BY`. All five (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) share one important rule: **they ignore `NULL` values**, except for the specific case of `COUNT(*)`, which counts rows regardless of whether any column is `NULL`. That distinction — `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(column)` counts non-`NULL` values in that column — trips people up constantly, and it's the same underlying reason `AVG` divides by the number of non-`NULL` values rather than the total row count. When an aggregate runs over zero matching rows, `COUNT` returns `0`, but `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, and `MAX` all return `NULL` — there's no sensible sum, average, minimum, or maximum of an empty set, but

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
there is a sensible count (zero).

title: Aggregate Queries

content:
## COUNT

<QuestionList topic="COUNT" storagePrefix="aggregate-queries-count">

<QuestionCard id="agg-count-01" number={1} question="What's the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?" difficulty="easy" topic="COUNT">
`COUNT(*)` counts every row in the group, regardless of `NULL` values in any column. `COUNT(column)` counts only the rows where that specific column is *not* `NULL` — so `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(email)` can return different numbers if some rows have a `NULL` email.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-count-02" number={2} question="What does COUNT(DISTINCT column) do?" difficulty="easy" topic="COUNT">
It counts the number of *unique*, non-`NULL` values in that column, rather than every non-`NULL` row. `COUNT(DISTINCT department_id)` on an employees table returns the num

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
ber of distinct departments represented, not the number of employees.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-count-03" number={3} question="What does COUNT return when applied to a group or table with zero matching rows?" difficulty="medium" topic="COUNT">
`0` — unlike the other aggregate functions, `COUNT` always has a well-defined answer for an empty set: there are zero rows (or zero non-`NULL` values), which is a valid, meaningful number rather than an undefined one.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
## SUM

<QuestionList topic="SUM" storagePrefix="aggregate-queries-sum">

<QuestionCard id="agg-sum-01" number={1} question="What does SUM do, and how does it treat NULL values?" difficulty="easy" topic="SUM">
`SUM` adds up all the non-`NULL` values in a numeric column. `NULL` values are simply skipped — they aren't treated as zero, they're excluded from the calculation entirely, which matters if you were assuming a `NULL` would contribute `0` to the total.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-sum-02" number={2} question="Why would you use COALESCE with SUM?" difficulty="medium" topic="SUM">
`COALESCE(SUM(column), 0)` substitutes `0` for the result when `SUM` would otherwise return `NULL` — which happens when there are no matching rows at all, or every value in the column is `NULL`. It's

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
common in reporting queries where downstream code expects a number, not a `NULL`, for groups with no activity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-sum-03" number={3} question="What does SUM return when there are no rows to sum?" difficulty="medium" topic="SUM">
`NULL` — an empty set has no sensible total, so `SUM` returns `NULL` rather than `0`. This is a common source of bugs when the result is used directly in arithmetic without a `COALESCE` guard, since anything added to `NULL` is also `NULL`.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Aggregate Queries

## AVG

<QuestionList topic="AVG" storagePrefix="aggregate-queries-avg">

<QuestionCard id="agg-avg-01" number={1} question="What does AVG compute, and how does it handle NULL values?" difficulty="easy" topic="AVG">
`AVG` computes the arithmetic mean of a numeric column, and like `SUM`, it automatically ignores `NULL` values — both in the total and in the count used as the divisor. So `AVG` effectively divides the sum of non-`NULL` values by the *count of non-`NULL` values*, not by the total row count.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-avg-02" number={2} question="How would AVG's result differ from manually computing SUM(column) / COUNT(*)?" difficulty="medium" topic="AVG">
If the column has any `NULL` values, `SUM(column) / COUNT(*)` divides by the *total* row count (including rows w

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
here the column is `NULL`), producing a smaller number than the true average of the non-`NULL` values. `AVG(column)` divides by `COUNT(column)` instead — the non-`NULL` count — so the two can diverge whenever `NULL`s are present.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-avg-03" number={3} question="What does AVG return over an empty set or a column of all NULLs?" difficulty="medium" topic="AVG">
`NULL` — with zero non-`NULL` values to average, there's no meaningful result to return, the same reasoning that applies to `SUM` and `MIN`/`MAX` over an empty set.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Aggregate Queries
description: Interview questions on SQL aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX — and how each one handles NULL values and interacts with GROUP BY.
content:
## MIN

<QuestionList topic="MIN" storagePrefix="aggregate-queries-min">

<QuestionCard id="agg-min-01" number={1} question="What does MIN do, and does it work on non-numeric columns?" difficulty="easy" topic="MIN">
`MIN` returns the smallest value in a column or expression across the group. It isn't limited to numbers — it works on dates (earliest date), strings (lexicographically first), and any other type that has a defined ordering, always ignoring `NULL` values in the comparison.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-min-02" number={2} question="How would you find the row with the minimum value in a column, not just the minimum value itself?" difficulty="medium" topic="MIN">
`MIN` alone only returns the value, not the rest of that row's data. To get the full row, either filter with a

content:
subquery (`WHERE price = (SELECT MIN(price) FROM products)`), or use `ORDER BY price ASC LIMIT 1`, which is often more efficient since it can stop scanning after finding the first match if an index supports the sort order.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-min-03" number={3} question="What does MIN return over an empty group?" difficulty="medium" topic="MIN">
`NULL` — there's no smallest value in an empty set, so `MIN` (like `MAX`, `SUM`, and `AVG`) returns `NULL` rather than some arbitrary default.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## MAX

<QuestionList topic="MAX" storagePrefix="aggregate-queries-max">

<QuestionCard id="agg-max-01" number={1} question="What does MAX do, and where does it commonly show up outside of pure reporting queries?" difficulty="easy" topic="MAX">
`MAX` returns the largest value in a column or expression across the group, ignoring `NULL`s, and works on any orderable type (numbers, dates, strings). Beyond reporting, it commonly shows up in finding the most recent record per group (`MAX(created_at)` per user) or the current version of a row in a slowly-changing or event-sourced table.
</QuestionCard>

Alternatively, a window function like `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY value DESC)` filtered to rank `1` avoids the self-join and handles ties more explicitly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="agg-max-03" number={3} question="Can MIN and MAX be used without GROUP BY?" difficulty="easy" topic="MAX">
Yes — without `GROUP BY`, the whole result set is treated as a single group, so `SELECT MAX(price) FROM products` returns one row with the single highest price across the entire table, the same way any aggregate function behaves without explicit grouping.

content:
## Basic SQL Syntax: Building the SELECT Statement Clause by Clause

**A SELECT statement is assembled from a small set of clauses — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, and JOINs to pull in more than one table — and the order you write them in isn't the order the database actually evaluates them in, which is where most "why doesn't this work" confusion starts.**

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## Key Concepts

SQL is written in this order: `SELECT` → `FROM` → `WHERE` → `GROUP BY` → `HAVING` → `ORDER BY`. But it's **evaluated** in a different order: `FROM` (and any `JOIN`s) first, then `WHERE`, then `GROUP BY`, then `HAVING`, then `SELECT`, then `ORDER BY` last. That gap between written order and evaluation order explains a whole category of SQL surprises — why you can't reference a `SELECT`-list alias in `WHERE` (it doesn't exist yet at that point), why `HAVING` can filter on an aggregate but `WHERE` can't (the aggregate isn't computed until `GROUP BY` runs), and why `ORDER BY` is the one clause allowed to reference a `SELECT`-list alias (everything above it has already run).

---

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## SELECT

<QuestionList topic="SELECT" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-select">

<QuestionCard id="sel-01" number={1} question="What does the SELECT clause do, and what can appear in its column list?" difficulty="easy" topic="SELECT">
`SELECT` specifies which columns (or computed expressions) appear in the result set. Its list can include column names, literal values, arithmetic expressions, function calls, and aggregate functions — anything that resolves to a single value per output row.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sel-02" number={2} question="What is a column alias, and how do you define one?" difficulty="easy" topic="SELECT">
A column alias renames a column or expression in the output using `AS` (often optional): `SELECT price * quantity AS total`. It makes computed or awkwardly

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
-named columns readable in the result set, and most databases let `ORDER BY` reference it — though, notably, `WHERE` cannot, since `WHERE` runs before the `SELECT` list is evaluated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sel-03" number={3} question="What does SELECT DISTINCT do, and how is it different from a plain SELECT?" difficulty="easy" topic="SELECT">
`SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result set, comparing the full combination of selected columns — two rows are only deduplicated if every selected column matches. A plain `SELECT` returns every row that satisfies the query, duplicates included.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sel-04" number={4} question="What does SELECT * do, and why is it discouraged in production queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="SELECT">
`SELECT

description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
*` returns every column in the table(s) referenced. It's discouraged in production because it transfers more data than usually needed, breaks silently if columns are added/removed/reordered upstream, and prevents the query planner from using certain optimizations (like an index-only scan) that are possible when only specific columns are requested.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## FROM

<QuestionList topic="FROM" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-from">

<QuestionCard id="frm-01" number={1} question="What does the FROM clause specify?" difficulty="easy" topic="FROM">
`FROM` specifies which table (or tables, via `JOIN`) the query reads from. It's logically the first clause evaluated — the database has to know the source rows before it can filter, group, or select from them, regardless of the order the clauses are written in.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="frm-02" number={2} question="What is a table alias, and why use one?" difficulty="easy" topic="FROM">
A table alias is a short name assigned to a table for the rest of the query: `FROM employees e`. It's used to shorten repeated references, and it's required (not just convenient) once a query joins a table to i

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
tself or references the same table more than once, since the database needs a way to distinguish which instance a column reference belongs to.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="frm-03" number={3} question="What does a schema-qualified table name look like, and why would you need one?" difficulty="medium" topic="FROM">
A schema-qualified name prefixes the table with its schema: `analytics.orders` rather than just `orders`. It's needed when the same table name exists in more than one schema and the default search path would otherwise resolve it ambiguously, or simply to make a query's data source explicit and unambiguous regardless of the connection's default schema setting.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## WHERE

<QuestionList topic="WHERE" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-where">

<QuestionCard id="whr-01" number={1} question="What does the WHERE clause do, and when in query execution is it evaluated?" difficulty="easy" topic="WHERE">
`WHERE` filters individual rows based on a condition, before any grouping happens. It's evaluated right after `FROM`/`JOIN` resolve the source rows and before `GROUP BY`, which is why it can only reference actual table columns — not aggregate results or `SELECT`-list aliases that don't exist yet at that point.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="whr-02" number={2} question="How do you combine multiple conditions in a WHERE clause?" difficulty="easy" topic="WHERE">
With logical operators — `AND` (both must be true), `OR` (at least one must be true), and `NOT`

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
(inverts a condition) — and parentheses to make the intended grouping explicit, since `AND` binds tighter than `OR` by default.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="whr-03" number={3} question="Can you use a column alias defined in SELECT inside the WHERE clause?" difficulty="medium" topic="WHERE">
No, in standard SQL you can't — `WHERE` is evaluated before the `SELECT` list, so the alias doesn't exist yet at that point in execution. To filter on a computed value, you either repeat the full expression in `WHERE`, or wrap the query in a subquery/CTE and filter in the outer query, where the alias is now a real column.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## ORDER BY

<QuestionList topic="ORDER BY" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-order-by">

<QuestionCard id="ord-01" number={1} question="What does ORDER BY do, and what's the default sort direction?" difficulty="easy" topic="ORDER BY">
`ORDER BY` sorts the final result set by one or more columns or expressions. The default direction is ascending (`ASC`); `DESC` sorts descending. It's the last clause logically evaluated, which is why it's the only clause that can freely reference `SELECT`-list aliases.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ord-02" number={2} question="How do you sort by multiple columns, and what does the ordering of columns in ORDER BY mean?" difficulty="easy" topic="ORDER BY">
List them comma-separated: `ORDER BY department, salary DESC`. The order matters — rows are sorted by

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
the first column, and only rows with equal values in that column get sorted by the second, and so on, exactly like a multi-level tiebreaker.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ord-03" number={3} question="Can you ORDER BY a column that's not in the SELECT list?" difficulty="medium" topic="ORDER BY">
In most databases, yes — as long as the column is available from the tables in `FROM`, you can sort by it without including it in the output. The one exception is when `DISTINCT` or `GROUP BY` is used: then `ORDER BY` is generally restricted to columns or expressions that also appear in the `SELECT` list, since sorting by something not part of the deduplicated/grouped output would be ambiguous.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## GROUP BY

<QuestionList topic="GROUP BY" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-group-by">

<QuestionCard id="grp-01" number={1} question="What does GROUP BY do?" difficulty="easy" topic="GROUP BY">
`GROUP BY` collapses rows that share the same value(s) in the specified column(s) into a single output row per group, typically so aggregate functions (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, etc.) can compute a summary value per group instead of across the whole table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="grp-02" number={2} question="What rule governs which columns can appear in the SELECT list alongside GROUP BY?" difficulty="medium" topic="GROUP BY">
Every column in the `SELECT` list must either be one of the `GROUP BY` columns, or be wrapped in an aggregate function. This is enforced because for any non-grouped,

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
non-aggregated column, the database would have no single, well-defined value to return for a group made up of multiple original rows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="grp-03" number={3} question="Can you GROUP BY multiple columns, and what does that produce?" difficulty="medium" topic="GROUP BY">
Yes — `GROUP BY department, job_title` groups rows by the unique combination of both columns, producing one output row per distinct `(department, job_title)` pair rather than per department alone. It's how you compute aggregates at a finer grain than a single column allows.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## HAVING

<QuestionList topic="HAVING" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-having">

<QuestionCard id="hav-01" number={1} question="What does HAVING do, and how is it different from WHERE?" difficulty="easy" topic="HAVING">
`HAVING` filters *groups* after `GROUP BY` has produced them, and unlike `WHERE`, it can reference aggregate functions (`HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`). `WHERE` filters individual rows before grouping happens and cannot reference aggregates, because they haven't been computed yet at that point in execution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hav-02" number={2} question="Why can't you filter on an aggregate function's result using WHERE?" difficulty="medium" topic="HAVING">
Because `WHERE` is evaluated before `GROUP BY` runs, at which point aggregate values (like a group's `COUNT` o

title: Basic SQL Syntax
description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
r `SUM`) don't exist yet — they're only computed once rows have been grouped. `HAVING` runs after grouping specifically so it has access to those computed aggregate values to filter on.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hav-03" number={3} question="Can HAVING be used without GROUP BY?" difficulty="hard" topic="HAVING">
Yes, in most databases — without a `GROUP BY`, the entire result set is treated as a single implicit group, so `HAVING` can filter based on an aggregate computed across all rows (e.g., `HAVING COUNT(*) > 100`), returning either the aggregated row or nothing at all.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

description: Interview questions on basic SQL syntax — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, and JOINs — and the order SQL actually evaluates them in.
content:
## JOINs

<QuestionList topic="JOINs" storagePrefix="basic-sql-syntax-joins">

<QuestionCard id="bjoin-01" number={1} question="What is a JOIN, and why is it needed?" difficulty="easy" topic="JOINs">
A `JOIN` combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column, most often a foreign key matching a primary key. It's needed because relational databases deliberately split related data across tables rather than duplicating it, and a join is how a query reassembles that data at read time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bjoin-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between an implicit join (comma-separated FROM) and explicit JOIN...ON syntax?" difficulty="medium" topic="JOINs">
`FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.a_id` (implicit) produces the same result as `FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b

content:
.a_id` (explicit), but the explicit form is strongly preferred: it keeps the join condition visually separate from filtering conditions, makes the join type explicit (`INNER`, `LEFT`, etc.), and is much harder to get wrong by accidentally omitting the join condition and producing a Cartesian product.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="bjoin-03" number={3} question="What's the most common join type, and what does it return?" difficulty="easy" topic="JOINs">
`INNER JOIN` is the default and most common type — it returns only rows that have a match in both tables. Rows on either side without a corresponding match are excluded entirely, which is different from `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL OUTER JOIN`, which preserve unmatched rows from one or both sides with `NULL` filling the missing columns.

content:
## Data Definition Language (DDL): Defining and Changing Schema

**DDL is the set of commands that shape the database's structure — creating, altering, and removing tables and their constraints — and it behaves differently from ordinary data changes in ways that matter: DDL is often auto-committing, harder to safely roll back, and riskier to run against a live production table.**

description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [CREATE TABLE](#create-table)
- [ALTER TABLE](#alter-table)
- [DROP TABLE](#drop-table)
- [TRUNCATE TABLE](#truncate-table)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)

title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
## Key Concepts

DDL commands — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` — define and modify the *structure* of the database, not the data inside it (that's DML's job). A defining trait of DDL is that in most databases it **auto-commits**: unlike a `DELETE` or `UPDATE`, a `CREATE TABLE` or `DROP TABLE` typically can't be wrapped in a transaction and rolled back the same way (PostgreSQL is a notable exception — it supports transactional DDL). That makes DDL commands inherently higher-risk to run against production: `DROP TABLE` and `TRUNCATE TABLE` in particular are close to irreversible outside of a backup restore, which is why production schema changes are usually reviewed and run through migration tooling rather than typed ad hoc.

---

title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
## CREATE TABLE

<QuestionList topic="CREATE TABLE" storagePrefix="sql-ddl-create-table">

<QuestionCard id="ddl-ct-01" number={1} question="What does CREATE TABLE do, and what can you define in it?" difficulty="easy" topic="CREATE TABLE">
`CREATE TABLE` defines a new table's structure: its columns, each column's data type, constraints (`PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`), and default values. Nothing about the table's data is specified here — only its shape, which every future `INSERT` into that table must conform to.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-ct-02" number={2} question="What's the syntax for defining a default value on a column?" difficulty="easy" topic="CREATE TABLE">
`DEFAULT` is specified after the column's type: `created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRE

title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
NT_TIMESTAMP`. If an `INSERT` doesn't provide a value for that column, the default is used automatically instead of leaving it `NULL` (unless the column also allows `NULL` and no default is set).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-ct-03" number={3} question="What does CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS do, and why use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="CREATE TABLE">
It creates the table only if a table with that name doesn't already exist, silently doing nothing (rather than throwing an error) if it does. It's useful in scripts or migrations that might run more than once, making the `CREATE TABLE` idempotent instead of failing on a second run.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.

## ALTER TABLE

<QuestionList topic="ALTER TABLE" storagePrefix="sql-ddl-alter-table">

<QuestionCard id="ddl-at-01" number={1} question="What does ALTER TABLE do, and what kinds of changes can it make?" difficulty="easy" topic="ALTER TABLE">
`ALTER TABLE` modifies an existing table's structure: adding a column (`ADD COLUMN`), dropping one (`DROP COLUMN`), changing a column's type or constraints (`ALTER COLUMN` / `MODIFY`), or renaming the table or a column. It changes structure only — existing data is preserved (and, where applicable, backfilled to fit the new structure).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-at-02" number={2} question="What happens to existing rows when you ADD COLUMN with a NOT NULL constraint and no default?" difficulty="medium" topic="ALTER TABLE">
It fails — existin

The usual fix is to add the column with a `DEFAULT` (so existing rows get backfilled automatically), or add it as nullable first, backfill values, then apply `NOT NULL` in a separate step.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-at-03" number={3} question="Why can ALTER TABLE be risky to run against a large, live production table?" difficulty="hard" topic="ALTER TABLE">
Depending on the database and the specific change, some `ALTER TABLE` operations rewrite the entire table (locking it, or at minimum consuming significant I/O) rather than making a cheap metadata-only change. On a large, high-traffic table, a blocking `ALTER TABLE` can cause a production outage — which is why many

title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
## DROP TABLE

<QuestionList topic="DROP TABLE" storagePrefix="sql-ddl-drop-table">

<QuestionCard id="ddl-dt-01" number={1} question="What does DROP TABLE do?" difficulty="easy" topic="DROP TABLE">
`DROP TABLE` permanently removes a table — its structure, all its data, and (depending on the database) its dependent objects like indexes — from the database. Unlike `DELETE`, there are no rows left afterward because the table itself no longer exists.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-dt-02" number={2} question="What happens if you try to DROP a table that other tables have foreign keys referencing?" difficulty="medium" topic="DROP TABLE">
By default, the database blocks the drop to protect referential integrity — other tables' foreign keys would be left pointing at nothing. Some database

title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
s support `DROP TABLE ... CASCADE`, which also drops the dependent foreign key constraints (or, in some systems, the dependent objects entirely) to force the operation through.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-dt-03" number={3} question="Can a DROP TABLE be rolled back?" difficulty="medium" topic="DROP TABLE">
It depends on the database: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so a `DROP TABLE` inside an explicit transaction can be rolled back if the transaction isn't committed. Many other databases (MySQL among them) auto-commit DDL, meaning the drop takes effect immediately and can't be undone by `ROLLBACK` — recovery would require restoring from a backup instead.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## TRUNCATE TABLE

<QuestionList topic="TRUNCATE TABLE" storagePrefix="sql-ddl-truncate-table">

<QuestionCard id="ddl-tt-01" number={1} question="What does TRUNCATE TABLE do?" difficulty="easy" topic="TRUNCATE TABLE">
`TRUNCATE TABLE` removes all rows from a table while keeping its structure (columns, constraints, indexes) intact — the table still exists afterward, just empty. It typically works by deallocating the table's data pages directly rather than deleting rows one at a time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-tt-02" number={2} question="Why is TRUNCATE generally faster than DELETE with no WHERE clause?" difficulty="medium" topic="TRUNCATE TABLE">
`DELETE` removes rows one at a time, logging each individual row deletion (so it can be rolled back and so row-level triggers can fi

title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
description: Interview questions on SQL DDL — CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE — and how each affects schema, data, and transactions.
content:
re), which has real overhead at large row counts. `TRUNCATE` deallocates the table's data pages as a single operation, generally logging far less and skipping row-level triggers, which makes it substantially faster for clearing a large table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddl-tt-03" number={3} question="Can you TRUNCATE a table that's referenced by a foreign key from another table?" difficulty="hard" topic="TRUNCATE TABLE">
Usually not directly, for the same referential-integrity reason as `DROP TABLE` — truncating would leave other tables' foreign keys pointing at rows that no longer exist. Some databases require truncating the referencing table first, support `TRUNCATE ... CASCADE` to truncate dependent tables together, or simply disallow it if any row is actually referenced.
</Ques

content:
## Data Manipulation Language (DML): Inserting, Updating, and Deleting Rows

**DML is the set of commands that change the data inside a table's existing structure — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — and unlike DDL, these are normal transactional operations: they can be batched together, rolled back, and safely undone as long as they haven't been committed yet.**

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)

- [UPDATE](#update)

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
## Key Concepts

DML commands operate on rows within a table whose structure already exists — `INSERT` adds rows, `UPDATE` modifies existing rows, `DELETE` removes rows. All three participate normally in transactions: they can be grouped with `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`, and a mistake caught before commit can be undone cleanly. The single most common real-world DML mistake is also the simplest to avoid: running `UPDATE` or `DELETE` **without a `WHERE` clause**, which applies the change to every row in the table instead of the intended subset — which is why testing the equivalent `SELECT ... WHERE ...` first, before switching to `UPDATE`/`DELETE`, is standard practice.

---

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
## INSERT

<QuestionList topic="INSERT" storagePrefix="sql-dml-insert">

<QuestionCard id="dml-ins-01" number={1} question="What does INSERT do, and what's the basic syntax for adding a single row?" difficulty="easy" topic="INSERT">
`INSERT` adds new rows to a table. The basic form is `INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (val1, val2)` — explicitly naming the columns being populated is safer than omitting them, since it doesn't depend on the table's column order staying the same over time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-ins-02" number={2} question="How do you insert multiple rows in a single statement?" difficulty="easy" topic="INSERT">
List multiple value tuples separated by commas: `INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (a1, a2), (b1, b2), (c1, c2)`. A single multi-row `INSERT`

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
is typically much faster than the same number of single-row `INSERT` statements, since it avoids per-statement overhead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-ins-03" number={3} question="What is the INSERT ... SELECT pattern, and when would you use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="INSERT">
`INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT cols FROM source WHERE ...` inserts rows produced by a query instead of a literal `VALUES` list. It's used to copy or migrate data between tables, populate a summary/staging table from a larger source, or archive rows into a separate table before deleting them from the original.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-ins-04" number={4} question="What happens if an INSERT violates a constraint, like a duplicate primary key or a NOT NULL column left unspecified?" difficul

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
ty="medium" topic="INSERT">
The database rejects the entire `INSERT` with a constraint-violation error, and no row is added — it doesn't partially insert with the violating column left blank. In a multi-row `INSERT`, whether the *whole statement* fails or only the offending row is skipped depends on the database and any `ON CONFLICT`/`ON DUPLICATE KEY` clause used.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
## UPDATE

<QuestionList topic="UPDATE" storagePrefix="sql-dml-update">

<QuestionCard id="dml-upd-01" number={1} question="What does UPDATE do, and why must it almost always be paired with WHERE?" difficulty="easy" topic="UPDATE">
`UPDATE` modifies the values of existing rows in a table. Without a `WHERE` clause, it applies to **every row in the table** — a `WHERE` clause is what scopes the change to the specific rows intended. Omitting it by accident is one of the most common and most damaging SQL mistakes in production.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-upd-02" number={2} question="Can you update multiple columns in a single UPDATE statement?" difficulty="easy" topic="UPDATE">
Yes — comma-separate the assignments: `UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.1, updated_at = CURRENT_TI

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
MESTAMP WHERE department_id = 2`. All assignments in one statement are applied together as part of the same atomic change.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-upd-03" number={3} question="What's a safe practice for testing an UPDATE before running it against production data?" difficulty="medium" topic="UPDATE">
Run the equivalent `SELECT * FROM table WHERE <same condition>` first, and check that it returns exactly the rows you intend to change. Once confirmed, swap `SELECT *` for the `UPDATE ... SET ...` with the identical `WHERE` clause, so the scoping has already been verified before any data changes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-upd-04" number={4} question="Can an UPDATE reference the table's current values as part of the new value, and can it join another table?" difficult

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
y="medium" topic="UPDATE">
Yes to both. `SET salary = salary * 1.1` reads the current value of `salary` before overwriting it. Most databases also support updating based on a join to another table (syntax varies — `UPDATE ... FROM ...` in PostgreSQL, `UPDATE ... JOIN ...` in MySQL), letting you set a column's value based on data that lives in a different table.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
## DELETE

<QuestionList topic="DELETE" storagePrefix="sql-dml-delete">

<QuestionCard id="dml-del-01" number={1} question="What does DELETE do, and how is it scoped?" difficulty="easy" topic="DELETE">
`DELETE FROM table WHERE condition` removes rows matching the condition. Like `UPDATE`, omitting `WHERE` deletes every row in the table — the table itself still exists afterward, just empty, which is one way it differs from `DROP TABLE`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-del-02" number={2} question="What are the differences between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP?" difficulty="medium" topic="DELETE">
`DELETE` is DML: it removes specific rows (filterable with `WHERE`), can be rolled back within a transaction, and fires row-level triggers. `TRUNCATE` is DDL: it removes all rows at once by deal

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
locating data pages, is faster, but typically can't be filtered and may auto-commit. `DROP` is also DDL: it removes the table entirely, structure included, not just the rows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-del-03" number={3} question="How does a DELETE interact with a foreign key relationship?" difficulty="medium" topic="DELETE">
By default, deleting a row that other rows still reference via a foreign key is blocked to preserve referential integrity. Depending on how the foreign key was defined, it may instead cascade (`ON DELETE CASCADE` — dependent rows are deleted too), set the reference to `NULL` (`ON DELETE SET NULL`), or explicitly restrict the delete (`ON DELETE RESTRICT`, the implicit default).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dml-del-04" number={4} question="Can a DELETE

title: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
description: Interview questions on SQL DML — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — multi-row patterns, safe update/delete practices, and transactional behavior.
content:
be rolled back?" difficulty="easy" topic="DELETE">
Yes — unlike most DDL, `DELETE` is a normal transactional DML operation. Inside an explicit transaction, a `DELETE` can be undone with `ROLLBACK` as long as the transaction hasn't been committed yet. Once committed, undoing it requires restoring from a backup or replaying an audit log, not `ROLLBACK`.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

- **"How would you archive and remove all orders older than 2 years?"** Walk through `INSERT INTO archive_orders SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date < ...` followed by a matching `D

title: SQL Practice | Core Concepts
description: Hands-on SQL query-writing challenges with worked solutions for data engineering interviews. Interactive Q&A with progress tracking.

import QuestionCard from '../../../../components/mdx/QuestionCard.astro';

Query-writing challenges with worked solutions — the format interviewers use to test whether you can actually write SQL, not just describe it. Mark them **done** ✓, **bookmark** 🔖 for review, and expand answers on demand.

---

## Ranking & Salary Queries

The classic "Nth highest value" family of problems, and the different ways to answer them.

<QuestionList topic="Ranking & Salary Queries" storagePrefix="sql-prac-rank">

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-rank-01" number={100} question="How would you find the second-highest salary in an Employee table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking">
Given an `Employee` table (`ID`, `Salary`), there are several ways to do this.

**Option 1 — subquery with `NOT IN`:** find the max, exclude it, find the new max.
```sql
SELECT MAX(Salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE Salary NOT IN (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee);
```

**Option 2 — not-equal operator**, efficient when excluding a single top value:
```sql
SELECT MAX(Salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
F

ROM Employee
WHERE Salary <> (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee);
```

**Option 3 — `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`** (best for row ordering); `DISTINCT` avoids ties breaking the logic:
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT Salary AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
ORDER BY Salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
```
*(SQL Server: `OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY`.)*
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-rank-02" number={101} question="How would you find the maximum salary by department, including departments with no employees?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ranking">
Given `Employee(ID, Salary, DeptID)` and `Department(ID, DeptName)` — **this is a trick question**: ask the interviewer whether departments with no employees should still appear. If yes, use `LEFT OUTER JOIN` (`NULL` salary for empty departm

ents); if no, `INNER JOIN` is enough.

```sql
SELECT d.DeptName, MAX(e.Salary) AS MaxSalary
FROM Department d
LEFT OUTER JOIN Employee e ON d.ID = e.DeptID
GROUP BY d.DeptName;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-rank-03" number={102} question="How would you find the maximum salary per department (without a Department table)?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ranking">
```sql
SELECT DeptID, MAX(Salary) AS MaxSalary
FROM Employee
GROUP BY DeptID;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-rank-04" number={103} question="How would you find the Nth highest salary, for an arbitrary N?" difficulty="hard" topic="Ranking">
**Correlated subquery** — counts how many distinct salaries are higher; when that count is `N-1`, you've found rank N:
```sql
SELECT * FROM Employ

ee emp1
WHERE (N - 1) = (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT emp2.Salary) FROM Employee emp2 WHERE emp2.Salary > emp1.Salary
);
```

**`ROW_NUMBER()` window function** (recommended — works across Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL):
```sql
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS rnum FROM Employee
) AS Subquery WHERE rnum = N;
```
*(Use `DENSE_RANK()` instead if duplicate salaries should share a rank.)*

**`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`** (MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQLite — shortest if supported):
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Employee ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET (N - 1);
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Filtering, Sets & Duplicates

Set comparisons between tables, and finding rows that don't belong.

<QuestionList topic="Filtering, Sets & Duplicates" storagePrefix="sql-prac-filter">

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-01" number={104} question="How would you select every other (alternate odd/even) record from a table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filtering">
Assign a row number with `ROW_NUMBER()`, then filter with modulo:

```sql
-- Even-numbered records
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) AS row_num
    FROM Employee
) AS Subquery
WHERE MOD(row_num, 2) = 0;

-- Odd-numbered: WHERE MOD(row_num, 2) = 1
```
*(No `MOD()` support? Use `WHERE row_num % 2 = 0`.)*
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-02" number={105} ques

tion="How would you find records in Table A that don't exist in Table B, without using NOT IN?" difficulty="medium" topic="Filtering">
**Set operators** — standard SQL/SQL Server/PostgreSQL/MySQL use `EXCEPT`, Oracle uses `MINUS`:
```sql
SELECT * FROM Table_A EXCEPT SELECT * FROM Table_B;   -- Oracle: MINUS instead of EXCEPT
```

**`LEFT JOIN`** (most universal — works across all SQL databases):
```sql
SELECT Table_A.* FROM Table_A
LEFT JOIN Table_B ON Table_A.ID = Table_B.ID
WHERE Table_B.ID IS NULL;
```
*(`NOT IN` is avoided here because it silently returns no rows if the subquery contains even one `NULL`.)*
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-03" number={106} question="How would you find employees who share both the same name and email?" difficulty="easy" t

opic="Filtering">
Group by both columns together — `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` isolates rows where both fields match exactly:
```sql
SELECT name, email, COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM Employee
GROUP BY name, email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-04" number={107} question="How would you find duplicate email addresses in an Employee table?" difficulty="easy" topic="Filtering">
```sql
SELECT EMAIL, COUNT(EMAIL) AS occurrence_count
FROM Employee
GROUP BY EMAIL
HAVING COUNT(EMAIL) > 1;
```
Note: with `GROUP BY`, only grouped or aggregated columns may appear in `SELECT`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-05" number={108} question="How would you select 10 employees with odd employee IDs?" difficulty="easy" topic="Filteri

ng">
```sql
-- Standard SQL / Oracle 12c+ / PostgreSQL / MySQL
SELECT ID FROM Employee WHERE ID % 2 = 1 FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;

-- SQL Server
SELECT TOP 10 ID FROM Employee WHERE ID % 2 = 1;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-filter-06" number={109} question="How would you do a case-insensitive name search?" difficulty="easy" topic="Filtering">
```sql
SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE UPPER(emp_name) LIKE '%RICH%';
-- Equivalent: WHERE LOWER(emp_name) LIKE '%rich%'
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Dates & Result Shaping

Date arithmetic and controlling how many rows come back.

<QuestionList topic="Dates & Result Shaping" storagePrefix="sql-prac-dates">

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-dates-01" number={110} question="How would you select employees born between two dates?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dates">
`BETWEEN` is inclusive of both endpoints:
```sql
SELECT EmpName FROM Employees WHERE birth_date BETWEEN '1990-01-01' AND '2000-12-31';
-- Equivalent: WHERE birth_date >= '1990-01-01' AND birth_date <= '2000-12-31'
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-dates-02" number={111} question="How would you extract the quarter from a date?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dates">
```sql
-- Standard SQL (most portable)
SELECT EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM DATE '2016-03-31') AS quarte

r;

-- Oracle
SELECT TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('03/31/2016', 'MM/DD/YYYY'), 'Q') AS quarter FROM DUAL;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-dates-03" number={112} question="How would you calculate the number of days between two dates?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dates">
```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT DATEDIFF('2016-12-31', '2015-01-01') AS DaysDifference;

-- SQL Server
SELECT DATEDIFF(day, '2015-01-01', '2016-12-31') AS DaysDifference;

-- PostgreSQL / Oracle
SELECT '2016-12-31'::date - '2015-01-01'::date AS DaysDifference;
```
Note: in MySQL the larger date goes first for a positive result; in SQL Server/PostgreSQL, second.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-dates-04" number={113} question="How do you get the current date and time in SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Da

tes">
```sql
SELECT CURRENT_DATE;       -- ANSI standard; MySQL: CURDATE()
SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;  -- ANSI standard; MySQL: NOW()
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-prac-dates-05" number={114} question="How do you limit the number of rows returned by a query, and how does pagination build on that?" difficulty="easy" topic="Result Shaping">
```sql
-- Standard SQL
SELECT * FROM table_name FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;
-- MySQL
SELECT * FROM table_name LIMIT 10;

-- Pagination: skip 3, take next 6
SELECT * FROM table_name OFFSET 3 ROWS FETCH NEXT 6 ROWS ONLY;   -- MySQL: LIMIT 3, 6
```
Always pair `LIMIT`/`FETCH` with `ORDER BY` — without it, row order (and your results) are unpredictable.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

content:
## RDBMS Benefits and Limitations: When to Choose (and Outgrow) a Relational Database

**An RDBMS trades some flexibility and horizontal scalability for strong consistency guarantees and a rigorously enforced schema — a trade that's right for most transactional systems and starts to strain only at a specific kind of scale.**

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Key Concepts

The core benefit of an RDBMS is **ACID** — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the set of guarantees that make a transaction either fully happen or not happen at all, even under concurrent access or a crash mid-write. That's paired with a **fixed, enforced schema** (bad data gets rejected at write time, not discovered later) and a mature, standardized query language with decades of tooling, optimizers, and operational experience behind it. The limitations show up as scale grows past what a single, more powerful machine can handle: RDBMSs traditionally scale **vertically** (a bigger server) rather than **horizontally** (more servers), a rigid schema makes fast-changing or semi-structured data awkward to model, and enforcing strong consistency across many machine

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
s gets expensive — which is exactly the gap NoSQL and distributed systems were built to fill.

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="RDBMS Benefits & Limitations" storagePrefix="rdbms-benefits-and-limitations">

<QuestionCard id="rbl-01" number={1} question="What are the core benefits of using an RDBMS?" difficulty="easy" topic="Benefits">
Strong consistency guarantees through ACID transactions, a schema that's enforced at write time rather than discovered as a runtime error later, a standardized and widely-known query language (SQL), and decades of mature tooling — query optimizers, replication, backup/recovery, monitoring — built around the relational model.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-02" number={2} question="What does ACID stand for, and why does it matter?" difficulty="easy" topic="ACID">
**Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.** Together they guarant
