description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
ee that a transaction either fully completes or has no effect at all, that the database moves from one valid state to another, that concurrent transactions don't corrupt each other's view of the data, and that a committed transaction survives a crash. It matters because it's what lets application code trust the database instead of re-implementing that safety itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-03" number={3} question="Explain atomicity with an example." difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Atomicity means a transaction is all-or-nothing. Classic example: transferring money between two bank accounts requires debiting one account and crediting another — atomicity guarantees that if the crediting step fails, the debit is rolled back too, so the transaction never leaves money "in trans

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
it" or duplicated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-04" number={4} question="Explain consistency in ACID." difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Consistency means a transaction can only bring the database from one valid state to another valid state — it can't violate constraints, foreign keys, or defined rules, even temporarily as far as anything outside the transaction can observe. If a transaction would break a constraint (e.g., insert an order for a customer that doesn't exist), the whole transaction is rejected rather than partially applied.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-05" number={5} question="Explain isolation and why isolation levels exist." difficulty="medium" topic="ACID">
Isolation means concurrent transactions shouldn't see each other's uncommitted changes, so the ou

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
tcome looks as if transactions ran one at a time even though they actually overlapped. Isolation levels (`READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ`, `SERIALIZABLE`, etc.) exist because full isolation is expensive — each level trades some strictness for performance, and picking the right one depends on what anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads) a given workload can tolerate.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-06" number={6} question="Explain durability." difficulty="easy" topic="ACID">
Durability means once a transaction is committed, its changes survive — even a power loss or crash immediately afterward won't lose it. RDBMSs typically achieve this by writing to a write-ahead log (WAL) on durable storage before acknowledging the commit, so the change can be replayed from

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
the log if the in-memory state is lost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-07" number={7} question="What are the main limitations of an RDBMS at scale?" difficulty="medium" topic="Limitations">
Traditional RDBMSs scale vertically more naturally than horizontally, so there's a ceiling set by how large a single machine can get. A fixed schema makes it awkward to store fast-changing, semi-structured, or highly variable data. And maintaining strong consistency across many nodes (if you do try to distribute an RDBMS) adds coordination overhead that limits write throughput compared to systems designed for eventual consistency.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-08" number={8} question="What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling, and why do RDBMSs traditionally favor v

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
ertical?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scaling">
Vertical scaling means adding more resources (CPU, RAM, faster disks) to a single machine; horizontal scaling means adding more machines and distributing the load across them. RDBMSs traditionally favor vertical scaling because ACID transactions and joins are much simpler to guarantee on a single node — distributing them across machines while preserving the same consistency guarantees is a genuinely hard distributed-systems problem, one that only some newer distributed SQL systems (e.g., CockroachDB, Google Spanner) have solved.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rbl-09" number={9} question="When would you choose an RDBMS over a NoSQL system, and vice versa?" difficulty="medium" topic="Trade-offs">
Choose an RDBMS when data is structured, rela

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
tionships matter (foreign keys, joins), and transactional correctness is critical — financial records, order systems, anything where "partially applied" is unacceptable. Lean toward NoSQL when the schema is highly variable or evolving fast, write throughput needs to scale horizontally beyond what a single machine can handle, or the access pattern is simple enough (key-value lookups, for example) that relational features add overhead without adding value.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: RDBMS Benefits & Limitations
description: Interview questions on RDBMS benefits and limitations — ACID properties, vertical vs horizontal scaling trade-offs, and when to choose a relational database.
content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Walk me through what ACID actually protects against, one letter at a time."** Use a concrete transaction (a bank transfer, an order placement) and show what specifically breaks if each property is missing.
- **"Your RDBMS is hitting a scaling wall — what are your options before rearchitecting to NoSQL?"** Talk through read replicas, caching, connection pooling, query/index optimization, and vertical scaling headroom before jumping to "switch databases."
- **"When would you deliberately choose a weaker isolation level than SERIALIZABLE?"** Explain the performance trade-off — most workloads use `READ COMMITTED` because full serializability adds locking overhead the application doesn't actually need.

content:
## What Are Relational Databases: Tables, Keys, and the Relational Model

**A relational database organizes data into tables of rows and columns, linked to each other through keys rather than duplicated everywhere they're needed — the structural idea every SQL query and every RDBMS is ultimately built on top of.**

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Key Concepts

The **relational model**, introduced by Edgar Codd in 1970, represents data as **tables** (also called relations) — each table a fixed set of columns (attributes) and any number of rows (records). A **primary key** uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a **foreign key** in one table points to a primary key in another, which is what lets related data live in separate tables instead of being duplicated everywhere it's needed. That separation is deliberate: it's how a relational database enforces **referential integrity** — the guarantee that a foreign key always points to a row that actually exists — and how it avoids the update anomalies that come from copying the same fact into a dozen places. Relationships between tables come in a few shapes: **one-to-many** (one d

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
epartment, many employees) needs only a foreign key on the "many" side, while **many-to-many** (students and courses) needs a third junction table holding a foreign key to each side.

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Relational Databases" storagePrefix="relational-databases">

<QuestionCard id="rdb-01" number={1} question="What is a relational database?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A relational database is a database that stores data in tables — structured collections of rows and columns — and represents relationships between different pieces of data through keys rather than by nesting or duplicating data. It's the model underlying virtually every SQL database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and the managed cloud warehouses built on similar principles.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-02" number={2} question="Who introduced the relational model, and what problem was it solving?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Edgar F. Codd

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
introduced the relational model in a 1970 paper while at IBM. Before it, databases were typically hierarchical or network-based, requiring applications to know the physical structure and navigation paths of the data. Codd's insight was that data could be represented purely as tables with logical relationships, letting a query language describe *what* data you want without specifying *how* to physically traverse it to get there.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-03" number={3} question="What are tables, rows, and columns in the relational model?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A **table** represents one entity type (e.g., `employees`). Each **column** defines an attribute of that entity with a fixed data type (e.g., `name`, `hire_date`, `salary`). Each **row** is one instance

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
of that entity — one specific employee, with a value for every column. Every row in a table shares the same columns, which is what makes the table queryable as a uniform set.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-04" number={4} question="What is a primary key, and why must it be unique?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
A primary key is one or more columns whose value uniquely identifies a row within a table — no two rows can share the same primary key value, and it can't be `NULL`. It has to be unique because it's the handle every other part of the system uses to refer to that exact row: foreign keys reference it, indexes are frequently built on it, and joins rely on it resolving to exactly one row.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-05" number={5} question="What is a foreign key, and

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
what does it enforce?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
A foreign key is a column (or columns) in one table that references the primary key of another table — for example, an `orders.customer_id` column referencing `customers.id`. It enforces **referential integrity**: the database won't let you insert an order with a `customer_id` that doesn't exist in the `customers` table, and by default won't let you delete a customer that still has orders referencing them (unless a cascade rule says otherwise).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-06" number={6} question="What's the difference between a one-to-many and a many-to-many relationship, and how is many-to-many implemented?" difficulty="medium" topic="Relationships">
A one-to-many relationship (one department has many employees) is impleme

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
nted with a single foreign key on the "many" side — `employees.department_id`. A many-to-many relationship (students enroll in many courses, courses have many students) can't be represented with a single foreign key on either side, since neither table has one row per relationship; instead it requires a **junction table** (e.g., `enrollments`) holding a foreign key to each side, with each row representing one specific student-course pairing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-07" number={7} question="What is a schema, and why does defining one upfront matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
A schema is the definition of a table's structure — its columns, their data types, and its constraints (primary key, foreign keys, `NOT NULL`, etc.) — declared before any data is inserted.

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
Defining it upfront matters because the database then enforces it on every write: a row that violates the schema (wrong type, missing required value, duplicate key) is rejected at insert time rather than silently corrupting downstream data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-08" number={8} question="Why store data across multiple related tables instead of one big table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Design">
Splitting data across related tables — normalization — avoids duplicating the same fact in many places. If a customer's address lived on every one of their orders instead of once in a `customers` table, updating it would mean rewriting every order row, and a partial update would leave the data inconsistent. Separate, related tables mean each fact is stored once and referenced everyw

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
here it's needed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="rdb-09" number={9} question="What is referential integrity?" difficulty="medium" topic="Keys">
Referential integrity is the guarantee that a foreign key value always corresponds to an existing row in the referenced table — no "dangling" foreign keys pointing at rows that were deleted or never existed. The database enforces it automatically once a foreign key constraint is declared, rejecting inserts/updates that would violate it and controlling what happens on delete via rules like `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `ON DELETE RESTRICT`.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: Relational Databases
description: Interview questions on what relational databases are, the relational model, tables, primary and foreign keys, and referential integrity.
content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a simple schema for an e-commerce system with customers, orders, and products."** Walk through identifying the entities, their primary keys, the one-to-many relationships (customer → orders), and the many-to-many relationship (orders ↔ products) that needs a junction table (`order_items`).
- **"What happens if you try to delete a customer who still has orders?"** Explain referential integrity — the database blocks the delete by default, unless a cascade or set-null rule was explicitly configured on the foreign key.
- **"Why not just store everything in one giant table?"** Use it to explain normalization's payoff: avoiding duplicated facts and the update anomalies that come with them, at the cost of needing joins to reassemble the full picture.

--

## SQL Data Types: Numeric, String, Date, and Beyond

**Every column in a relational table has a declared data type, and that choice isn't a formality — it determines how much space a value takes, what operations are valid on it, and whether bad data gets rejected at the door or silently corrupts a downstream calculation.**

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
## Key Concepts

SQL data types fall into a few core families: **numeric** (`INT`, `DECIMAL`, `FLOAT` — whole numbers, exact decimals, and approximate floating-point respectively), **string** (`CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT` — fixed-length, variable-length, and unbounded text), **date/time** (`DATE`, `DATETIME`/`TIMESTAMP` — a calendar date versus a specific instant), and **boolean** (true/false, though not every SQL dialect has a native boolean type). The choice between similar-looking types has real consequences: `DECIMAL` stores an exact value while `FLOAT` stores an approximation, which matters enormously for money; `CHAR` pads to a fixed length while `VARCHAR` doesn't, trading a little flexibility for storage predictability. Most databases also offer **vendor-specific types** beyond the SQL

description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
standard — PostgreSQL's `JSONB` and `ARRAY` being common examples — for cases the standard types don't cover well.

content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="SQL Data Types" storagePrefix="sql-data-types">

<QuestionCard id="dt-01" number={1} question="What are the main categories of SQL data types?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
**Numeric** (`INT`, `DECIMAL`, `FLOAT`), **string/character** (`CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`), **date/time** (`DATE`, `DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP`), and **boolean** (`BOOLEAN`, though support varies by database). Most vendors also add their own extended types — JSON, arrays, UUIDs — layered on top of this common core.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-02" number={2} question="What's the difference between INT and DECIMAL, and when would you use DECIMAL over FLOAT?" difficulty="medium" topic="Numeric Types">
`INT` stores whole numbers with no fractional component. `DECIM

content:
AL(precision, scale)` stores an exact fixed-point number — no rounding error — which is why it's the right choice for money and anything requiring exact arithmetic. `FLOAT` stores an approximate floating-point value, which is faster and more compact but can introduce tiny rounding errors that make it unsuitable for financial calculations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-03" number={3} question="What's the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR, and TEXT?" difficulty="easy" topic="String Types">
`CHAR(n)` is fixed-length — a value shorter than `n` is padded with spaces, and storage is always exactly `n` characters. `VARCHAR(n)` is variable-length up to a maximum of `n`, storing only the actual length used. `TEXT` stores effectively unbounded-length text with no declared maximum, generally u

description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
sed for large free-form content like descriptions or comments.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-04" number={4} question="What date/time types does SQL typically offer, and how do DATE and DATETIME/TIMESTAMP differ?" difficulty="medium" topic="Date/Time Types">
`DATE` stores just a calendar date (year, month, day) with no time component. `DATETIME`/`TIMESTAMP` stores a specific date and time down to some precision, and in some databases `TIMESTAMP` additionally tracks time zone information while `DATETIME` doesn't — the exact behavior varies by vendor, which is worth checking before assuming.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-05" number={5} question="How does BOOLEAN work across different SQL dialects?" difficulty="medium" topic="Boolean">
PostgreSQL has a native `BOOLEAN` type. My

title: SQL Data Types
description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.
content:
SQL doesn't — it typically represents booleans as `TINYINT(1)` (0 or 1) under the hood, with `BOOLEAN` accepted as a synonym. This is a common source of confusion when porting schemas between databases, since code that assumes a real boolean type may behave differently against a database emulating one with an integer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-06" number={6} question="What happens if you insert a value that doesn't match a column's data type?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Depends on the database and the mismatch: many databases reject the insert outright with a type error (e.g., inserting text into an `INT` column). Some perform implicit conversion when it's unambiguous (e.g., inserting the string `'5'` into an `INT` column). Relying on implicit conversion is general

description: Interview questions on SQL data types — numeric, string, date/time, boolean, vendor-specific types, and how type choice affects storage and correctness.

ly discouraged — it's a common source of subtle bugs when the conversion doesn't behave the way you'd expect.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-07" number={7} question="Why does picking the right data type matter for storage and query performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
A narrower, well-chosen type takes less disk space and memory, which means more rows fit in a page and more of the working set fits in cache — both directly speed up scans and index lookups. Using an oversized type "just in case" (e.g., `BIGINT` for a column that will only ever hold small numbers) wastes space across every row and every index built on that column, at scale.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-08" number={8} question="What are vendor-specific data types, and give an example." difficu

Types beyond the ANSI SQL standard that a specific database vendor adds to cover cases the standard types handle poorly. PostgreSQL's `JSONB` (binary-indexed JSON, queryable with operators) and `ARRAY` (a column holding a list of values) are common examples — both let you store semi-structured or multi-valued data inside an otherwise relational table without a separate junction table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dt-09" number={9} question="What's the difference between implicit and explicit type conversion?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Implicit conversion happens automatically when the database can unambiguously reinterpret a value as another type (e.g., comparing an `INT` column to the string `'5'`). Explicit conversion uses a functi

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"How would you store a list of tags on a post — a comma-separated string, a JSON array, or a separate table?"** Walk through the trade-offs: a delimited string is simple but unqueryable, a native array/JSON type (where supported) is queryable but less po

## SQL Keywords: DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL Explained

**Every SQL keyword falls into one of a small number of categories based on what it actually changes — schema, data, permissions, or transaction state — and recognizing which bucket a statement belongs to is a fast way to reason about its blast radius before running it.**

## Key Concepts

SQL keywords are **reserved words** the database parser assigns special meaning to — they can't be used as ordinary identifiers (table or column names) without special quoting, because the parser needs to recognize them unambiguously. They group into four categories: **DDL** (Data Definition Language: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP` — manages schema structure), **DML** (Data Manipulation Language: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and often `SELECT` — manages the data itself), **DCL** (Data Control Language: `GRANT`, `REVOKE` — manages who can do what), and **TCL** (Transaction Control Language: `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT` — manages transaction boundaries). The category matters practically, not just academically: DDL statements typically auto-commit and can't be rolled back th

They're reserved because the parser needs to distinguish them unambiguously from identifiers (table names, column names); if `SELECT` could also be a column name without special handling, the parser couldn't tell which meaning was intended in a given position.

It depends on the classification scheme. Many textbooks and vendors group `SELECT` under DML since it operates on data. Others carve out a separate category, DQL (Data Query Language), specifically for `SELECT`, on the reasoning that it only reads data and never modifies it — a meaningfully different risk profile than `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`. ## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Categorize these five keywords: CREATE, SELECT, GRANT, COMMIT, DELETE."** A quick fluency check — `CREATE` is DDL, `SELECT` is DML/DQL, `GRANT` is DCL, `COMMIT` is TCL, `DELETE` is DML.
- **"Why might TRUNCATE be riskier to run in production than DELETE, even though both remove data?"** Explain that `TRUNCATE`'s DDL status often means it can't be rolled back the same way, may skip row-level triggers, and removes everything at once with no `WHERE` clause to scope it.
- **"A junior engineer asks why they can't run a GRANT statement — what do you tell them?"** Use it to explain DCL's privilege requirements, and why permission management is deliberately separated from everyday DML access.

## SQL Operators: Comparison, Logical, and Pattern Matching

**Operators are what turn a SQL statement's raw values into the conditions that decide which rows get selected, updated, or deleted — and a surprising number of query bugs trace back to a single operator behaving differently than expected, especially around NULL.**

title: SQL Operators
description: Interview questions on SQL operators — arithmetic, comparison, logical, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE wildcards, and NULL-safe comparisons.
content:
## Table of Contents

- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

title: SQL Operators
description: Interview questions on SQL operators — arithmetic, comparison, logical, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE wildcards, and NULL-safe comparisons.
content:
## Key Concepts

SQL operators split into a few functional groups: **arithmetic** (`+ - * / %`) for numeric calculation, **comparison** (`= <> < > <= >=`) for evaluating conditions, **logical** (`AND`, `OR`, `NOT`) for combining conditions, and a set of purpose-built operators for common filtering patterns — `BETWEEN` for inclusive ranges, `IN` for membership in a list, and `LIKE` with wildcards (`%`, `_`) for pattern matching on text. The one recurring trap across almost all of them is **NULL**: it represents "unknown," not a value, so any comparison against `NULL` using `=` or `<>` evaluates to unknown (effectively excluded) rather than true or false — which is why SQL provides the dedicated `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` operators instead of relying on standard comparison.

---

title: SQL Operators
description: Interview questions on SQL operators — arithmetic, comparison, logical, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE wildcards, and NULL-safe comparisons.
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="SQL Operators" storagePrefix="sql-operators">

<QuestionCard id="op-01" number={1} question="What categories of operators does SQL provide?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
**Arithmetic** (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`), **comparison** (`=`, `<>`/`!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`), **logical** (`AND`, `OR`, `NOT`), and a set of specialized filtering operators: `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `LIKE`, and the NULL-safe `IS NULL`/`IS NOT NULL`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-02" number={2} question="What are the arithmetic operators, and where do they commonly show up in queries?" difficulty="easy" topic="Arithmetic">
`+`, `-`, `*`, `/` for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, and `%` (or `MOD`) for remainder. They show up most often in computed

content:

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-03" number={3} question="What are the comparison operators, and how does NULL interact with them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
`=`, `<>`/`!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` compare two values. `NULL` breaks the usual true/false logic: `NULL = NULL` does not evaluate to true — it evaluates to unknown, because `NULL` represents an unknown value, and comparing two unknowns can't logically resolve to "equal." Any row where a comparison involving `NULL` evaluates to unknown gets excluded from the result, which surprises people who expect `WHERE col = NULL` to match NULL rows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op

`AND` requires both conditions to be true, `OR` requires at least one, `NOT` inverts a condition. `AND` has higher precedence than `OR`, so `WHERE a OR b AND c` evaluates as `WHERE a OR (b AND c)`, not `(a OR b) AND c` — a common source of bugs when a query mixes both without explicit parentheses to force the intended grouping.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-05" number={5} question="What does the BETWEEN operator do, and is it inclusive or exclusive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Filtering">
`BETWEEN a AND b` filters for values in the range from `a` to `b`, **inclusive** on both ends — `price BETWEEN 10 AND 20`

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-06" number={6} question="What does the IN operator do, and when is it preferable to a chain of OR conditions?" difficulty="easy" topic="Filtering">
`IN (v1, v2, v3, ...)` matches a column against any value in a given list — shorthand for `col = v1 OR col = v2 OR col = v3`. It's preferable whenever the list has more than a couple of values: it's more readable, less error-prone to write correctly, and can also take a subquery (`IN (SELECT ...)`) rather than a static list.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-07" number={7} question="How does the LIKE operator

`LIKE` performs pattern matching on text. `%` matches any sequence of characters (including zero), and `_` matches exactly one character. `name LIKE 'A%'` matches any name starting with "A"; `name LIKE '_ohn'` matches any 4-character name ending in "ohn" (like "John"). Matching is case-sensitive or insensitive depending on the database's default collation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="op-08" number={8} question="Why must you use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL instead of = NULL?" difficulty="medium" topic="NULL Handling">
Because `NULL` represents an unknown value rather than a comparable value, standard comparison operators (`=`, `<>`) against `NULL` always evaluate to unknown rather than true, even when c

<QuestionCard id="op-09" number={9} question="Does SQL short-circuit AND/OR the way general-purpose programming languages do?" difficulty="hard" topic="Logical">
Not reliably — unlike languages like Python or JavaScript, standard SQL doesn't guarantee left-to-right short-circuit evaluation of `AND`/`OR`, because the query optimizer is free to reorder or evaluate conditions in whatever order it determines is most efficient. ## SQL vs NoSQL Databases: Choosing the Right Data Model

**SQL and NoSQL aren't two competing databases — they're different families of data model, each suited to a different shape of data and access pattern, and most real systems at scale end up using more than one.**

title: SQL vs NoSQL Databases

title: SQL vs NoSQL Databases
description: Interview questions on SQL vs NoSQL databases — the four NoSQL data models, consistency trade-offs, polyglot persistence, and when to choose each.
content:
## Key Concepts

**SQL databases** are relational: fixed schema, tables linked by keys, strong ACID consistency. **NoSQL databases** cover four broad, distinct data models rather than one alternative: **document** stores (MongoDB — flexible, JSON-like records), **key-value** stores (Redis, DynamoDB — the simplest and fastest lookup pattern), **column-family/wide-column** stores (Cassandra, BigTable — optimized for high write throughput and horizontal scale), and **graph** databases (Neo4j — optimized for traversing relationships). The real trade-off isn't "SQL is better" or "NoSQL is better" — it's schema flexibility and horizontal scalability (NoSQL's strengths) against strong consistency and relational query power (SQL's strengths). Most systems past a certain size practice **polyglot pe

content:
rsistence** — a relational database for transactional core data, plus one or more NoSQL stores for the access patterns SQL handles poorly (caching, session storage, high-velocity event ingestion).

<QuestionList topic="SQL vs NoSQL Databases" storagePrefix="sql-vs-nosql">

<QuestionCard id="svn-01" number={1} question="What's the fundamental difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
SQL databases are relational — fixed schema, structured tables, relationships enforced through keys, strong ACID consistency. NoSQL databases trade some of that structure and consistency for schema flexibility and easier horizontal scaling, and cover several different underlying data models rather than one alternative approach.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="svn-02" number={2} question="What are the four main categories of NoSQL databases?" difficulty="easy" topic="NoSQL Models">
**Document** stores (flexible, semi-structured JSON-like

Each is built for a different access pattern, not as a general-purpose SQL substitute.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="svn-03" number={3} question="What is a document database, and when is it a good fit?" difficulty="medium" topic="NoSQL Models">
A document database (e.g., MongoDB) stores records as flexible, JSON-like documents rather than fixed rows — different documents in the same collection can have different fields. It's a good fit when the schema varies between records or evolves quickly, and when an app

<QuestionCard id="svn-04" number={4} question="What is a key-value store, and when is it a good fit?" difficulty="medium" topic="NoSQL Models">
A key-value store (e.g., Redis, DynamoDB) is the simplest NoSQL model — every value is retrieved by a unique key, with no query language beyond that lookup. It's a good fit for caching, session storage, and any workload where the access pattern is genuinely "get this exact thing by its ID" at very high speed and volume.

<QuestionCard id="svn-05" number={5} question="What is a column-family/wide-column store, and when is it a good fit?" difficulty="medium" topic="NoSQL Models">
A wide-column store (e.g., Cassandra

It's a good fit for very high write throughput at large scale — time-series data, event logs, sensor data — where horizontal scalability matters more than relational query flexibility.

<QuestionCard id="svn-06" number={6} question="What is a graph database, and when is it a good fit?" difficulty="medium" topic="NoSQL Models">

<QuestionCard id="svn-07" number={7} question="How do consistency guarantees typically differ between SQL and NoSQL systems?" difficulty="medium" topic="Consistency">
SQL databases default to strong consistency — a read always sees the latest committed write. Many NoSQL systems default to (or offer as an option) eventual consistency, where a read might briefly return stale data after a write, in exchange for lower latency and easier horizontal scaling. Some NoSQL systems (e.g., DynamoDB, Cassandra) let you tune this per-query, trading consistency for speed or vice versa.

Polyglot persistence is using different databases for different parts of the same system, matched to each part's access pattern — a relational database for transactional core data (orders, accounts), Redis for session caching, Cassandra for high-volume event ingestion. Systems adopt it because no single database model is optimal for every workload, and forcing one database to handle all of them usually means compromising on whichever workload doesn't fit its strengths.
</QuestionCard>

Some do, to varying degrees — MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions and `$lookup` (a join-like aggregation stage), for example — but it's generally not the primary design goal the way it is for an RDBMS, and performance/scale trade-offs usually still apply. ## Quick Reference

A refresher on the syntax the questions below assume. For a from-scratch walkthrough of SQL, see the [SQL Roadmap](/roadmaps/sql/) — this page focuses on what interviewers ask, not how to learn SQL from zero.

### Reading data
`SELECT` retrieves columns, `WHERE` filters rows, `ORDER BY` sorts, `GROUP BY`/`HAVING` aggregate and filter groups, `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` paginate:

```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

### Joins
`INNER JOIN` returns only matching rows; `LEFT`/`RIGHT JOIN` keep all rows from one side (NULL where unmatched); `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps all rows from both; `CROSS JOIN` produces a Cartesian product; a self join joins a table to itself via an alias.

```sql
SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id;
```

### Modifying data & schema
`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` (DML) manipulate rows; `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP TABLE` (DDL) manage schema. Always scope `UPDATE`/`DELETE` with `WHERE` — omitting it applies to every row.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    salary DECIMAL(10, 2),
    department_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(id)
);

UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department_id = 2;
```

### Constraints & data types
`PRIMARY KEY` (unique row identifier), `FOREIGN KEY` (referential integrity), `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` (validates values), `DEFAULT`. Common types: `INT`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `DECIMAL(precision, scale)`, `DATE`, `DATETIME`, `BOOLEAN`, `TEXT`.

### Common mistakes

| Mistake | Problem | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| `WHERE col = NULL` | Always returns no rows | Use `WHERE col IS NULL` |
| Missing `WHERE` on `UPDATE`/`DELETE` | Modifies/deletes every row | Always scope with `WHERE` |
| `SELECT *` on large tables | Slow, excess data transfer | Select only needed columns |
| Using a column alias in `WHERE` | Alias isn't resolved yet at that stage | Only usable in `ORDER BY`/`SELECT` |

## Relational Database Fundamentals

Before the command-level questions below, interviewers sometimes start one level up — what a relational database actually is, and why you'd reach for one over the alternatives.

<QuestionList topic="Relational Database Fundamentals" storagePrefix="sql-relational-db">

<QuestionCard id="sql-rdb-01" number={1} question="What is a relational database, and what does the relational model organize data into?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A relational database stores data in **tables** made up of rows (records) and columns (attributes), based on the relational model Edgar Codd introduced in 1970. Relationships between tables are expressed through keys — a **primary key** uniquely identifies a row, and a **foreign key** in one table references

a primary key in another — which is what lets you split data across tables without duplicating it and still reconstruct any relationship through a join.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-rdb-02" number={2} question="What are the main benefits of an RDBMS, and where does it start to show its limitations?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
The core benefits are **ACID guarantees** (reliable transactions), a **fixed schema** that enforces data consistency at write time, and a mature, standardized query language (SQL) with decades of tooling built around it. The limitations show up at scale: RDBMSs traditionally scale **vertically** (a bigger machine) rather than horizontally, a rigid schema makes fast-changing or semi-structured data awkward to model, and very high write thr

oughput or massive horizontal scale is where NoSQL and distributed systems typically take over.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-rdb-03" number={3} question="How are SQL keywords typically categorized, and what does each category do?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
SQL keywords fall into four categories: **DDL** (Data Definition Language — `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, which manage schema), **DML** (Data Manipulation Language — `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, which manage rows), **DCL** (Data Control Language — `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, which manage permissions), and **TCL** (Transaction Control Language — `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`, which manage transaction boundaries). Recognizing which bucket a keyword falls into is a quick way to reason about what a statement ac

tually affects — schema, data, access, or transaction state.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## SQL Fundamentals

The core vocabulary and commands every SQL interview starts with.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Fundamentals" storagePrefix="sql-fundamentals">

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-01" number={1} question="What is SQL and what is it used for?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard programming language for managing relational databases. It enables data professionals to create, read, update, and delete data (CRUD), manage schemas, and perform data analysis.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-02" number={2} question="Describe the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **SQL** — relational, structured schema, ACID compliance, tables with rows/columns
- **NoSQL** — non-

relational, flexible schema, eventual consistency, document/key-value/graph models
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-03" number={3} question="What are the different types of SQL commands?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **DDL** — Data Definition (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`)
- **DML** — Data Manipulation (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`)
- **DCL** — Data Control (`GRANT`, `REVOKE`)
- **TCL** — Transaction Control (`COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-04" number={4} question="Explain the purpose of the SELECT statement." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Retrieves data from tables.

```sql
SELECT columns FROM table WHERE conditions ORDER BY columns;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-05"

number={5} question="What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clauses?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **`WHERE`** — filters rows *before* `GROUP BY`
- **`HAVING`** — filters groups *after* aggregation
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-06" number={6} question="Define what a JOIN is in SQL and list its types." difficulty="easy" topic="Joins">
JOINs combine rows based on related columns.

- **`INNER JOIN`** — matching rows only
- **`LEFT`/`RIGHT JOIN`** — all rows from one side + matching from the other
- **`FULL OUTER JOIN`** — all rows from both tables
- **`CROSS JOIN`** — Cartesian product
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-07" number={7} question="What is a primary key in a database?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
The unique

identifier for each row. Cannot be `NULL`, must be unique — enforces entity integrity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-08" number={8} question="Explain what a foreign key is and how it is used." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A column referencing another table's primary key. Enforces referential integrity and creates relationships between tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-09" number={9} question="How can you prevent SQL injections?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Parameterized queries (prepared statements), input validation, least-privilege database accounts, and stored procedures used cautiously — never build queries by concatenating raw user input.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-10" number={10} question="What is normal

ization? Explain with examples." difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
Organizing data to reduce redundancy:

- **1NF** — atomic values, no repeating groups
- **2NF** — every non-key column fully depends on the whole primary key
- **3NF** — no transitive dependencies (non-key columns depend only on the key)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-11" number={11} question="Describe the concept of denormalization and when you would use it." difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
Deliberately adding redundant data to improve read performance, at the cost of write complexity and storage. Common in data warehouses and read-heavy applications where join cost outweighs storage cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-12" number={12} question="What are indexes and

how can they improve query performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
B-tree structures that enable fast lookups. They speed up `WHERE`/`JOIN`/`ORDER BY`, but slow down `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` since the index has to be maintained on every write.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-13" number={13} question="Explain the purpose of the GROUP BY clause." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Groups rows into summary rows so aggregate functions (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, ...) can be applied per group instead of across the whole table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-14" number={14} question="What is a subquery, and when would you use one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
A query nested inside `SELECT`, `WHERE`, or `FROM`. Used for complex fi

ltering that depends on the result of another query — for example, filtering rows above an aggregate computed elsewhere.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-15" number={15} question="Describe the functions of the ORDER BY clause." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Sorts the result set in ascending (`ASC`, default) or descending (`DESC`) order, by one or more columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-16" number={16} question="What are aggregate functions in SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Functions that compute a single value from multiple rows: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-17" number={17} question="Explain the differences between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and FULL JOIN." difficult

y="easy" topic="Joins">
- **`INNER`** — only matching rows
- **`LEFT`** — all left rows + matching right rows (`NULL` if no match)
- **`RIGHT`** — all right rows + matching left rows (`NULL` if no match)
- **`FULL`** — all rows from both tables
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-18" number={18} question="How do you insert a new row into a database table?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
```sql
INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (val1, val2);
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-fund-19" number={19} question="Explain how to update records in a database table." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
```sql
UPDATE table SET col1 = val1 WHERE condition;
```
Always scope with `WHERE` — omitting it updates every row.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard i

d="sql-fund-20" number={20} question="What is a SQL View and what are its advantages?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
A virtual table based on a stored `SELECT` query. Advantages: simplifies repeated complex queries, provides a security layer (expose only certain columns/rows), and centralizes reusable logic.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## SQL Data Types and Operators

Types, comparison operators, and NULL handling that show up in almost every query.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Data Types and Operators" storagePrefix="sql-types">

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-01" number={21} question="List the different data types available in SQL." difficulty="easy" topic="Data Types">
- **Numeric** — `INT`, `DECIMAL`
- **String** — `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`
- **Date/Time** — `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-02" number={22} question="What are the differences between CHAR, VARCHAR, and TEXT data types?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Types">
- **`CHAR`** — fixed length, padded with spaces
- **`VARCHAR`** — variable length, up to a defined limit
- **`TEXT`** — large variable-length text, typically

no practical limit
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-03" number={23} question="How do you use the BETWEEN operator in SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operators">
```sql
SELECT * FROM table WHERE column BETWEEN 10 AND 20;
```
Inclusive of both endpoints.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-04" number={24} question="Describe the use of the IN operator." difficulty="easy" topic="Operators">
```sql
SELECT * FROM table WHERE column IN (val1, val2, val3);
```
Shorthand for chaining several `OR` conditions on the same column.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-05" number={25} question="Explain the use of wildcard characters in SQL." difficulty="easy" topic="Operators">
`%` matches any sequence of characters, `_` matches exactly one character. Used w

ith `LIKE`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-06" number={26} question="What is the purpose of the LIKE operator?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operators">
Pattern matching on strings:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'J%';
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-07" number={27} question="How do you handle NULL values in SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="NULL Handling">
Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` for comparisons — `= NULL` never matches. Functions like `COALESCE` and `ISNULL` substitute a default when a value is `NULL`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-08" number={28} question="What does the COALESCE function do?" difficulty="easy" topic="NULL Handling">
Returns the first non-`NULL` value in its argument list:

```sql
SELECT COALESC

E(phone, email, 'N/A');
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-09" number={29} question="What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operators">
- **`UNION`** — combines result sets, removes duplicates (extra sort/dedup cost)
- **`UNION ALL`** — combines result sets, keeps duplicates (faster, no dedup pass)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-types-10" number={30} question="Describe the use of arithmetic operators in SQL queries." difficulty="easy" topic="Operators">
Standard operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`) can be used directly in `SELECT` and `WHERE` clauses to compute or filter on derived numeric values.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## SQL Advanced Queries

Patterns that go beyond basic filtering — conditional logic, self joins, CTEs, and window functions.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Advanced Queries" storagePrefix="sql-advanced">

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-01" number={31} question="Explain how to use the CASE statement in SQL." difficulty="medium" topic="Advanced Queries">
```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN age < 18 THEN 'Minor' ELSE 'Adult' END FROM users;
```
Works like an inline if/else — usable in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, and `ORDER BY`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-02" number={32} question="How would you perform a self JOIN?" difficulty="medium" topic="Joins">
```sql
SELECT e1.name, e2.name
FROM employees e1
JOIN employees e2 ON e1.manager_id = e2.id;
```
Joins a table to itself via two aliases — c

ommon for hierarchical relationships like employee/manager.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-03" number={33} question="What is a cross JOIN and when would you use it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Joins">
Produces the Cartesian product of two tables (every row of A paired with every row of B). Used for generating test data or combining independent dimensions (e.g. all product/color combinations).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-04" number={34} question="How to implement pagination in SQL queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="Advanced Queries">
```sql
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL
SELECT * FROM table ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

-- SQL Server
SELECT * FROM table ORDER BY id OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
```
Always pair with `ORDER BY` — without it, pag

e boundaries aren't guaranteed to be stable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-05" number={35} question="Explain the concept of Common Table Expressions (CTEs) and recursive CTEs." difficulty="medium" topic="Advanced Queries">
A CTE (`WITH` clause) creates a temporary named result set scoped to one query, improving readability over nested subqueries. A **recursive CTE** references itself to walk hierarchical data (org charts, category trees) level by level.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-06" number={36} question="What are window functions and how are they used?" difficulty="medium" topic="Window Functions">
Functions that compute a value across a "window" of related rows without collapsing them into one row, unlike `GROUP BY`.

```sql
SELECT name, salary,

RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees;
```
Common ones: `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, `LAG()`, `LEAD()`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-07" number={37} question="How can you concatenate column values in SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Advanced Queries">
- **Standard SQL / PostgreSQL** — `||`
- **MySQL** — `CONCAT(a, b)`
- **SQL Server** — `+`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-08" number={38} question="What is the PIVOT operation and how would you apply it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Advanced Queries">
Transforms distinct row values into columns. SQL Server has a native `PIVOT` keyword; most other databases emulate it with conditional aggregation:

```sql
SELECT
    department,
    SUM(CASE WHEN quarte

r = 'Q1' THEN revenue END) AS q1,
    SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q2' THEN revenue END) AS q2
FROM sales
GROUP BY department;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-09" number={39} question="Explain combining GROUP BY with ORDER BY." difficulty="easy" topic="Advanced Queries">
`ORDER BY` runs after `GROUP BY` (and after `HAVING`), so it sorts the already-aggregated result rows — you can order by an aggregate expression like `COUNT(*)`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-adv-10" number={40} question="How would you find duplicate records in a table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Advanced Queries">
```sql
SELECT col, COUNT(*)
FROM table
GROUP BY col
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Database Design & Architecture

Modeling, schema strategy, and the objects that support them.

<QuestionList topic="Database Design & Architecture" storagePrefix="sql-design">

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-01" number={41} question="What is the Entity-Relationship Model?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Modeling">
A conceptual model using entities (tables), attributes (columns), and relationships between entities to design a database before implementation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-02" number={42} question="Explain the different types of database schema." difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
- **Conceptual** — high-level business view, no implementation detail
- **Logical** — structure (entities, relationships, attributes) without DBMS-specific detail

- **Physical** — the actual implementation: tables, indexes, storage
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-03" number={43} question="What are Stored Procedures and how are they beneficial?" difficulty="medium" topic="Database Objects">
Precompiled, named blocks of SQL stored in the database. Benefits: reduced network round trips, centralized/reusable logic, tighter access control, and execution plan caching.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-04" number={44} question="What is a trigger in SQL and when should it be used?" difficulty="medium" topic="Database Objects">
Code that runs automatically in response to a DML event (`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`) on a table. Used for audit trails, enforcing complex validation, or keeping denormalized data in sync.
</Question

Card>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-05" number={45} question="Describe the concept of ACID in databases." difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
**Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability** — the guarantees that make a transaction reliable: it fully completes or fully rolls back, leaves the database in a valid state, is isolated from concurrent transactions, and survives a crash once committed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-06" number={46} question="What is database sharding?" difficulty="hard" topic="Scalability">
Horizontal partitioning of data across multiple database instances (shards), typically by a key like customer ID or region, to scale writes and storage beyond a single machine.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-07" number={47} questi

on="How do database indexes work and what types are there?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
Most commonly a **B-tree** structure that keeps sorted keys for fast range/equality lookups. Other types: **Hash** (equality-only, O(1) lookup), **Bitmap** (low-cardinality columns), **GiST**/**GIN** (PostgreSQL — full-text search, geometric data).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-08" number={48} question="Describe the process of data warehousing." difficulty="medium" topic="Data Warehousing">
ETL processes move data from operational systems into a warehouse, modeled dimensionally (star/snowflake schema), and queried through OLAP cubes or SQL for reporting and analysis.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-09" number={49} question="Explain the difference betwee

n OLTP and OLAP systems." difficulty="medium" topic="Data Warehousing">
- **OLTP** — transactional, frequent small writes, operational (e.g. order processing)
- **OLAP** — analytical, read-heavy, large scans over historical data (e.g. reporting)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-design-10" number={50} question="What are materialized views and how do they differ from standard views?" difficulty="medium" topic="Database Objects">
A materialized view stores the query result physically and must be refreshed to stay current, trading staleness for read speed. A standard (virtual) view re-runs its underlying query on every access.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## SQL Optimization and Performance

Reading execution plans and making queries faster.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Optimization and Performance" storagePrefix="sql-optimization">

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-01" number={51} question="How do you identify and optimize slow-running queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Use `EXPLAIN`/`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to find the bottleneck, add targeted indexes, avoid `SELECT *`, and restructure `JOIN`s so the database can use indexes and smaller intermediate result sets.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-02" number={52} question="What is query execution plan in SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
The database's chosen strategy for running a query — which scans, joins, and indexes it will use, and their estimated (or

actual) cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-03" number={53} question="Explain how to use EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE." difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
- **`EXPLAIN`** — shows the planned execution strategy without running the query
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`** — actually executes the query and shows real timings and row counts alongside the plan
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-04" number={54} question="How can indexing affect performance both positively and negatively?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
- **Positive** — much faster `SELECT`/`JOIN`/`ORDER BY` on indexed columns
- **Negative** — slower `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`, since every index has to be updated too, plus extra storage
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-05" number=

{55} question="Describe how to measure the performance of SQL queries." difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Execution time, rows examined vs. rows returned, whether indexes are actually used (from `EXPLAIN` output), and I/O cost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-06" number={56} question="How would you rewrite a query to improve its performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Prefer `JOIN`s over correlated subqueries where possible, select only needed columns instead of `SELECT *`, filter early, and add indexes that match the query's `WHERE`/`JOIN` columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-opt-07" number={57} question="What are partitioned tables and how can they optimize performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Tables physically spl

it by a key (date, range, or hash). Queries that filter on the partition key only scan relevant partitions ("partition pruning"), dramatically reducing I/O on large tables.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## SQL Security

Protecting access to data.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Security" storagePrefix="sql-security">

<QuestionCard id="sql-sec-01" number={58} question="How do you implement database encryption in SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
**TDE** (Transparent Data Encryption) for data at rest, column-level encryption for specific sensitive fields, and **SSL/TLS** for data in transit.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-sec-02" number={59} question="What are roles and how do they manage database access?" difficulty="easy" topic="Security">
Named collections of privileges. Users are assigned roles and inherit the underlying permissions — simplifies access control at scale versus granting permissions per-user.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-sec-03" number=

{60} question="Explain the concept of row-level security." difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Restricts which rows a user can see or modify based on their identity or context (e.g. a sales rep only sees their own region's rows), enforced by the database rather than application code.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## SQL Functions and Expressions

Scalar/table-valued functions and stored procedures.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Functions and Expressions" storagePrefix="sql-functions">

<QuestionCard id="sql-func-01" number={61} question="Describe scalar-valued and table-valued functions." difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
- **Scalar** — returns a single value, usable inline in `SELECT`/`WHERE`
- **Table-valued** — returns a table, usable in a `FROM` clause like a regular table
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-func-02" number={62} question="How would you define a stored procedure with input and output parameters?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE proc(@input INT, @output INT OUTPUT) AS
BEGIN
    SET @output = @input * 2;
END;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-func-03" number={63} question="What is the difference between a function and a stored procedure?" difficulty="medium" topic="Functions">
- **Function** — returns a value, callable inline within a query, generally can't perform DML on the tables it reads
- **Procedure** — supports `OUTPUT` parameters, can perform full DML, but can't be called inline inside a `SELECT`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-func-04" number={64} question="How do you use the CAST and CONVERT functions?" difficulty="easy" topic="Functions">
```sql
SELECT CAST(col AS INT);       -- ANSI standard
SELECT CONVERT(INT, col);      -- SQL Server style
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Transaction Control and Locking

Concurrency guarantees and how the database enforces them.

<QuestionList topic="Transaction Control and Locking" storagePrefix="sql-transactions">

<QuestionCard id="sql-txn-01" number={65} question="What is a database transaction?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transactions">
An atomic unit of work that either commits fully or rolls back fully, preserving the database's ACID guarantees.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-txn-02" number={66} question="Explain the concept of locking and its types in SQL databases." difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
Locks prevent conflicting concurrent access to the same data. Granularity ranges from **row-level** (fine-grained, more concurrency) to **page-level** to **table-level** (coarse, less concurr

ency but cheaper to manage).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-txn-03" number={67} question="What are the properties of transactions?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transactions">
**ACID**: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-txn-04" number={68} question="How do you manage transaction isolation levels?" difficulty="hard" topic="Transactions">
```sql
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
```
Levels range from `READ UNCOMMITTED` (weakest, allows dirty reads) through `READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ`, to `SERIALIZABLE` (strongest, fully isolated but least concurrent).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-txn-05" number={69} question="What does it mean to commit or roll back a transaction?" difficulty="easy" topic="T

ransactions">
- **`COMMIT`** — permanently saves all changes made in the transaction
- **`ROLLBACK`** — undoes all changes made in the transaction, as if it never happened
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## SQL and Modern Data Ecosystems

Where SQL sits alongside big data and cloud platforms.

<QuestionList topic="SQL and Modern Data Ecosystems" storagePrefix="sql-ecosystems">

<QuestionCard id="sql-eco-01" number={70} question="How can SQL be integrated with big data technologies?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystems">
SQL-on-Hadoop engines (Hive, Spark SQL), external/federated tables, and JDBC/ODBC connectors all let SQL query data sitting in big-data storage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-eco-02" number={71} question="Discuss the interoperability of SQL with cloud-based data stores." difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystems">
Cloud databases and warehouses (RDS, BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) all expose standard-ish SQL interfaces, so most SQL knowledge transfers direct

ly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-eco-03" number={72} question="What is Data Lake and how can SQL interact with it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystems">
A centralized repository of raw data in its native format. Query engines like Presto/Trino and Athena let you run SQL directly against files in the lake without a separate load step.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-eco-04" number={73} question="Explain the interaction between SQL and NoSQL within the same application." difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystems">
Polyglot persistence — using SQL databases for transactional/relational data and NoSQL stores for scale or flexible schema, within the same system.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-eco-05" number={74} question="How does SQL work within a microservic

es architecture?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystems">
Each service typically owns its own database (often SQL), and shares data with other services through APIs or events rather than direct cross-service queries — avoiding a shared-schema coupling problem.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## SQL Best Practices and Standards

Writing SQL that's maintainable and portable.

<QuestionList topic="SQL Best Practices and Standards" storagePrefix="sql-best-practices">

<QuestionCard id="sql-best-01" number={75} question="What are some common SQL coding practices you follow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Best Practices">
Consistent naming conventions, indexing based on actual query patterns, avoiding `SELECT *`, and always using parameterized queries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-best-02" number={76} question="How can you ensure the portability of SQL scripts across systems?" difficulty="medium" topic="Best Practices">
Stick to ANSI SQL where possible, avoid vendor-specific functions, and abstract vendor differences behind views where you can't avoid them.
</Questi

onCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-best-03" number={77} question="What methods do you use for version controlling SQL scripts?" difficulty="easy" topic="Best Practices">
Git for the SQL files themselves, plus migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase, or a dbt-style migrations folder) to apply schema changes as ordered, repeatable steps — "database as code."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-best-04" number={78} question="What are the benefits of using stored procedures instead of embedded SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Best Practices">
Fewer network round trips, cached execution plans, centralized logic that's easier to secure and audit than SQL scattered across application code.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-best-05" number={79} question="How do you document SQL code effec

tively?" difficulty="easy" topic="Best Practices">
Inline comments explaining *why* (not what), ER diagrams for schema relationships, and a data dictionary describing tables/columns for anyone querying the data later.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Analytical SQL Questions

Ranking, running totals, and other analysis-oriented patterns.

<QuestionList topic="Analytical SQL Questions" storagePrefix="sql-analytical">

<QuestionCard id="sql-analytic-01" number={80} question="How would you find the Nth highest salary from a table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Analytics">
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-analytic-02" number={81} question="How do you count occurrences of a specific value in a column?" difficulty="easy" topic="Analytics">
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table WHERE column = 'value';
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-analytic-03" number={82} question="How can you calculate running totals in SQL?" difficulty

="medium" topic="Analytics">
```sql
SELECT order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM orders;
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-analytic-04" number={83} question="Explain how to reverse the contents of a column without a reverse function." difficulty="hard" topic="Analytics">
When the database has no built-in `REVERSE()`, fall back to application-level processing, or a stored procedure/recursive query that rebuilds the string character by character in reverse order.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-analytic-05" number={84} question="What approach do you use for creating a calendar table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Analytics">
Generate a contiguous date range (via a recursive CTE or a numbers table joined to a base da

te) and add derived flag columns — weekday, is_weekend, fiscal_quarter — for fast time-based joins and analysis.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-analytic-06" number={99} question="Explain how to use SQL for predictive analysis and machine learning." difficulty="hard" topic="Analytics">
Window functions and statistical aggregates can compute trend features directly in SQL. Warehouse-native ML (BigQuery ML, Redshift ML) and extensions like MADlib go further, letting you train and score models without leaving SQL.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Data Manipulation and ETL

Moving and cleaning data with SQL.

<QuestionList topic="Data Manipulation and ETL" storagePrefix="sql-etl">

<QuestionCard id="sql-etl-01" number={85} question="What is the process of Extract, Transform, Load (ETL)?" difficulty="easy" topic="ETL">
Extract data from source systems, transform it (clean, join, aggregate), and load it into a target system — the foundation of most data warehousing pipelines.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-etl-02" number={86} question="How do you import/export data from/to a flat file using SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="ETL">
- **PostgreSQL** — `COPY`
- **MySQL** — `LOAD DATA INFILE`
- **SQL Server** — `BULK INSERT`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-etl-03" number={87} question="Explain the steps for

a basic ETL process." difficulty="medium" topic="ETL">
Extract → clean → validate → load to a staging table → load to the warehouse → (re)build indexes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-etl-04" number={88} question="How do you cleanse and format data using SQL queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="ETL">
`TRIM` to remove stray whitespace, `UPPER`/`LOWER` to normalize case, `REPLACE` for known bad patterns, and regex functions (`REGEXP_REPLACE`, etc.) for more complex cleanup.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-etl-05" number={89} question="What tools do you use for automating data import/export?" difficulty="easy" topic="ETL">
Apache Airflow or dbt for orchestration/transformation, Talend or Informatica for GUI-driven ETL, or plain cron-scheduled scripts for simpler pipel

ines.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Domain-Specific SQL Scenarios

Modeling patterns for relationships, hierarchies, and time.

<QuestionList topic="Domain-Specific SQL Scenarios" storagePrefix="sql-domain">

<QuestionCard id="sql-domain-01" number={90} question="How would you model a many-to-many relationship in SQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
A junction (bridge) table holding foreign keys to both related tables — e.g. `student_id` and `course_id` in an `enrollments` table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-domain-02" number={91} question="Describe how to manage hierarchical data in SQL." difficulty="hard" topic="Data Modeling">
- **Adjacency list** — each row stores its `parent_id`; simple, but multi-level queries need recursion
- **Nested sets** — stores left/right bounds; fast subtree

reads, expensive writes
- **Recursive CTEs** — walk an adjacency list to arbitrary depth in a single query
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-domain-03" number={92} question="How would you approach writing SQL queries for reporting?" difficulty="medium" topic="Reporting">
Query against a dimensional model (star/snowflake) rather than raw OLTP tables, aggregate with `GROUP BY`, and optimize for read patterns since reporting queries are run far more often than the underlying data changes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-domain-04" number={93} question="Explain how to handle temporal data and time zones in SQL." difficulty="hard" topic="Data Modeling">
Store timestamps in UTC using a timezone-aware type (`TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`), and convert to a local zone only at dis

play time with `AT TIME ZONE`. Storing local time directly makes cross-region comparisons and DST transitions error-prone.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-domain-05" number={94} question="How do you use SQL in financial applications for risk analysis?" difficulty="hard" topic="Reporting">
Time-series queries over historical prices/positions, window functions for rolling metrics (moving average, volatility), and aggregate risk measures computed directly in the warehouse close to the data.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Troubleshooting and Debugging

Diagnosing failures, corruption, and concurrency issues.

<QuestionList topic="Troubleshooting and Debugging" storagePrefix="sql-debugging">

<QuestionCard id="sql-debug-01" number={95} question="What steps do you take to troubleshoot a failed SQL query?" difficulty="medium" topic="Troubleshooting">
Check syntax first, verify table/column names exist, validate data types match, then isolate the problem by simplifying the query (remove joins/conditions one at a time) until it runs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-debug-02" number={96} question="How can you recover data from a corrupt SQL database?" difficulty="hard" topic="Troubleshooting">
Restore from the most recent clean backup, replay transaction logs to minimize data loss, and for en

gine-level corruption run integrity checks like `DBCC CHECKDB` (SQL Server) to identify and, where possible, repair the damage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-debug-03" number={97} question="What methods do you employ to ensure data integrity?" difficulty="medium" topic="Troubleshooting">
Primary/foreign key constraints, `CHECK` constraints for value rules, unique indexes to prevent duplicates, and triggers for cross-row validation that constraints alone can't express.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="sql-debug-04" number={98} question="How do you decipher and resolve deadlocks in SQL?" difficulty="hard" topic="Troubleshooting">
Analyze the deadlock graph the database produces to see which transactions were holding/waiting on which locks, identify the resource contention

pattern, then fix it by keeping transactions short, accessing tables in a consistent order, and reducing lock scope.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Choosing the Right Technologies: A Trade-Off Framework

**Picking a data technology is rarely about which tool is "best" in the abstract — it's about matching a tool's trade-offs (managed vs. self-hosted, cost vs. control, latency vs. complexity) against a team's actual scale, skill set, and budget, which is why the same problem can have a different right answer at two different companies.**
