## Practical Validation Techniques

Specific problems that come up once you move past "check for nulls" into real production datasets.

<QuestionList topic="Practical Validation Techniques" storagePrefix="dq-practical">

<QuestionCard id="dq-21" number={21} question="How do you check referential integrity in a warehouse that doesn't enforce foreign keys?" difficulty="medium" topic="Referential Integrity">
Most analytical warehouses accept (but don't enforce) foreign key declarations, so referential integrity has to be checked explicitly — typically an anti-join: rows in the child table whose key doesn't exist in the parent table.

```sql
SELECT o.customer_id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL   -- orphaned foreign k

eys
```

Run this as a scheduled check (or a dbt `relationships` test) rather than relying on the database to reject bad writes, since the warehouse itself won't.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-22" number={22} question="What techniques do you use to detect duplicate records at scale?" difficulty="hard" topic="Deduplication">
For exact duplicates, hash the row's relevant columns and check for repeated hash values — cheaper than comparing every column pairwise. For duplicates that differ slightly (a retry that changed a timestamp), define a business key (the columns that should uniquely identify a record) and check *that* for uniqueness instead of the whole row. At large scale, a window function is the standard SQL pattern for both detecting and resolving duplicates:

```sql

SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY business_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
FROM table
QUALIFY rn = 1   -- keep only the most recent version of each key
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-23" number={23} question="How do you detect distribution drift in a column's values over time?" difficulty="hard" topic="Statistical Checks">
Compare a statistical summary of today's batch against a rolling historical baseline — mean/median/standard deviation for numeric columns, or the distribution of category frequencies for categorical ones — and alert when the difference exceeds a threshold (a fixed percentage, or a statistical distance measure like population stability index for more rigorous setups). This catches problems row-level checks can't: every row can individually b

e "valid" while the overall shape of the data has still shifted in a way that signals an upstream change.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-24" number={24} question="What data quality challenges are unique to streaming pipelines compared to batch?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Batch checks run against a complete, stable dataset; streaming checks have to work against data that's still arriving, with no natural "batch is done" moment to validate against. This means checks need to run over rolling windows rather than a fixed dataset, tolerate legitimately late/out-of-order events without false-alarming, and use approximate techniques (sketches for distinct counts, running aggregates) since holding the full stream in memory to validate it isn't an option.
</QuestionCard>

<Q

uestionCard id="dq-25" number={25} question="How do you decide between NULL, an empty string, and a sentinel value for missing data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Modeling">
Use **NULL** for "value doesn't exist / unknown," reserving it for genuine absence rather than overloading it with multiple meanings. Use an **empty string** only when "known to be empty" is itself meaningful and distinct from "unknown" (a middle name field where you've confirmed the person has none, vs. one you simply haven't collected). Avoid ad-hoc **sentinel values** ("N/A", -1, 9999) in the data itself wherever possible — they're invisible to standard NULL-handling logic (COUNT, aggregates, joins) and silently corrupt results unless every downstream consumer knows to filter them out; if you need a placeholder

in a dimension for exactly this reason, use the "Unknown member" pattern instead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-26" number={26} question="Where in a medallion (bronze/silver/gold) pipeline should quality gates actually enforce checks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Pipeline Design">
Light structural checks (can it be parsed, does it match the expected raw schema) belong at bronze, right on ingestion, so malformed source data is caught immediately rather than propagating. The bulk of validation — not-null, referential integrity, business rules, deduplication — belongs at the bronze-to-silver transition, since silver is meant to be the clean, trusted layer everything else builds on. Gold-layer checks are usually reconciliation-style (do these aggregates tie back to silver correctly)

rather than re-validating row-level rules that should have already been caught upstream.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Metrics, Ownership & Trust

Beyond individual checks — how you decide how much quality investment a dataset deserves, and who's responsible when it fails.

<QuestionList topic="Metrics, Ownership & Trust" storagePrefix="dq-trust">

<QuestionCard id="dq-27" number={27} question="How do you build a data quality score, and what would it be based on?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metrics">
A simple, defensible approach: weight each quality dimension (completeness, validity, freshness, uniqueness) by how much it matters for that specific dataset, compute a pass rate for each from your existing checks, and combine into a single 0-100 score per table. The value isn't the exact number — it's giving stakeholders a trend line ("this table's score dropped from 98 to 85 last week") that's easi

er to act on than a wall of individual pass/fail check results.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-28" number={28} question="How do you decide how much quality investment a dataset actually needs?" difficulty="medium" topic="Prioritization">
Scale checks to the dataset's actual blast radius: a table feeding an executive dashboard or a financial report justifies deep validation, reconciliation, and tight SLAs; an internal exploratory table a few analysts use occasionally doesn't need the same investment. Treating every table as equally critical is how quality programs burn effort on low-value checks while genuinely important tables stay under-covered — usage and downstream dependency count are the practical signals for where to spend the effort.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="

dq-29" number={29} question="Who should own a data quality failure — the producing team or the consuming team?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ownership">
The producing team owns fixing the *source* of the problem (a broken upstream job, a schema change that wasn't communicated), since they're the only ones who can actually correct it at the root. The consuming team typically owns detecting and surfacing the failure fast (their checks, their dashboards break first) and communicating impact — a data contract is what ties these together in advance, so this isn't negotiated fresh during every incident.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dq-30" number={30} question="How do you build stakeholder trust in data after a high-profile quality incident?" difficulty="medium" topic="Trust">
Be transpa

rent about what happened and why, rather than quietly fixing it — a short incident writeup (what broke, what was affected, what's changing) does more for trust than silence. Follow up with a durable fix (a new check that would have caught it, not just a one-time patch), and make quality *visible* going forward — a quality score, a status page, or a badge on documented tables — so trust is rebuilt on demonstrated reliability over time rather than a single reassurance.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

ar ownership.

## Data Warehousing: Architecture, Schemas & ETL

**A data warehouse is the architectural layer that turns raw, write-optimized operational data into a structure built for fast, reliable analytics — this page covers OLAP/OLTP fundamentals, star and snowflake schema design, ETL, dimensional modeling, and the platform-level trade-offs data engineers are expected to reason through in interviews.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

A data warehouse exists to answer one question well: how do you turn scattered, write-optimized operational data into a structure that's fast and reliable to query for analytics? The foundational split is **OLTP vs. OLAP** — OLTP systems (the applications generating your data) are normalized and optimized for many small, concurrent writes; OLAP systems are denormalized and optimized for large, read-heavy aggregations across history. Warehouses exist because running analytical queries directly against an OLTP system either degrades it or gives you an incomplete, historyless answer.

Getting data from source to warehouse is the job of **ETL/ELT** — extract from source systems, transform (clean, conform, apply business rules), and load into the warehouse, or in the ELT va

riant, load raw and transform inside the warehouse using its own compute. Once data lands, **dimensional modeling** — star and snowflake schemas, fact/dimension tables, slowly changing dimensions — is the standard way warehouses organize data for query performance and business usability; see the [Data Modeling](/level-2-core-concepts/data-modeling/) page for schema-design specifics, since this page stays at the platform and architecture layer around it.

The landscape has also evolved beyond a single "data warehouse" box: **data lakes** store raw, schema-on-read data cheaply at scale, and **lakehouses** try to combine lake economics with warehouse-style transactions and performance. Vendor-specific implementation details for Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and Databricks live on their own

pages — this page stays at the concepts and trade-offs level that shows up across all of them.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-fund-07" number={7} question="What is Data Warehousing Hierarchy?" difficulty="hard" topic="Dimensions">
Hierarchies are logical structures that use ordered levels as a means of organizing data. A hierarchy can be used to define data aggregation. For example, in a time dimension, a hierarchy might aggregate data from the month level to the quarter level to the year level. A hierarchy can

also be used to define a navigational drill path and to establish a family structure. Within a hierarchy, each level is logically connected to the levels above and below it. For example, in the product dimension, there might be two hierarchies--one for product categories and one for product suppliers. Dimension hierarchies also group levels from general to granular. ension values. For a particular level value, a value at the next higher level is its parent, and values at the next lower level are its children. These familial relationships enable analysts to access data quickly.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-schema-05" number={19} question="What is the difference between star and snowflake schema, and when is each better?" difficulty="medium" topic="Star Schema">
- **Star schema** — dimension tables are mapped directly around one or more fact tables. It's a renormalized (denormalized) model, so no complicated joins are needed and queries run fast. It's the default choice when raw query performance matters most.
- **Snowflake schema** — the normalized form of a star schema: dimension tables are split into multiple related tables, which reduces redundancy and makes direct modification of dimension data eas

ier, at the cost of more, more complex joins and somewhat slower queries.

In short: pick snowflake when you have genuine one-to-many hierarchies within a dimension and want easier maintenance/browsing; pick star when query performance and simplicity are the priority, which is most analytics/BI workloads.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-schema-07" number={21} question="What data type should a surrogate key use?" difficulty="medium" topic="Surrogate Keys">

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-schema-09" number={23} question="What is Surrogate Key and where we use it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Surrogate Keys">

Data warehouses typically use a surrogate, (also known as artificial or identity key), key for the dimension tables primary keys. They can use Info sequence generator, or Oracle sequence, or SQL Server Identity values for the surrogate key.
It is useful because the natural primary key (i.e. Customer Number in Customer table) can change and this makes updates more difficult.
Some tables have columns such as AIRPORT_NAME OR CITY_NAME which are stated as the primary keys (according to the business users) but ,not only can these ch

<QuestionCard id="dwh-dim-20" number={51} question="What are Semi additive and Factless Facts?" difficulty="hard" topic="Fact Tables">
Semi-Additive: Semi-additive facts are facts that can be summed up for some dimensions in the fact t

able, but not the others. For example:
Current_Balance and Profit_Margin are the facts. Current_Balance is a semi-additive fact, as it makes sense to add them up for all accounts (what's the total current balance for all accounts in the bank?), but it does not make sense to add them up through time (adding up all current balances for a given account for each day of the month does not give us any useful information). A factless fact table captures the many-to-many relationships between dimensions, but contains no numeric or textual facts. They are often used to record events or coverage information.
Common examples of factless fact tables include:

- Identifying product promotion events (to determine promoted products that didn't sell)
- Tracking student attendance or registration even

ts

<QuestionCard id="dwh-dim-22" number={53} question="What are the different methods of loading dimension tables?" difficulty="medium" topic="Dimensional Modeling">
There are two common methods for loading data into dimension tables:

- **Direct load (faster)** — all constraints and keys are disabled before loading. Once loaded, the data is validated against the constraints; any rows found invalid are excluded from indexing and skipped in downstream processing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-etl-12" number={94} question="What is Brodcasting and Replicate?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transformations">
- **Broadcast** — takes data from multiple inputs, combines it, and sends it to all the output ports. Eg: you have 2 incoming flows (this can be data parallelism or component parallelism) on a Broadcast component, one with 10 records and the other with 20 records — every outgoing flow (any number of flows) will have 10 + 20 = 30 records.

### Normalization & Relational Theory

<QuestionList topic="Normalization & Relational Theory" storagePrefix="dwh-norm">

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-01" number={123} question="What is Normalization?" difficulty="medium" topic="Normalization">
Database normalization is a data design and organization process applied to data structures based on rules that help build relational databases. In relational database design, the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy. Normalization usually involves dividing a database into two or more tables and defining relationships between the tables. The objective is to isolate data so that additions, deletions, and modifications of a field can be made in just one table and then propagated through the rest of the database via the defined relation

ships.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-02" number={124} question="What are different Normalization Forms?" difficulty="hard" topic="Normalization">
- 1NF: Eliminate Repeating Groups Make a separate table for each set of related attributes, and give each table a primary key. Each field contains at most one value from its attribute domain.
- 2NF: Eliminate Redundant Data If an attribute depends on only part of a multi-valued key, remove it to a separate table.
- 3NF: Eliminate Columns Not Dependent On Key If attributes do not contribute to a description of the key, remove them to a separate table. All attributes must be directly dependent on the primary key.
- BCNF: Boyce-Codd Normal Form If there are non-trivial dependencies between candidate key attributes, separate them

out into distinct tables.
- 4NF: Isolate Independent Multiple Relationships No table may contain two or more 1:n or n:m relationships that are not directly related.
- 5NF: Isolate Semantically Related Multiple Relationships There may be practical constrains on information that justify separating logically related many-to-many relationships.
- ONF: Optimal Normal Form A model limited to only simple (elemental) facts, as expressed in Object Role Model notation.
- DKNF: Domain-Key Normal Form A model free from all modification anomalies. Remember, these normalization guidelines are cumulative. For a database to be in 3NF, it must first fulfill all the criteria of a 2NF and 1NF database.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-03" number={125} question="What is Relational Algebra?"

difficulty="medium" topic="Relational Theory">
It is procedural query language. It consists of a set of operations that take one or two relations as input and produce a new relation.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-04" number={126} question="What is Relational Calculus?" difficulty="hard" topic="Relational Theory">
It is an applied predicate calculus specifically tailored for relational databases proposed by E. F. Codd.
E.g. of languages based on it are DSL ALPHA, QUEL.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-05" number={127} question="How does Tuple oriented Relational calculus differ from Domain oriented Relational Calculus?" difficulty="hard" topic="Relational Theory">
The tuple-oriented calculus uses a tuple variables i.e., variable whose only permitted value

s are tuples of that relation. E.g. QUEL
The domain-oriented calculus has domain variables i.e., variables that range over the underlying domains instead of over relation. E.g. ILL, DEDUCE.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-06" number={128} question="What is Functional Dependency?" difficulty="hard" topic="Relational Theory">
A Functional dependency is denoted by X → Y between two sets of attributes X and Y that are subsets of R specifies a constraint on the possible tuple that can form a relation state r of R. The constraint is for any two tuples t1 and t2 in r if t1[X] = t2[X] then they have t1[Y] = t2[Y]. This means the value of X component of a tuple uniquely determines the value of component Y.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-07" number={129} question="Wh

at is Multivalued Dependency?" difficulty="hard" topic="Relational Theory">
Multivalued dependency denoted by X → Y specified on relation schema R, where X and Y are both subsets of R, specifies the following constraint on any relation r of R: if two tuples t1 and t2 exist in r such that t1[X] = t2[X] then t3 and t4 should also exist in r with the following properties

t3[x] = t4[X] = t1[X] = t2[X]
t3[Y] = t1[Y] and t4[Y] = t2[Y]
t3[Z] = t2[Z] and t4[Z] = t1[Z]
where [Z = (R-(X U Y)) ]
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-08" number={130} question="What is Lossless Join Property?" difficulty="hard" topic="Normalization">
It guarantees that the spurious tuple generation does not occur with respect to relation schemas after decomposition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id

="dwh-norm-09" number={131} question="What Is 1NF?" difficulty="easy" topic="Normalization">

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-10" number={132} question="What is Fully Functional Dependency?" difficulty="hard" topic="Relational Theory">
It is based on concept of full functional dependency. A functional dependency X → Y is full functional dependency if removal of any attribute A from X means that the dependency does not hold any more.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-11" number={133} question="What is 2NF?" difficulty="medium" topic="Normalization">
A relation schema R is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute A in R is fully functionally dependent on primary key.
</Qu

estionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-12" number={134} question="What is 3NF?" difficulty="hard" topic="Normalization">
A relation schema R is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and for every FD X → A either of the following is true

X is a Super-key of R.
A is a prime attribute of R.
In other words, if every non prime attribute is non-transitively dependent on primary key.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-13" number={135} question="What is BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)?" difficulty="hard" topic="Normalization">
A relation schema R is in BCNF if it is in 3NF and satisfies an additional constraint that for every FD X → A, X must be a candidate key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-14" number={136} question="What is 4NF?" difficulty="hard" topic="Normalization">
A

relation schema R is said to be in 4NF if for every Multivalued dependency X → Y that holds over R, one of following is true
X is subset or equal to (or) XY = R.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-15" number={137} question="What is 5NF?" difficulty="hard" topic="Normalization">

Ri = R for some i.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-norm-17" number={139} question="What is Join Dependency and Inclusion Dependency?" difficulty="hard" topic="Relational Theory">

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-01" number={164} question="What is the difference between a view and a materialized view?" difficulty="medium" topic="Views">
- **View** — a logical, virtual structure with no data of its own; every query against it re-runs the underlying `SELECT` against the base tables, so changes to the base tables are always reflected immediately. A view occupies no storage space beyond its stored definition.
- **Materialized view** — stores the pre-calculated result of the query physically on disk. The query only executes once (at creation/refresh time); afterward every read hits the stored result set, which is why materialized views a

re much faster to query but need an explicit refresh to pick up changes in the base tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-02" number={165} question="What is Rollback Segment?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
A Database contains one or more Rollback Segments to temporarily store "undo" information.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-03" number={166} question="What is a Table Space?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
A database is divided into Logical Storage Unit called table spaces. A table space is used to grouped related logical structures together.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-04" number={167} question="What is Database Link?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
A database link is a named object that describes a "path" from one datab

ase to another.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-05" number={168} question="What is a Hash Cluster?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
A row is stored in a hash cluster based on the result of applying a hash function to the row's cluster key value. All rows with the same hash key value are stores together on disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-06" number={169} question="What is Schema?" difficulty="easy" topic="Database Objects">
A schema is collection of database objects of a User.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-07" number={170} question="What is Table?" difficulty="medium" topic="Database Objects">
A table is the basic unit of data storage in an ORACLE database. The tables of a database hold all of the user accessible data. Table data is

stored in rows and columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-08" number={171} question="What is a View?" difficulty="medium" topic="Views">
A view is a virtual table. Every view has a Query attached to it. (The Query is a SELECT statement that identifies the columns and rows of the table(s) the view uses.)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-09" number={172} question="What is an Extent?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
An Extent is a specific number of contiguous data blocks, obtained in a single allocation, and used to store a specific type of information.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-10" number={173} question="What is an Index?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexing">
An Index is an optional structure associated with a table to have direct ac

cess to rows, which can be created to increase the performance of data retrieval. Index can be created on one or more columns of a table.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-11" number={174} question="What are Clusters?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
Clusters are groups of one or more tables physically stores together to share common columns and are often used together.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-12" number={175} question="What are the different types of Segments?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
Data Segment,
Index Segment,
Rollback Segment and Temporary Segment.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-13" number={176} question="Explain the Relationship among database and Table Space and Data File?" difficulty="medium" topic="Relational Mod

el">
Each database logically divided into one or more table spaces one or more data files are explicitly created for each table space.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-14" number={177} question="What is an Index Segment?" difficulty="easy" topic="Indexing">
Each Index has an Index segment that stores all of its data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-15" number={178} question="Do you View contain Data?" difficulty="easy" topic="Views">
Views do not contain or store data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-16" number={179} question="What is the use of Control File?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
When an instance of an ORACLE database is started, its control file is used to identify the database and redo log files that must be opened for databas

e operation to proceed. It is also used in database recovery.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-17" number={180} question="Can Objects of the same Schema reside in different Table Spaces?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
Yes
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-20" number={183} question="What is Mirrored on line redo Log?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
A mirrored on-line redo log consists of copies of on-line redo log files physically located on se

parate disks; changes made to one member of the group are made to all members.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-21" number={184} question="What is Online redo Log?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
The On-line Redo Log is a set of tow or more on-line redo files that record all committed changes made to the database. Whenever a transaction is committed, the corresponding redo entries temporarily stores in redo log buffers of the SGA are written to an on-line redo log file by the background process LGWR. The on-line redo log files are used in cyclical fashion.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-22" number={185} question="What is Log Switch?" difficulty="medium" topic="Database Objects">
The point at which ORACLE ends writing to one online redo log file and begin

s writing to another is called a log switch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-23" number={186} question="What Type of Indexing Mechanism do we need use for a typical Data Warehouse?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexing">
On the fact table it is best to use bitmap indexes. Dimension tables can use bitmap and/or the other types of clustered/non-clustered, unique/non-unique indexes.
To my knowledge, SQLServer does not support bitmap indexes. Only Oracle supports bitmaps.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-24" number={187} question="What is View?" difficulty="medium" topic="Views">
A simple view can be thought of as a subset of a table. It can be used for retrieving data, as well as updating or deleting rows. Rows updated or deleted in the view are updated or deleted

in the table the view was created with. It should also be noted that as data in the original table changes, so does data in the view, as views are the way to look at part of the original table. The results of using a view are not permanently stored in the database. The data accessed through a view is actually constructed using standard T-SQL select command and can come from one to many different base tables or even other views.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-25" number={188} question="What is Indexing and what are the different kinds of Indexing?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexing">
Indexing is a technique for determining how quickly specific data can be found.
Types:
- Binary search style indexing
- B-Tree indexing
- Inverted list indexing
M+ emory resident table

- Table indexing
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-obj-26" number={189} question="What is ROWID?" difficulty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
The ROWID is a unique database-wide physical address for every row on every table. Once assigned (when the row is first inserted into the database), it never changes until the row is deleted or the table is dropped.
The ROWID consists of the following three components, the combination of which uniquely identifies the physical storage location of the row.
Oracle database file number, which contains the block with the rows
Oracle block address, which contains the row
The row within the block (because each block can hold many rows)
The ROWID is used internally in indexes as a quick means of retrieving rows with a particular key value. Appl

ication developers also use it in SQL statements as a quick way to access a row once they know the ROWID.
</QuestionCard>

### Transactions & DBMS Internals

<QuestionList topic="Transactions & DBMS Internals" storagePrefix="dwh-txn">

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-01" number={203} question="Describe Three Levels of Data Abstraction?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
There are three levels of abstraction:
- **Physical level** — the lowest level of abstraction, describes how data are stored.
- **Logical level** — the next higher level of abstraction, describes what data are stored in the database and what relationships exist among that data.
- **View level** — the highest level of abstraction, describes only part of the entire database.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-02" number={204} question="What is Data Independence?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
Data independence me

ans that “the application is independent of the storage structure and access strategy of data”. In other words, The ability to modify the schema definition in one level should not affect the schema definition in the next higher level.
Two types of Data Independence:
Physical Data Independence: Modification in physical level should not affect the logical level.
Logical Data Independence: Modification in logical level should affect the view level.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-03" number={205} question="What is a View and how it is related to Data Independence?" difficulty="medium" topic="Views">
A view may be thought of as a virtual table, that is, a table that does not really exist in its own right but is instead derived from one or more underlying base table. In other

words, there is no stored file that direct represents the view instead a definition of view is stored in data dictionary. Growth and restructuring of base tables is not reflected in views. Thus the view can insulate users from the effects of restructuring and growth in the database. Hence accounts for logical data independence.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-04" number={206} question="What Is DDL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
A data base schema is specifies by a set of definitions expressed by a special language called DDL.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-05" number={207} question="What Is VDL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
It specifies user views and their mappings to the conceptual schema (View Definition Language)
</QuestionCard

>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-06" number={208} question="What is SDL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
This language is to specify the internal schema. This language may specify the mapping between two schemas. (Storage Definition Language)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-07" number={209} question="What Is Data Storage Definition Language?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
The storage structures and access methods used by database system are specified by a set of definition in a special type of DDL called data storage-definition language.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-08" number={210} question="What Is DML?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
This language that enable user to access or manipulate data as organized by appropriate d

ata model.
Procedural DML or Low level: DML requires a user to specify what data are needed and how to get those data.
Non-Procedural DML or High level: DML requires a user to specify what data are needed without specifying how to get those data.
(Data Manipulation Language)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-09" number={211} question="What is Query Evaluation Engine?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transactions">
It executes low-level instruction generated by compiler.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-10" number={212} question="What is DDL Interpreter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transactions">
It interprets DDL statements and record them in tables containing metadata.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-11" number={213} question="What is Record at a time?"

difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
The Low level or Procedural DML can specify and retrieve each record from a set of records. This retrieve of a record is said to be Record-at-a-time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-12" number={214} question="What is Set at a time or Set oriented?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
The High level or Non-procedural DML can specify and retrieve many records in a single DML statement. This retrieve of a record is said to be Set-at-a-time or Set-oriented.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-13" number={215} question="What is Durability in DBMS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
Once the DBMS informs the user that a transaction has successfully completed, its effects should persist even if the system crashes b

efore all its changes are reflected on disk. This property is called durability.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-14" number={216} question="What do you mean by Atomicity and Aggregation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
Atomicity:
Either all actions are carried out or none are. Users should not have to worry about the effect of incomplete transactions. DBMS ensures this by undoing the actions of incomplete transactions.
Aggregation:
A concept which is used to model a relationship between a collection of entities and relationships. It is used when we need to express a relationship among relationships.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-15" number={217} question="What is Phantom Deadlock?" difficulty="hard" topic="Transactions">
In distributed deadlock

detection, the delay in propagating local information might cause the deadlock detection algorithms to identify deadlocks that do not really exist. Such situations are called phantom deadlocks and they lead to unnecessary aborts.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-16" number={218} question="What is Checkpoint and when does it cccur?" difficulty="hard" topic="Transactions">
A Checkpoint is like a snapshot of the DBMS state. By taking checkpoints, the DBMS can reduce the amount of work to be done during restart in the event of subsequent crashes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-17" number={219} question="What are different Phases of Transaction?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transactions">
Different phases are
Analysis phase
Redo Phase
Undo phase
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-18" number={220} question="What do you mean by Flat File Database?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
It is a database in which there are no programs or user access languages. It has no cross-file capabilities but is user-friendly and provides user-interface management.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-19" number={221} question="What is transparent DBMS?" difficulty="easy" topic="Transactions">
It is one, which keeps its Physical Structure hidden from user.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-20" number={222} question="What is RDBMS Kernel?" difficulty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
Two important pieces of RDBMS architecture are the kernel, which is the software, and the data dictionary, which consists of the system-level data

structures used by the kernel to manage the database
You might think of an RDBMS as an operating system (or set of subsystems), designed specifically for controlling data access; its primary functions are storing, retrieving, and securing data. An RDBMS maintains its own list of authorized users and their associated privileges; manages memory caches and paging; controls locking for concurrent resource usage; dispatches and schedules user requests; and manages space usage within its table-space structures.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-21" number={223} question="Name the Sub systems of RDBMS?" difficulty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
I/O, Security, Language Processing, Process Control, Storage Management, Logging and Recovery, Distribution Control, Transaction Control,

Memory Management, Lock Management.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-22" number={224} question="What is Storage Manager?" difficulty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
It is a program module that provides the interface between the low-level data stored in database, application programs and queries submitted to the system.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-23" number={225} question="What is Buffer Manager?" difficulty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
It is a program module, which is responsible for fetching data from disk storage into main memory and deciding what data to be cache in memory.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-24" number={226} question="What is Transaction Manager?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
It is a program module, which

ensures that database, remains in a consistent state despite system failures and concurrent transaction execution proceeds without conflicting.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-25" number={227} question="What is File Manager?" difficulty="medium" topic="DBMS Internals">
It is a program module, which manages the allocation of space on disk storage and data structure used to represent information stored on a disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-txn-26" number={228} question="What is Authorization and Integrity Manager?" difficulty="medium" topic="Transactions">
It is the program module, which tests for the satisfaction of integrity constraint and checks the authority of user to access data.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-sql-09" number={237} question="What is a Query?" difficulty="medium" topic="SQL">
A query is one or more statements that request data from a database. If the data is available, then the requested data returns in the form of a table which contains rows and columns. Queries are sent to the databases in a language called SQL. However, when using the Report Panel, SQL knowledge is not required.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-sql-10" number={238} question="What is Stored Procedure?" difficulty="medium

" topic="Stored Procedures">
A stored procedure is a named group of SQL statements that have been previously created and stored in the server database. Stored procedures accept input parameters so that a single procedure can be used over the network by several clients using different input data. And when the procedure is modified, all clients automatically get the new version. Stored procedures reduce network traffic and improve performance. Stored procedures can be used to help ensure the integrity of the database.
e.g. sp_helpdb, sp_renamedb, sp_depends etc.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-sql-11" number={239} question="What is Trigger?" difficulty="medium" topic="Triggers">
A trigger is an SQL procedure that initiates an action when an event (INSERT, DELETE or UPDATE) occur

s. Triggers are stored in and managed by the DBMS. Triggers are used to maintain the referential integrity of data by changing the data in a systematic fashion. A trigger cannot be called or executed; the DBMS automatically fires the trigger as a result of a data modification to the associated table. Triggers can be viewed as similar to stored procedures in that both consist of procedural logic that is stored at the database level. Stored procedures, however, are not event-drive and are not attached to a specific table as triggers are. Stored procedures are explicitly executed by invoking a CALL to the procedure while triggers are implicitly executed. In addition, triggers can also execute stored procedures.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-sql-12" number={240} question="What is m

eant by Query Optimization?" difficulty="hard" topic="SQL">
The phase that identifies an efficient execution plan for evaluating a query that has the least estimated cost is referred to as query optimization.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-sql-13" number={241} question="What do you mean by Correlated Subquery?" difficulty="hard" topic="SQL">
Subqueries, or nested queries, are used to bring back a set of rows to be used by the parent query. Depending on how the subquery is written, it can be executed once for the parent query or it can be executed once for each row returned by the parent query. If the subquery is executed for each row of the parent, this is called a correlated subquery.
A correlated subquery can be easily identified if it contains any references to the parent

subquery columns in its WHERE clause. Columns from the subquery cannot be referenced anywhere else in the parent query. The following example demonstrates a non-correlated subquery.
E.g. Select * From CUST Where '10/03/1990' IN (Select ODATE From ORDER Where CUST. CNUM = ORDER. CNUM)
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-sql-14" number={242} question="What are Stand alone procedures?" difficulty="medium" topic="SQL">
Procedures that are not part of a package are known as stand-alone because they independently defined. A good example of a stand-alone procedure is one written in a SQL*Forms application. These types of procedures are not available for reference from other Oracle tools. Another limitation of stand-alone procedures is that they are compiled at run time, which slows execut

ion.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-bi-04" number={246} question="What is batch processing in Business Objects?" difficulty="medium" topic="Business Objects">

The batch can be run as a transaction in which if one process fails, the entire batch is rolled back or it can be run as a ser

ies of jobs.

<QuestionCard id="dwh-bi-05" number={247} question="What is Business Intelligence?" difficulty="medium" topic="BI Tools">
Business Intelligence is a process for increasing the competitive advantage of a business by intelligent use of available data in decision-making.
The five key stages of Business Intelligence:

<QuestionCard id="dwh-bi-06" number={248} question="What is a Universe in Business Intelligence?" difficulty="medium" topic="BI Concepts">

niverse defines the relationship among the various tables in the datawarehouse.
Or Universe is a semantic layer between the database and the user interface (reports).

<QuestionCard id="dwh-bi-07" number={249} question="What is OLAP in Business Intelligence?" difficulty="medium" topic="OLAP">
Online Analytical Processing, a category of software tools that provides analysis of data stored in a database. OLAP tools enable users to analyze different dimensions of multidimensional data. For example, it provides time series and trend analysis views. The chief component of OLAP is the OLAP server, which sits between a client and a database management systems (DBMS). The OLAP server understands how data is organized in the database and has special functions analyzing the data

.
A good OLAP interface has writes an efficient SQL and reads an accurate data from db. To design and architect having good knowledge on DB understanding the report requirements.

ion="Why an Infocube has maximum of 16 dimensions?" difficulty="medium" topic="OLAP">

ard id="dwh-bi-11" number={253} question="What are Dashboards?" difficulty="medium" topic="BI Concepts">

<QuestionCard id="dwh-bi-12" number={254} question="What are Adhoc reports and Static Reports?" difficulty="medium" topic="BI Concepts">
Adhoc reports run in real time based on the input parameters provided by the user at the run time. In Microstrategy, adhoc reports are created using Prompts.
In static reports, users won't be provide any input parameters. These reports are usaully schedule to run overnight and ready to view immediatley in the mornings using cache.

### Data Marts, Metadata & Enterprise Concepts

<QuestionList topic="Data Marts, Metadata & Enterprise Concepts" storagePrefix="dwh-ent">

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-01" number={255} question="Why is that Data Architect actually monitor and enforce compliance data standards?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
The primary idea of keeping the standards high on compliance for data standards is because it will help to reduce the data redundancy and helps the team to have a quality data. As this information is actually carried out or used throughout the organization.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-02" number={256} question="What are Data Modeling and Data Mining?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Mining">
Data modeling is the process of designing a data base model. In t

his data model data will be stored in two types of table fact table and dimension table.
Fact table contains the transaction data and dimension table contains the master data. Data mining is process of finding the hidden trends is called the data mining.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-03" number={257} question="What is the difference between Dependent Data Warehouse and Independent Data Warehouse?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
Dependent departments are those, which depend on a data ware to for their data. Independent department are those, which get their data directly from the operational data sources in the organization.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-04" number={258} question="What is the difference between Metadata and Data Dictionary?" difficu

lty="medium" topic="Metadata">
Meta data is nothing but information about data. It contains the information (i.e. data) about the graphs, its related files, abinitio commands, server information etc i.e. all kinds of information about project related information etc.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-05" number={259} question="What are Data Marts?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
A data mart is a collection of tables focused on specific business group/department. It may have multi-dimensional or normalized. Data marts are usually built from a bigger data warehouse or from operational data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-06" number={260} question="What are the advantages of Data Mining over traditional approaches?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Mining"

>
Data Mining is used for the estimation of the future. For example, for a company/business organization, using Data Mining we can predict the future of the business in terms of Revenue, Employees, Customers, or Orders, etc. Traditional approaches use simple algorithms for estimating the future, but they don't give results as accurate as Data Mining does.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-07" number={261} question="What is the main difference between Inmon and Kimball Philosophies of Data Warehousing?" difficulty="medium" topic="DW Philosophy">
Both differed in the concept of building the data warehouse. According to Kimball, Kimball views data warehousing as a constituency of data marts. Data marts are focused on delivering business objectives for departments in the organiza

tion. And the data warehouse is a conformed dimension of the data marts. Hence, a unified view of the enterprise can be obtained from the dimension modeling on a local departmental level. Inmon beliefs in creating a data warehouse on a subject-by-subject area basis. Hence, the development of the data warehouse can start with data from the online store. Other subject areas can be added to the data warehouse as their needs arise. Point-of-sale (POS) data can be added later if management decides it is necessary.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-08" number={262} question="What are the data validation strategies for Data Mart validation after the loading process?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Quality">
Data validation makes sure the loaded data is accurate and meets business re

quirements; the "strategy" is really just picking the right method for the source and volume involved:

- Validation in a data warehouse is typically done manually rather than through a dedicated tool.
- If the source and target are both relational, write SQL scripts that compare row counts, key sets, and aggregate values between source and target.
- If the source is a flat file or non-relational and the data volume is small, spreadsheet checks (e.g. Excel) are often enough.
- For larger or more complex loads, build dummy/staging tables to validate the ETL logic before trusting the mart.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-09" number={263} question="What is metadata in the context of a Data Warehouse, and why does it matter?" difficulty="hard" topic="Metadata">
Metadata is

"data about data" — a business analyst or data modeler captures information about the data itself: its source (where and how it originated), its nature (data type, nullability, valid values, etc.), and its behavior (how it's modified or derived, and its life cycle). This is captured in a data dictionary.

Examples of metadata include data element descriptions, data type descriptions, attribute/property descriptions, range/domain descriptions, and process/method descriptions. The repository environment encompasses all corporate metadata resources — database catalogs, data dictionaries, and navigation services.

Metadata is also presented at the data mart level: subsets, facts, dimensions, ODS, etc. For a data warehouse user, metadata provides vital information for analysis and decision

support, and it insulates the warehouse from changes in the schema of operational systems.

**Metadata synchronization** is the process of consolidating, relating, and synchronizing data elements with the same or similar meaning across different systems, joining these differing elements together in the warehouse for easier access.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-10" number={264} question="What are the possible Data Marts in Retail Sales?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Marts">
Product information and sales information.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-11" number={265} question="What is Data Cleaning?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Quality">
Data cleaning is a self-explanatory term. Most of the data warehouses in the world source data from multiple systems -

number={266} question="Briefly state different between Data Ware House and Data Mart?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
Data warehouse is made up of many datamarts. DWH contain many subject areas. However, data mart focuses on one subject area generally. E.g. If there will be DHW of bank then there can be one data mart for accounts, one for Loans etc. This is high-level definitions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-13" number={267} question="What is MetaData?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metadata">
Metadata is data about data. E.g. if in data mart we are receiving any file. Then metadata will contain information like how many columns, file is fix width/limited, ordering of fields, data types of field etc.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-14" number={268} q

uestion="What is the Definitions for Data Warehouse And Datamart?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
Datamart is subset of Data Warehouse we can say a datamart is collection of individual departmental information... Where as datawarehouse in collection of datamart.
Data mart is a single subject and datawarehouse is a integration of multiple subjects.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-15" number={269} question="What is Data Mining?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Mining">
Data Mining is the process of analyzing data from different perspectives and summarizing it into useful information.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-16" number={270} question="Is it correct develop a Data Mart using an ODS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
Yes it is correct to d

evelop a Data Mart using an ODS, because ODS which is used to store transaction data and few Days (less historical data) this is what datamart is required, so it is correct to develop datamart using ODS.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-17" number={271} question="Which automation tool is used in Data Warehouse testing?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Marts">
No Tool testing in done in DWH, only manual testing is done.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-18" number={272} question="What is Data Cardinality?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Quality">
Cardinality is the term used in database relations to denote the occurrences of data on either side of the relation.
There are 3 basic types of cardinality:
High data cardinality:
Values of a data column are very uncomm

on.
e.g.: email ids and the user names

Normal data cardinality:
Values of a data column are somewhat uncommon but never unique.
e.g.: A data column containing LAST_NAME (there may be several entries of the same last name)

Low data cardinality:
Values of a data column are very usual.
e.g.: flag statuses: 0/1
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-19" number={273} question="What is Chained Data Replication?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Quality">
In Chain Data Replication, the non-official data set distributed among many disks provides for load balancing among the servers within the data warehouse.
Blocks of data are spread across clusters and each cluster can contain a complete set of replicated data. All data block in every cluster is a unique permutation of the data i

n other clusters.
When a disk fails then all the calls made to the data in that disk are redirected to the other disks when the data has been replicated.
At times replicas and disks are added online without having to move around the data in the existing copy or affect the arm movement of the disk.
In load balancing, Chain Data Replication has multiple servers within the data warehouse share data request processing since data already have replicas in each server disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dwh-ent-20" number={274} question="What is the difference between Enterprise Data Warehouse and Data Warehouse?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Marts">
Big Organizations have a lot of diversified sources of data. There might be a data warehouse exclusively for transport and others for

data related to the project the company runs. In such case the complete enterprise's (company's) data warehouse is a big combination of all and is known as the Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW)
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a data warehouse for a retail company's sales reporting."** Start by nailing down the source systems and grain, then walk through staging, a star schema for the sales fact table (product, store, date, promotion dimensions), and how OLTP data gets denormalized for reporting performance.
- **"Our OLAP queries are slow — where do you start?"** Probe fact table grain, aggregation/rollup strategy, indexing choice (bitmap vs. B-tree), and whether the underlying MOLAP/ROLAP/HOLAP trade-offs actually fit the data volume and query patterns.
- **"How would you choose between a data warehouse, a data lake, and a lakehouse for a new analytics platform?"** Talk through schema-on-write vs. schema-on-read, cost profile, data variety, and the query patterns e

ach is actually good at.
- **"A dimension needs to track history — how do you model that, and how does it flow through the ETL?"** Walk through SCD Type 2 (or a hybrid approach) plus the load logic — surrogate keys, effective-dating, detecting changes — that keeps it correct.
- **"How would you migrate an on-prem warehouse to the cloud without breaking downstream BI reports?"** Discuss re-architecting ETL/ELT, keeping schema parity during the transition, and a reconciliation/validation strategy before cutting reports over.

---

## Further Reading

- [Data Modeling](/level-2-core-concepts/data-modeling/) — schema design specifics: star/snowflake, SCD types, fact/dimension patterns
- [Snowflake](/level-3-technologies/data-warehouses/snowflake/) and [BigQuery](/level-3-technologies/data-warehouses/bigquery/) — vendor-specific cloud warehouse implementations
- [Data Engineering Roadmap](/roadmaps/data-engineering/) — where warehousing fits into the broader curriculum

## Level 2 - Core Concepts: Data Engineering Discipline

This section covers the core concepts and disciplines that define modern data engineering. These topics are essential for building reliable, scalable data systems.

## Topics Covered

- **Data Modeling**: Designing effective data models with star schemas, dimension tables, and slowly changing dimensions
- **Data Warehousing**: Architecture and design patterns for building data warehouses and marts
- **Data Quality**: Ensuring data reliability through validation, testing, and monitoring
- **Data Governance**: Managing data responsibly with policies, catalogs, and access controls

A strong understanding of these concepts is necessary for designing and managing enterprise data systems.

## What is Data Engineering: Role, Responsibilities, and Lifecycle

**Data engineering is the discipline of designing, building, and maintaining the infrastructure that stores, processes, and serves data at scale — the foundation every downstream analytics, reporting, and machine learning workload depends on.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

At its core, data engineering is about **building and maintaining data pipelines** — systems that move data from source systems through transformation layers so it's reliably available for analysis, reporting, and machine learning. That work spans four recurring responsibilities: **data infrastructure** (reliable, scalable storage and processing systems), **pipeline architecture** (designing the ETL/ELT workflows that move data), **data quality** (ensuring accuracy and consistency), and **performance optimization** (keeping queries and transformations efficient as volume grows). The role leans on a specific skill set — SQL, Python, cloud platforms, data modeling, and system design — and the work itself follows a repeatable lifecycle: data is generated, ingested, processe

d, stored, served, and finally consumed by analysts, data scientists, and applications.

---

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="What is Data Engineering" storagePrefix="what-is-data-engineering">

<QuestionCard id="wde-01" number={1} question="What is data engineering, and why does it matter to an organization?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Data engineering is the practice of designing, building, and maintaining the infrastructure that stores, processes, and serves data at scale. It matters because data engineers create the foundation that lets an organization collect, transform, and analyze data reliably — without that foundation, analytics, reporting, and machine learning all sit on unreliable ground.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-02" number={2} question="What is a data engineer's primary responsibility?" difficulty="easy" topic="Role">
A d

ata engineer's primary responsibility is to build and maintain data pipelines — systems that move data from source systems, through transformation layers, to make it available for analysis, reporting, and machine learning. The emphasis is on the plumbing and infrastructure that gets data where it needs to go, reliably and repeatably.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-03" number={3} question="How does a data engineer's focus differ from a data scientist's?" difficulty="easy" topic="Role">
Data scientists focus on extracting insights from data — analysis, modeling, prediction. Data engineers focus on the infrastructure and pipelines that make that data available and trustworthy in the first place: data infrastructure, pipeline architecture, data quality, and performance optimization

. One builds the foundation; the other builds on top of it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-04" number={4} question="What does “data infrastructure” mean as one of a data engineer's core responsibilities?" difficulty="easy" topic="Responsibilities">
Data infrastructure refers to building reliable, scalable systems for data storage and processing — the databases, warehouses, lakes, and compute platforms that everything else is built on top of. If this layer isn't reliable or doesn't scale, every downstream pipeline and analysis inherits that fragility.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-05" number={5} question="What does “pipeline architecture” involve, and why does the ETL/ELT design choice matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Responsibilities">
Pipeline architecture is d

esigning the ETL/ELT workflows that handle data movement — deciding where data gets extracted from, where and when it gets transformed, and how it lands in its final destination. Getting this design right determines how maintainable, debuggable, and cost-efficient the whole data flow is, since it dictates where complexity and compute cost actually live.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-06" number={6} question="Why is data quality treated as one of the four core responsibilities of a data engineer?" difficulty="easy" topic="Responsibilities">
Data quality means ensuring accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data as it flows through the platform. It's called out as a core responsibility — not a nice-to-have — because every downstream consumer (dashboards, models, reports) inher

its whatever quality problems exist upstream; fixing quality at the source is far cheaper than firefighting it in a hundred dashboards later.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-07" number={7} question="What does “performance optimization” mean in a data engineering context?" difficulty="medium" topic="Responsibilities">
Performance optimization means making queries and transformations efficient at scale — the same pipeline that works fine on a small dataset needs to keep working as data volume, query concurrency, and complexity grow. It's a continuous responsibility rather than a one-time task, since data volumes and usage patterns keep shifting.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-08" number={8} question="Why are SQL and Python considered the core languages for data engineer

ing?" difficulty="easy" topic="Skills">
SQL is the lingua franca for data transformation and querying — nearly every warehouse, lake engine, and BI tool speaks it. Python is the most common language for pipeline scripting and automation — orchestration logic, custom transformations, and integrations are typically written in it. Together they cover both the "what data should look like" and "how do I move and shape it" sides of the job.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-09" number={9} question="Why do data engineers also need cloud platform knowledge, data modeling skills, and system design skills?" difficulty="medium" topic="Skills">
- **Cloud platforms** — modern data infrastructure runs on AWS, GCP, or Azure, so operating there is a baseline expectation, not a bonus skill.
- **

Data modeling** — structuring data for efficient querying and analysis determines whether downstream consumers get clean, fast answers or confusing, slow ones.
- **System design** — building scalable, resilient data architectures is what lets a platform keep working as data volume and the number of consumers grow.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-10" number={10} question="Walk through the stages of the data engineering lifecycle, from generation to consumption." difficulty="medium" topic="Lifecycle">
The lifecycle runs: **Data Generation → Ingestion → Processing → Storage → Serving → Consumption**.

1. **Generation** — data is created in source systems (databases, APIs, logs, IoT devices)
2. **Ingestion** — data is collected and brought into the platform, either batch or stre

aming
3. **Processing** — data is cleaned, transformed, and enriched
4. **Storage** — data is stored in warehouses, lakes, or databases
5. **Serving** — data is made available to consumers via APIs or query engines
6. **Consumption** — analysts, data scientists, and applications use the data

Each stage hands off to the next, so a failure or quality issue early in the chain propagates through everything downstream of it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="wde-11" number={11} question="What topics does a typical data engineering learning roadmap cover?" difficulty="easy" topic="Roadmap">
A typical roadmap covers: programming fundamentals (Python, SQL, Java/Scala), database systems (RDBMS, NoSQL, data warehouses), cloud platforms and infrastructure, pipeline orchestration (Airflow,

dbt), big data tools (Spark, Kafka), and monitoring and testing practices. It's designed to build from language and database fundamentals up through orchestration and operational maturity.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Explain data engineering to a non-technical stakeholder."** Frame it around the plumbing analogy: you're the one making sure clean water (data) reliably reaches every tap (dashboard, model, report) in the building, even as usage grows.
- **"Walk me through what happens to a single event, from the moment it's generated to the moment an analyst sees it in a dashboard."** Trace it through the six lifecycle stages — generation, ingestion, processing, storage, serving, consumption — naming a concrete tool or pattern at each step.
- **"Why do we need a dedicated data engineer instead of having analysts or data scientists build their own pipelines?"** Anchor the answer in the four core responsibilities — infrastructure, pipeline architecture, data quality,

performance — and explain why treating those as first-class, owned work (rather than side projects) is what keeps a platform reliable at scale.
- **"What skills would you look for when hiring a data engineer?"** Walk through SQL, Python, cloud platforms, data modeling, and system design, and explain what gap each one closes.

## Hadoop: Distributed Processing Framework

**Hadoop is a framework for storing and processing very large datasets across clusters of commodity hardware — HDFS handles distributed storage and MapReduce/YARN handle distributed computation, with fault tolerance built in through replication rather than expensive hardware.**

## Key Concepts

Hadoop is built around two ideas: distribute the data, and move the computation to where the data already lives rather than moving data to the computation. **HDFS** breaks files into fixed-size blocks (64MB or 128MB) and replicates each block — three copies by default — across **DataNodes**, using rack-aware placement (two replicas on one rack, a third on a different rack) so that a single node or rack failure never loses data. A single **NameNode** holds all filesystem metadata (the directory tree and block locations) in memory; it never stores actual file data. DataNodes report their health back to the NameNode via periodic **heartbeats** and **block reports**, and a **Secondary/Checkpoint NameNode** periodically merges the edit log into the filesystem image so restart

title: Set replication factor of a single file to 5
content:
s stay fast — but it is *not* a hot standby, which made the NameNode a single point of failure in Hadoop 1.

**MapReduce** processes data in phases: an optional input split, a map phase (filter/transform), an optional combiner (local pre-aggregation to cut network traffic), a shuffle-and-sort phase (group by key), and a reduce phase (aggregate). In Hadoop 1 this was coordinated by a single **JobTracker** and per-node **TaskTrackers**; YARN later generalized resource management beyond just MapReduce. Across almost every question below, the recurring themes are: how fault tolerance is achieved through replication and heartbeats, why data locality drives performance, and where the classic single points of failure sit.

Core concepts of the Hadoop Distributed File System — blocks, storage design, and how it differs from traditional and network-attached file systems.

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-01" number={1} question="What are the main components of a Hadoop Application?" difficulty="easy" topic="HDFS">
A Hadoop application has four core components:
- **HDFS** — the distributed file system in which Hadoop data is stored, offering very high bandwidth.
- **Hadoop Common** — the common set of libraries and utilities used across Hadoop.
- **Hadoop MapReduce** — the algorithm used for large-scale data processing.
- **Hadoop YARN** — resource management for the cluster; it also schedules tas

ks for users.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-02" number={2} question="What do you know about Block and Block scanner in HDFS?" difficulty="easy" topic="HDFS">
A large file in HDFS is broken into multiple parts, and each part is stored as a **Block**. By default, a block is 64MB.

A **Block Scanner** is a program every DataNode runs periodically to verify the checksum of every block it stores, in order to detect data corruption on that DataNode.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-03" number={3} question="How will you disable a Block Scanner on HDFS DataNode?" difficulty="medium" topic="HDFS">
`hdfs-site.xml` has a configuration property `dfs.datanode.scan.period.hours` that controls how often, in hours, the Block Scanner runs. Setting it to `0` disables

content:
the Block Scanner entirely.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-04" number={4} question="How can we update a file at an arbitrary location in HDFS?" difficulty="medium" topic="HDFS">
This is a trick question — HDFS does not allow updating a file at an arbitrary location. All files are written in append-only mode, meaning every write happens at the end of the file. There is no way to update a random location in an existing file.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-05" number={5} question="What is the difference between NAS and DAS in Hadoop cluster?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
- **NAS (Network Attached Storage)** — compute and storage are separated; storage is distributed over servers on a network.
- **DAS (Direct Attached Storage)** — storage is at

title: Set replication factor of a single file to 5
content:
tached directly to the node doing the computation.

Hadoop is built on the principle of moving processing near the data, so it needs storage local to computation. DAS gives very good performance and can run on commodity hardware, making it more cost-effective. NAS is only preferable when very high bandwidth (around 10 GbE) is available.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-06" number={6} question="How does indexing work in Hadoop?" difficulty="medium" topic="HDFS">
Hadoop indexing works at two levels:
- **Index based on File URI** — data is indexed by file; a search returns the files containing the data.
- **Index based on InputSplit** — data is indexed by the locations where the input split resides.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-07" number={7} questio

Use the `hadoop fs -test` command, generally used for testing purposes:

```bash

```

- `-e` checks existence of the file
- `-z` checks the file has non-zero size
- `-d` checks whether the path is a directory
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-08" number={8} question="How much storage is allocated by HDFS for storing a file of 25 MB size?" difficulty="medium" topic="Blocks">
HDFS stores all data in blocks, and the block size is configurable. With the default 64MB block size, storing a 25MB file still allocates at least one full block — so at least 64MB is allocated, even though only 25MB is actually used.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hd

fs-09" number={9} question="Why does HDFS store data in Block structure?" difficulty="medium" topic="Blocks">
Storing data in fixed-size blocks gives HDFS several benefits:
- **Fault tolerance** — replicating the same block across multiple locations means the data is still available even if one copy is inaccessible.
- **Large files** — files too large for a single disk can be split across blocks and stored across many machines.
- **Storage management** — fixed-size blocks make it easier to calculate storage usage and optimize algorithms that minimize data transfer across the network.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-10" number={10} question="What is a Balancer in HDFS?" difficulty="medium" topic="HDFS">
Data in HDFS can end up unevenly spread across DataNodes — for ex

content:
ample, right after a new DataNode is added to the cluster. The **Balancer** (sometimes called the Rebalancer) is an administrative tool that analyzes block placement and redistributes blocks to spread them more uniformly across DataNodes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-11" number={11} question="Why does the Hadoop Framework read a file in parallel but not write in parallel?" difficulty="hard" topic="HDFS I/O">
Reading is done in parallel because it lets Hadoop access data faster — the whole point of distributing storage.

Writing is *not* done in parallel because concurrent parallel writes to the same file would cause data inconsistency: if two nodes write to a file at the same time, neither knows what the other has written. For example, if 100MB of data (one 64MB blo

title: Set replication factor of a single file to 5
content:
ck, one 36MB block) were written in parallel, the first block wouldn't know where the remaining data belongs. So Hadoop reads in parallel but writes sequentially.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-12" number={12} question="If you change block size from 64MB to 128MB, what happens to existing data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Blocks">
Changing the block size does not affect data already written. After the change, every new file is chunked using the new 128MB block size, while existing data remains stored in its original 64MB chunks.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-13" number={13} question="What is the maximum and minimum block size Hadoop allows?" difficulty="medium" topic="Blocks">
- **Minimum** — 512 bytes, which is the local OS file system's block size

; you cannot go smaller.
- **Maximum** — there is no hard upper bound; it depends entirely on the environment/configuration.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-14" number={14} question="What is NAS?" difficulty="easy" topic="Storage">
NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a file system where data resides on one centralized machine, and every cluster member reads and writes to that shared storage over the network. It is not as efficient as HDFS for Hadoop-style workloads.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-15" number={15} question="How does HDFS differ from NAS?" difficulty="medium" topic="Storage">
- In **HDFS**, data blocks are distributed across the local drives of all machines in the cluster; in **NAS**, data sits on dedicated hardware.
- HDFS is designed t

o work with MapReduce, since computation moves to the data; NAS is not suited to this, since data is stored separately from computation.
- HDFS runs on a cluster of machines and provides redundancy via replication; NAS is served by a single machine and therefore doesn't provide the same data redundancy.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-16" number={16} question="How is HDFS different from traditional file systems?" difficulty="medium" topic="HDFS">
HDFS is responsible for storing huge volumes of data across a cluster and is designed to run on commodity hardware. While it shares similarities with other distributed file systems, the differences matter:
- Highly fault-tolerant, designed for low-cost hardware.
- Provides high-throughput access to application data, suited to

large data sets.
- Designed for applications that write data once and read it many times, requiring streaming-speed reads — "write-once, read-many" semantics.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-17" number={17} question="What is HDFS block size, and how does it differ from a traditional file system's block size?" difficulty="medium" topic="Blocks">
In HDFS, data is split into blocks (typically 64MB or 128MB) distributed across the cluster, and each block is replicated multiple times (three, by default) across different nodes. HDFS stores each block as a separate file on the underlying local file system. Because of this scale and replication model, HDFS block size isn't directly comparable to a traditional file system's block size.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="hadoop-hdfs-19" number={19} question="Can you give some examples of Big Data?" difficulty="easy" topic="Big Data">
Real-world examples include: Facebook generating 500+ terabytes of data per day, the New York Stock Exchange generating about 1 terabyte of new trade data per day, and a jet airliner collecting 10 terabytes of s
