### Partitioning, Shuffling & Performance

<QuestionList topic="Performance" storagePrefix="spark-perf">

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-01" number={63} question="Define partitions in Apache Spark." difficulty="easy" topic="Partitioning">
A partition is a smaller, logical division of data, similar to a split in MapReduce — a logical chunk of a large distributed dataset. Partitioning derives these logical units to speed up processing; everything in Spark is, in effect, a partitioned RDD. By default, Spark tries to read data into an RDD from nodes close to it, and creates one partition per HDFS block unless told otherwise.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-02" number={64} question="Describe Partition and Partitioner in Apache Spark." difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">

A **partition** is the basic unit of parallelism — a logical division of data stored on a cluster node, similar to an HDFS split; RDDs are collections of partitions, and Spark launches one task per partition when an action runs. If `spark.default.parallelism` is set, Spark uses that value; otherwise it uses the max number of upstream partitions (or matches the largest upstream RDD), which is least likely to cause out-of-memory errors.

A **partitioner** is an object that defines how key-value pairs are distributed across partitions — it maps each key to a partition ID between `0` and `numPartitions - 1`, and its contract guarantees that all records for a given key live on a single partition. This lets the scheduler optimize downstream operations. Spark has three kinds:
- **Hash Partiti

oner** — spreads data evenly across partitions based on a hash of the key.
- **Range Partitioner** — keys within the same range land on the same partition.
- **Custom Partitioner** — user-defined partitioning logic.

You can set one explicitly via `partitionBy()`, or get one implicitly from a transformation that preserves partitioning. For cogroup-like operations, Spark prefers an existing partitioner on one of the RDDs, falling back to a default `HashPartitioner` otherwise.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-03" number={65} question="How can you manually partition an RDD?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
By default, Spark creates one partition per HDFS block — a 1280 MB file with 128 MB blocks becomes 10 partitions:

```scala
val data = context.textFile("/u

ser/dataflair/file-name")
```

To request more partitions than there are blocks, pass a partition count explicitly:

```scala
val data = context.textFile("/user/dataflair/file-name", 20)
```

This creates 20 partitions (2 per block, in this example). Having somewhat more partitions than blocks is generally recommended for better performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-04" number={66} question="What is the difference between repartition and coalesce?" difficulty="medium" topic="Partitioning">
- **`repartition`** — can both increase and decrease the number of partitions; it creates entirely new partitions and does a full shuffle to evenly redistribute the data. It internally calls `coalesce` with the shuffle flag set, which makes it slower than `coalesce`.
-

**`coalesce`** — can only *reduce* the number of partitions; it reuses existing partitions to minimize (though not eliminate) the amount of data shuffled. It's generally faster than `repartition`, though speed can suffer if the input partitions are very unevenly sized.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-05" number={67} question="Describe the coalesce operation. When can you coalesce to a larger number of partitions?" difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">
`coalesce` is a transformation, in `org.apache.spark.rdd.ShuffledRDD`, that returns a new RDD reduced to `numPartitions` partitions:

```scala
def coalesce(numPartitions: Int, shuffle: Boolean = false): RDD[T]
```

Going from, say, 1000 partitions to 100 creates a **narrow dependency** — no shuffle occurs, since each

of the 100 new partitions simply claims 10 of the existing ones. But a drastic coalesce (e.g., down to `numPartitions = 1`) can leave your computation running on far fewer nodes than you'd like. Passing `shuffle = true` adds a shuffle step so the current upstream partitions still run in parallel.

With `shuffle = true`, you can actually coalesce *up* to a larger number of partitions too — useful if you have a small number of partitions (say 100), some of which are abnormally large: `coalesce(1000, shuffle = true)` redistributes the data across 1000 partitions using a hash partitioner. `coalesce` is generally an optimized `repartition` for the specific case of reducing partition count, and runs more efficiently after filtering has shrunk a large dataset.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

id="spark-perf-06" number={68} question="What is a shuffle operation in Spark, and when does it occur?" difficulty="medium" topic="Shuffling">
Shuffling is the redistribution of data across partitions — an all-to-all operation that may or may not move data between JVM processes/executors on different machines. Spark has no control over exactly which partition a given record ends up on. It's costly because, unlike most Spark tasks (which operate on one partition), a shuffle has to touch every partition. Shuffles are triggered by operations like `join`, `groupByKey`, and `reduceByKey`. Two configuration parameters affect shuffle compression: `spark.shuffle.compress` (whether to compress shuffle map output) and `spark.shuffle.spill.compress` (whether to compress intermediate spill files).

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-07" number={69} question="What operations can cause a shuffle in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Shuffling">
`repartition`, `coalesce` (with `shuffle = true`), `groupByKey`, `reduceByKey`, `cogroup`, and `join`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-08" number={70} question="How will you minimize data transfer while working with Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
- **Broadcast variables** — cache a read-only variable on every machine instead of shipping a copy with every task; improves the efficiency of joins between a large and a small RDD, and reduces communication cost via Spark's broadcast algorithm.
- **Accumulators** — update a shared variable's value in parallel across executors (e.g. counters/sums)

without shuffling data around to do it.
- **Avoid `ByKey` operations, `repartition`, and other shuffle-triggering calls** where they aren't necessary.
- **Enable shuffle compression** — set `spark.shuffle.compress = true` to reduce the volume of data transferred when a shuffle is unavoidable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-09" number={71} question="What is the default level of parallelism in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Optimization">
When not explicitly configured, the default level of parallelism is simply the number of partitions in the RDD being operated on.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-10" number={72} question="What is lazy evaluation in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Optimization">
Lazy evaluation ("call-by-need") delays

execution until a result is actually required. Transformations on an RDD aren't run when they're called — Spark just records what has to happen, building a DAG of pending work. Only when an action is called does Spark execute that DAG. This means data isn't loaded until it's actually needed, and Spark gets the chance to optimize the whole pipeline before running any of it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-11" number={73} question="What are the benefits of lazy evaluation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
- Increases the manageability of the program by letting Spark reason about the whole computation graph at once.
- Reduces computation overhead and increases overall system speed.
- Reduces time and space complexity.
- Enables optimization by reducing the numbe

r of passes/queries needed over the data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-12" number={74} question="What is a Broadcast variable in Spark, and why do we need it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
A broadcast variable lets you keep a read-only value cached on every machine, instead of shipping a fresh copy of it with every task — created via `SparkContext.broadcast(v)` and read via `.value`. Spark distributes it using an efficient broadcast algorithm to reduce communication cost. It's especially useful in shuffle operations that need the same reference data everywhere (e.g. join keys), and is recommended over a plain closure variable whenever the same data is needed by many tasks running on a cluster. The data is serialized before distribution and deserialized bef

ore use.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-13" number={75} question="What is an Accumulator in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
An accumulator is a variable that can only be updated through an associative and commutative operation, making it safe to add to in parallel across executors — commonly used to implement counters or running sums. Workers only ever write to it; the driver reads the final value. Spark provides numeric accumulators out of the box (`SparkContext.longAccumulator()`, `SparkContext.doubleAccumulator()`), and accumulators can be named or unnamed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-perf-14" number={76} question="How are automatic clean-ups triggered in Spark to handle accumulated metadata?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimiz

ation">
Clean-up can be triggered automatically by setting the `spark.cleaner.ttl` parameter (a periodic cleaner; the default is infinite, meaning metadata is remembered indefinitely). Metadata older than the configured duration is dropped, which is what lets long-running Spark applications keep running for many hours without accumulating unbounded metadata. Alternatively, you can batch-divide long-running jobs and write intermediary results to disk periodically.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### DataFrames, Datasets & Spark SQL

<QuestionList topic="Spark SQL" storagePrefix="spark-sql">

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-01" number={77} question="What is the purpose of Spark SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Spark SQL">
Spark SQL is Spark's module for running SQL queries and for interacting with structured data through the Dataset API — both use the same underlying computation engine, which gives Spark visibility into both the structure of the data and the computation being performed. It can also read data from an existing Hive installation, and it can be accessed via the JDBC/ODBC API or the command line, not just from within a Spark program.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-02" number={78} question="What are the functions/capabilities of Spark SQL?" difficulty="me

dium" topic="Spark SQL">
- Loading data from a wide range of structured sources.
- Querying data using SQL, both from inside a Spark program and from external tools that connect over JDBC/ODBC (e.g. BI tools like Tableau).
- Rich integration between SQL and regular Python/Java/Scala code — joining RDDs with SQL tables, exposing custom functions (UDFs) to SQL, and more.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-03" number={79} question="What module is used for implementing SQL in Apache Spark, and what are its libraries?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark SQL">
The **Spark SQL** module combines relational data processing with the power of Spark's functional programming API, and supports both SQL and Hive Query Language. It's made up of four main libraries:
- **Data Source API**
-

**DataFrame API**
- **Interpreter & Catalyst Optimizer**
- **SQL Service**

It's the recommended way to load data, query it from within Spark applications, and write results out to a destination.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-04" number={80} question="What is Hive on Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark SQL">
Hive has significant built-in support for running its execution engine on Spark instead of MapReduce/Tez:

```sql
hive> set spark.home=/location/to/sparkHome;
hive> set hive.execution.engine=spark;
```

More broadly, Spark's commonly-used ecosystem components include **Spark SQL** (originally "Shark") for developers, **Spark Streaming** for live data, **GraphX** for graph computation, **MLlib** for machine learning algorithms, and **SparkR** to work

with Spark from R.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-05" number={81} question="What is a DataFrame in Spark SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="DataFrames">
A DataFrame is a Dataset organized into named columns — conceptually similar to a table in a relational database, or a data frame in R/Python, but with richer optimization under the hood. In Java and Scala, a DataFrame is represented as a `Dataset` of `Row` objects. You can build one from an existing RDD, a Hive table, structured data files, or another Spark data source, and like RDDs, DataFrames are evaluated lazily.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-06" number={82} question="What are the advantages of DataFrame (over RDD)?" difficulty="medium" topic="DataFrames">
- Imposes structure on a distributed collectio

n of data, enabling higher-level abstractions and easier large-dataset processing.
- Space- and performance-efficient compared to raw RDDs.
- Supports both structured and unstructured formats (Avro, CSV, JSON, Parquet, etc.) and storage systems (HDFS, Hive, MySQL, and more).
- APIs available across Java, Scala, Python, and R.
- Provides Hive compatibility, so unmodified Hive queries can run against an existing Hive warehouse.
- Uses the **Catalyst optimizer**, which transforms a query through four phases: analyzing the logical plan to resolve references, logical plan optimization, physical planning, and code generation (compiling part of the query to JVM bytecode).
- Scales from kilobytes of data on a laptop to petabytes on a large cluster.

DataFrames can be created from Hive tabl

es, structured data files, or other Spark data sources.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-07" number={83} question="What is a Dataset in Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Datasets">
Introduced in Spark 1.6, a Dataset is a typed extension of the DataFrame API that gives you an object-oriented interface and compile-time type safety on top of DataFrame's Catalyst/Tungsten-optimized execution. Internally, a Dataset represents a logical plan describing the computation needed to produce the data; once that plan is analyzed and resolved, Spark builds a physical query plan to execute it. **Encoders** handle translation between JVM objects and Spark's internal binary format, enabling on-demand access to individual fields without fully deserializing an object, and Spark's built-in en

coders are advanced enough to generate bytecode for interacting with off-heap data directly. Datasets are interconvertible with DataFrames via `toDS(): Dataset[T]` and `toDF(): DataFrame`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-08" number={84} question="What are the advantages of Datasets?" difficulty="medium" topic="Datasets">
- **Compile-time type safety** — syntax errors surface at compile time, unlike RDDs, DataFrames, or plain SQL queries.
- **Fast in-memory encoding** via Tungsten, plus optimized queries via the Catalyst optimizer.
- **Less memory used** — because Spark knows the dataset's structure ahead of time, it can build an optimal in-memory layout while caching.
- **Object-oriented interface** with a custom view over structured and semi-structured data, and a rich

set of domain-specific operations.
- **Combines the strengths of RDDs and DataFrames** — RDD's convenience and static (Scala) type safety, plus DataFrame's performance optimization.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-09" number={85} question="On what basis can you differentiate RDD, DataFrame, and Dataset?" difficulty="hard" topic="Comparison">
| Criteria | RDD | DataFrame | Dataset |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Representation** | Distributed collection of data with no schema | Distributed collection organized into named columns | Combines DataFrame and RDD — static type safety plus an object-oriented interface |
| **Optimization** | No built-in optimizer | Uses the Catalyst optimizer | Also uses the Catalyst optimizer |
| **Schema** | Must be defined manually | Discovered au

tomatically | Discovered automatically via the SQL engine |
| **Aggregation speed** | Slowest of the three, even for simple grouping | Fastest, thanks to easy, powerful APIs | Faster than RDD, slightly slower than DataFrame |
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-10" number={86} question="What is the Catalyst framework/optimizer?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Catalyst is Spark SQL's optimization framework — it represents and manipulates a data-flow graph made up of relational operators and expressions. It has three main pieces: a **TreeNode library** for transforming trees (expressed as Scala case classes), a **logical plan representation** for relational operators, and an **expression library**. It supports both rule-based optimization (apply a fixed set of rules

to decide how to execute a query) and cost-based optimization (generate multiple candidate plans via rules, then pick the cheapest), and leans on Scala language features like pattern matching internally.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-11" number={87} question="What do you understand by SchemaRDD?" difficulty="easy" topic="Spark SQL">
SchemaRDD — the predecessor to DataFrame — is an RDD made up of `Row` objects (wrappers around basic string/integer arrays) along with schema information describing each column's data type. It was designed to make debugging code and unit-testing the SparkSQL module easier, and provides relational query interfaces on top of the standard RDD functionality. For example, given an RDD of `Person` records with `name` and `age` fields, the SchemaRDD

captures that column structure.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-12" number={88} question="Explain the createOrReplaceTempView API." difficulty="easy" topic="Spark SQL">
`createOrReplaceTempView` is a Dataset method (`org.apache.spark.sql`) that registers a temporary SQL view over a DataFrame/Dataset:

```scala
def createOrReplaceTempView(viewName: String): Unit

df.createOrReplaceTempView("titanicdata")
```

Once registered, you can run SQL queries directly against `titanicdata`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-13" number={89} question="Is it possible to do real-time processing directly with SparkSQL?" difficulty="medium" topic="Spark SQL">
Not directly — SparkSQL itself isn't a real-time engine. The common approach is to register the existing RDD

as a SQL table and run SQL queries against it on demand; for genuine real-time stream processing on top of the SQL engine, use Structured Streaming instead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-14" number={90} question="What are the various data sources available in Spark SQL?" difficulty="easy" topic="Spark SQL">
The three most commonly cited built-in sources are **Parquet files**, **JSON datasets**, and **Hive tables** — Spark SQL's Data Source API also extends to CSV, Avro, JDBC-connected databases, and other third-party formats.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-15" number={91} question="What data formats does Spark support for reading and processing?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Formats">
Spark supports both raw and structured file formats for efficient r

eading and processing, including Parquet, JSON, XML, CSV, RC, Avro, and TSV.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-16" number={92} question="What is a Parquet file, and why use it in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Formats">
Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format available to any project in the Hadoop ecosystem — any processing framework, data model, or language can use it. It's compressed and efficiently encoded, and it's a strong choice specifically for storing large volumes of data long-term for analytics. Spark SQL supports both reading and writing Parquet natively, performs both scan and write operations directly against it, and automatically preserves the schema of the original data (writing all columns as nullable by default).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

id="spark-sql-17" number={93} question="What are the advantages of using a Parquet file?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Formats">
- Lets you fetch only the specific columns you need for access.
- Consumes less storage space than row-based formats.
- Uses type-specific encoding.
- Supports (and limits) I/O to only what's required, reducing I/O operations overall.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-18" number={94} question="What are the two ways to attain a schema from data?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Formats">
Let Spark **infer** the schema from your data, or supply your own **user-defined schema**. Schema inference is the recommended starting point, but a user-defined schema typically increases performance by 2-3x (depending on cluster size), since Spark doesn't hav

e to scan all the data to infer types — and, correspondingly, fewer jobs are needed, since Spark no longer needs one inference job per data partition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-19" number={95} question="Why should you define your own schema?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Formats">
- Avoids the extra scan of your data that schema inference requires.
- Lets you specify alternative data types than what would otherwise be inferred.
- Lets you parse only the fields you actually need.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-20" number={96} question="Why is JSON a common format in big data pipelines?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Formats">
JSON is semi-structured, which suits hierarchical data and schemas that need to evolve over time, and it natively support

s composite data types such as arrays and maps.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-21" number={97} question="By default, how are corrupt records handled by spark.read.json()?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Formats">
They're routed into a column called `_corrupt_record` — this captures the records Spark can't parse, for example when characters are missing from a JSON string.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-sql-22" number={98} question="How do you parse XML data, and what class would you use in Java?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Formats">
In Java, a common approach is the **JDOM** library — download it and import it into your project. Scala has built-in XML parsing support via its `scala-xml` library (check for the current version for your Scala release).
</Qu

estionCard>

### Memory Management & Persistence

<QuestionList topic="Memory Management" storagePrefix="spark-mem">

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-01" number={99} question="How will you do memory tuning in Spark?" difficulty="hard" topic="Memory">
Memory tuning has to account for the amount of memory objects consume, the cost of accessing them, and garbage-collection overhead. Since Spark caches objects in memory, start by measuring usage: cache a representative RDD and check its size on the Storage page of the Web UI, then estimate memory needs from there. To reduce usage where needed:
- Prefer arrays of primitives/objects over linked lists or `HashMap`s — the `fastutil` library provides convenient primitive-friendly collection classes for Java.
- Reduce nested data structures with many small ob

jects and pointers (a linked list, for example, carries a pointer per node).
- Use numeric IDs instead of Strings for keys where possible.
- Pass the JVM flag `-XX:+UseCompressedOops` to shrink pointers from eight bytes to four.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-02" number={100} question="What is the difference between cache() and persist()?" difficulty="easy" topic="Persistence">
Both persist an RDD in memory across operations. The difference is that `persist()` lets you choose the storage level explicitly, while `cache()` always uses the default storage level, `MEMORY_ONLY`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-03" number={101} question="How will you remove data from cache in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="Persistence">
Spark automatically evicts unu

sed cached objects using a Least Recently Used (LRU) policy, and it monitors cache usage on each node to do this. To forcibly remove an object from cache yourself, call `RDD.unpersist()`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-04" number={102} question="What are the different Persistence/Storage levels in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Persistence">
- **`MEMORY_ONLY`** — stores the RDD as deserialized Java objects in the JVM; if it doesn't fit in memory, it's recomputed on demand.
- **`MEMORY_AND_DISK`** — deserialized in the JVM; spills to disk if it doesn't fit in memory.
- **`MEMORY_ONLY_SER`** — stores the RDD as serialized Java objects, more space-efficient than the deserialized form.
- **`MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER`** — serialized in the JVM; spills to disk if it doe

sn't fit in memory.
- **`DISK_ONLY`** — stored only on disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-05" number={103} question="How will you select the storage level in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Persistence">
The choice is a trade-off between CPU efficiency and memory usage. If your RDD fits comfortably in memory, use `MEMORY_ONLY` for the best performance. If it doesn't fit, try `MEMORY_ONLY_SER` with a compact serialization library — still fast, with real space savings. If there's a big gap between available memory and total object size, fall back to `MEMORY_AND_DISK`. Where fast fault recovery matters, replicate objects across multiple partitions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-06" number={104} question="What do you mean by Persistence in Spark

?" difficulty="medium" topic="Persistence">
RDD persistence is an optimization technique that saves the result of evaluating an RDD so it can be reused, avoiding recomputation and reducing overall computation overhead. It's implemented via `cache()` and `persist()`, and is a key tool for iterative algorithms: once persisted, each node keeps in memory whatever partitions of the RDD it computed, ready for reuse — which can speed up subsequent computations by roughly 10x.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-07" number={105} question="What is Executor Memory in a Spark application, and how do you calculate it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Memory">
Every Spark application has a fixed heap size and fixed core count per executor — the heap size is the **executor memory**, controlled by

the `spark.executor.memory` property (or the `--executor-memory` flag), and each worker node runs one executor per application. It's effectively a measure of how much of a worker node's memory the application is allowed to use.

**Worked example** — given 10 nodes, 15 cores per node, and 61 GB RAM per node, with a rule-of-thumb target of 5 concurrent tasks per executor:

```text
Number of executors per node = cores per node / concurrent tasks = 15 / 5 = 3
Total executors for the job   = nodes × executors per node = 10 × 3 = 30
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-mem-08" number={106} question="What is spark.executor.memory in a Spark application?" difficulty="easy" topic="Memory">
`spark.executor.memory` sets the amount of memory used per executor process; its default v

alue is 1 GB.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### Spark Streaming

<QuestionList topic="Spark Streaming" storagePrefix="spark-stream">

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-01" number={107} question="What is Spark Streaming?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming is an extension of the core Spark API for processing live data streams with high throughput and fault tolerance. It ingests data from sources like Kafka, Kinesis, and Flume, lets you apply familiar Spark functions (`map`, `reduce`, `join`, etc.) to the incoming data, and writes the processed results to a filesystem, a database, or a live dashboard.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-02" number={108} question="How does Spark Streaming work internally?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming listens to live data streams from variou

s sources and, as data arrives, divides it into small batches the Spark engine can handle. Internally, this uses an abstraction called a **DStream** (discretized stream) — a continuous stream of data that is, under the hood, simply a sequence of RDDs. Spark applies the usual transformations and actions to that sequence of RDDs to produce a resulting output stream.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-03" number={109} question="What is a DStream (Discretized Stream)?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streaming">
A DStream is the high-level abstraction Spark Streaming uses to represent a continuous stream of data — internally, just a sequence of RDDs. You can create a DStream either from a source like Kafka, Flume, or Kinesis, or by applying transformations to another DStream.
</Ques

tionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-04" number={110} question="What are the different types of transformations on DStreams?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
- **Stateless transformations** — processing of the current batch doesn't depend on the output of the previous batch. Examples: `map()`, `filter()`, `reduceByKey()`.
- **Stateful transformations** — processing depends on the intermediary results of the previous batch, such as transformations built on sliding windows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-05" number={111} question="What are receivers in Apache Spark Streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Receivers consume data from external sources and hand it off to Spark for processing. They're created as long-running tasks scheduled by the s

treaming context in a round-robin fashion across executors, with each receiver using a single core. There are two kinds:
- **Reliable receivers** — send an acknowledgment back to the data source once the data has been received and replicated in Spark's storage.
- **Unreliable receivers** — send no acknowledgment.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-06" number={112} question="What is Structured Streaming in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Introduced in Spark 2.1, Structured Streaming is a scalable, fault-tolerant stream-processing engine built directly on the Spark SQL engine. You express streaming aggregations, event-time windows, and similar logic using the Dataset/DataFrame API, and the computation runs on the same optimized Spark SQL execution eng

ine used for batch queries.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-07" number={113} question="What is Checkpointing in Spark Streaming?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
Checkpointing adds resiliency to a streaming application so it can recover after a failure. There are two types:
- **Metadata checkpointing** — saves the configuration and other information that defines the streaming application (configuration, DStream operations, incomplete batches), used to recover the driver after a failure.
- **Data checkpointing** — saves RDDs themselves to reliable storage; useful for stateful transformations where a generated RDD depends on the RDD from the previous batch, since that dependency chain can otherwise grow very long. Checkpointing intermediate RDDs bounds the recovery

time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-08" number={114} question="What is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) / journaling in Spark Streaming?" difficulty="hard" topic="Streaming">
There are two kinds of failure in a Spark job: driver failure and worker failure. When a **worker** fails, its executor processes are killed and their scheduled tasks are automatically moved to other running worker nodes. When the **driver** fails, every associated executor is killed along with whatever data was sitting in its memory — in a streaming application, that data hasn't necessarily been persisted anywhere yet, so it can be lost for good, unlike batch jobs reading from a reliable filesystem like HDFS (where zero data loss is guaranteed since the data can always be re-read).

**Write-Ahead Lo

gging**, introduced in Spark 1.2, solves this: the intent of every operation is first written to a log file, so if the driver fails and restarts, it can replay the logged operations against the data. For streaming sources like Kafka or Flume, receivers also write the data they receive into these log files, not just into executor memory. Enable it with:
1. `streamingContext.checkpoint(path)` — sets the checkpoint directory.
2. `spark.stream.receiver.WriteAheadLog.enable = true` — enables WAL logging.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-09" number={115} question="How is caching relevant in Spark Streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming divides a data stream into DStream batches, and those batches can be cached in memory — very useful when the same

DStream feeds multiple downstream computations. Caching uses `cache()` or `persist(StorageLevel)`:

```scala
val cacheDf   = dframe.cache()
val persistDf = dframe.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY)
```

For network-based input streams (Kafka, Flume, etc.), the default persistence level replicates data to 2 nodes for fault tolerance. Caching's main advantages: cost efficiency (avoids recomputation), time efficiency, and more jobs completed per unit of time since worker nodes spend less time recomputing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-10" number={116} question="What is the significance of the Sliding Window operation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
Spark Streaming's windowed computations apply transformations over a sliding window of RDDs rather than a sin

gle batch. As the window slides, the RDDs that fall inside it are combined and processed together, producing new RDDs for the windowed DStream — useful for aggregations that need to look back over a recent time span rather than just the latest micro-batch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-11" number={117} question="Explain the level of parallelism in Spark Streaming." difficulty="medium" topic="Streaming">
To reduce processing time, you generally need to increase parallelism, in one of three ways:
- **Increase the number of receivers** — if a single receiver can't read and distribute records fast enough, it becomes a bottleneck; add more receivers as the scenario demands.
- **Re-partition the received data** — if you can't add more receivers, redistribute the data you

already have by re-partitioning it.
- **Increase parallelism in aggregation** — raise the parallelism of the aggregation stage itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-stream-12" number={118} question="Which companies use Spark Streaming?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streaming">
Well-known adopters include Uber, Netflix, and Pinterest.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### MLlib & GraphX

<QuestionList topic="MLlib & GraphX" storagePrefix="spark-ml">

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-01" number={119} question="What is the main use of MLlib in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="MLlib">
MLlib is Spark's machine-learning library, delivering both speed (up to 100x faster than MapReduce for some workloads) and a broad set of algorithms usable from Java, Scala, or Python as part of a larger Spark workflow:
- **ML Algorithms** — classification, regression, clustering, collaborative filtering.
- **Featurization** — feature extraction, transformation, dimensionality reduction, and selection.
- **Pipelines** — tools for constructing, evaluating, and tuning ML pipelines.
- **Persistence** — saving and loading algorithms, models, and pipelines.
- **Utilitie

s** — linear algebra, statistics, and data-handling helpers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-02" number={120} question="List some commonly used Machine Learning algorithms available via MLlib." difficulty="easy" topic="MLlib">
Machine learning algorithms broadly fall into three categories: **supervised**, **unsupervised**, and **reinforcement learning**. Commonly used algorithms in MLlib and the wider Spark ML ecosystem include Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, K-Means, KNN, SVM, Random Forest, Naive Bayes, dimensionality-reduction algorithms, and gradient boosting/AdaBoost.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-03" number={121} question="How is machine learning implemented in Apache Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="MLlib">
Through **MLlib**,

Spark's scalable machine-learning library, which aims to make common ML algorithms and workflows (classification, clustering, regression, dimensionality reduction, and more) both easy to use and scalable across a cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-04" number={122} question="Is Apache Spark a good fit for reinforcement learning?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLlib">
Not really — Spark works best for comparatively simple machine learning algorithms like clustering, regression, and classification; reinforcement learning's sequential, stateful nature doesn't map cleanly onto Spark's execution model.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-05" number={123} question="What is a Pipeline in Apache Spark (ML)?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLlib">
A Pipeline is a machine-

learning concept representing a sequence of algorithms — one or more stages — executed in order to process and learn from data, similar to a workflow. A DataFrame is passed in as input and is progressively transformed as it moves through each stage; Spark typically performs runtime checks on the DataFrame as it flows through the pipeline. Pipelines can also be saved to disk and reloaded later.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-06" number={124} question="What is the difference between a Transformer and an Estimator in Apache Spark?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLlib">
A **Transformer** is an abstraction for a feature transformer or a learned model — it implements `transform()`, converting one DataFrame into another (typically by appending one or more new columns). An **Estimato

r** is an abstraction for a learning algorithm that fits/trains on data — it implements `fit()`, which takes a DataFrame as input and produces a Model (itself a Transformer).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-07" number={125} question="What are the two main types of Vector in Spark, and how do dense and sparse vectors differ?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLlib">
- **Dense Vector** — backed by a plain array of `double` values holding every entry, e.g. a vector like `(1.0, 0.0, 3.0)`.
- **Sparse Vector** — backed by two parallel arrays, one for indices and one for values, storing only the non-zero entries to save space.

```scala
val sparseVec: Vector = Vectors.sparse(5, Array(0, 4), Array(1.0, 2.0))
val denseVec: Vector  = Vectors.dense(4405d, 260100d, 400d, 5.0, 4.0, 198.

0, 9070d, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.0)
```

`sparseVec` above is a size-5 vector with non-zero values only at indices 0 and 4. Sparse vectors are worthwhile when most entries are zero; used on data with only a few zero values, they actually hurt performance, since the extra index bookkeeping adds overhead without saving meaningful space. Either representation gives identical calculation results — the difference is purely about memory and speed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-08" number={126} question="What is GraphX, and is there an API for implementing graphs in Spark?" difficulty="easy" topic="GraphX">
GraphX is Spark's API for graphs and graph-parallel computation. It extends the Spark RDD abstraction with a **Resilient Distributed Property Graph** — a directed multigraph tha

t can have multiple parallel edges, with user-defined properties attached to every vertex and edge. To support graph computation, GraphX exposes operators such as `subgraph`, `joinVertices`, and `mapReduceTriplets`, along with an optimized variant of the Pregel API, plus a growing collection of graph algorithms and builders for common analytics tasks.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-09" number={127} question="What is a Property Graph?" difficulty="medium" topic="GraphX">
A Property Graph is a directed multigraph, where you can attach an object (properties) to every vertex and edge. Because it's a multigraph, it allows multiple parallel edges sharing the same source and destination — useful for modeling more than one relationship between the same pair of vertices at once (e.

g., two people who are both "boss" and "mentor" to each other).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-10" number={128} question="What are the options in Spark to create a Graph?" difficulty="easy" topic="GraphX">
- **`Graph.apply`** — the simplest option; builds a graph from RDDs of vertices and edges.
- **`Graph.fromEdges`** — builds a graph from just an RDD of edges; vertices are created automatically with a default value.
- **`Graph.fromEdgeTuples`** — builds a graph from an RDD of tuples alone.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-11" number={129} question="What are the basic Graph operators in Spark GraphX?" difficulty="easy" topic="GraphX">
`numEdges`, `numVertices`, `inDegrees`, `outDegrees`, `degrees`, `vertices`, `edges`, `persist`, `cache`, `unpersistVertic

es`, and `partitionBy`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-12" number={130} question="What partitioning approach does GraphX use?" difficulty="hard" topic="GraphX">
GraphX uses a **vertex-cut** approach to distributed graph partitioning: instead of splitting a graph along its edges, it partitions along vertices, which can then span multiple machines. Edges are assigned to partitions according to whichever partition strategy is selected. This reduces communication and storage overhead compared to edge-cut partitioning.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-13" number={131} question="What is Neighborhood Aggregation in Spark GraphX?" difficulty="hard" topic="GraphX">
Neighborhood Aggregation is the task of aggregating information about each vertex's local neighborhood

— for example, counting how many books a given book references, or how many times a tweet has been retweeted. It's a building block for iterative graph algorithms like PageRank and shortest-path, implemented in GraphX via the `aggregateMessages[]` and `mergeMsg[]` operations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-14" number={132} question="What is PageRank in GraphX?" difficulty="medium" topic="GraphX">
PageRank measures the importance of each vertex in a graph, treating an edge from `u` to `v` as `u` endorsing `v`'s importance — a Twitter user followed by many others ends up ranked highly, for instance. GraphX ships both a **static** implementation (runs for a fixed number of iterations) and a **dynamic** one (runs until ranks converge within a tolerance) as methods on the PageR

ank object, and `GraphOps` lets you call either directly as a method on a `Graph`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-15" number={133} question="What makes Apache Spark well-suited to low-latency workloads like graph processing and machine learning?" difficulty="medium" topic="MLlib">
Spark keeps data in memory, which speeds up both model building/training and graph traversal — machine learning algorithms typically need multiple iterations to converge on an optimal model, and graph algorithms need to traverse all nodes and edges, often repeatedly. Workloads that require many iterations benefit the most from Spark's in-memory model: less disk access and more controlled network traffic make a large difference once there's a meaningful amount of data to process.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="spark-ml-16" number={134} question="Is it possible to use Spark to access and analyze data stored in Cassandra databases?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
Yes — Spark can access and analyze data in Cassandra using the Cassandra Connector.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Walk me through what happens when I call `.count()` on a chain of `.filter()` and `.map()` calls."** Trace the lazy-evaluation story: nothing runs until `count()` (an action) is called, at which point Spark builds a DAG, the DAG Scheduler splits it into stages at shuffle boundaries, and the Task Scheduler dispatches tasks to executors — one task per partition.
- **"A join in my Spark job is taking forever and spilling to disk — how do you debug it?"** Talk through checking for data skew across partitions, whether a shuffle is unavoidable given the join keys, whether a broadcast join would work if one side is small enough, and whether `repartition`/`coalesce` are being used appropriately before the join.
- **"Design a Spark job to process a stream of

clickstream events and maintain a running count per user."** This is a stateful-streaming question — expect to discuss DStreams vs. Structured Streaming, windowing, checkpointing for fault tolerance, and how state gets persisted across micro-batches.
- **"Why is this Spark application running out of memory?"** Walk through executor memory sizing (`spark.executor.memory`, cores per executor), storage level choice (`MEMORY_ONLY` vs. `MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER`), and whether the job is caching more than it needs to or shuffling more data than necessary.
- **"When would you reach for RDDs instead of DataFrames?"** A good answer touches on low-level control over partitioning, working with unstructured data that doesn't fit a schema, and cases needing fine-grained transformations the Catalyst optimi

zer doesn't help with — while acknowledging that DataFrames/Datasets are the default choice for structured data in modern Spark.

## Business Intelligence: Analytics & Visualization Platforms

BI tools enable analytics and visualization for end users and stakeholders.

## Platforms Covered

- **Tableau**: Enterprise BI and visualization
- **Looker**: Business intelligence and exploration
- **Superset**: Open-source BI and visualization

## Looker: Business Intelligence & Exploration

**Looker is a modeling-first BI platform: instead of pulling data into its own engine, it defines reusable metrics and relationships in LookML and pushes queries down to the warehouse — which shapes almost every answer about performance, governance, and real-time capability.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Looker's defining trait is that it doesn't store or move data — it's a semantic layer written in **LookML** that defines dimensions, measures, and relationships between tables, then compiles user interactions in an **Explore** into SQL run directly against the underlying warehouse. That "push-down" architecture explains most of Looker's trade-offs: it inherits the warehouse's scalability and real-time limits rather than imposing its own, relies on the warehouse (or **PDTs** — Persistent Derived Tables — materialized back into it) for performance, and depends on the warehouse's own security and partitioning features rather than reinventing them. Governance in Looker is mostly about **access control** (roles, Explore permissions, row-level filters) and **change management*

* (LookML in Git, Development Mode for safe iteration), since the modeling logic — not the data itself — is what Looker actually owns. Most interview questions boil down to: what does Looker do itself, and what does it delegate to the connected database?

---
## Interview Questions

### Fundamentals & Core Concepts

<QuestionList topic="Looker Fundamentals" storagePrefix="looker-fund">

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-01" number={1} question="What is Looker?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Looker is a business intelligence (BI) and data visualization platform that lets users explore, analyze, and share data insights, built around a modeling layer (LookML) rather than its own data engine.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-02" number={2} question="How does Looker handle data integration?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Looker connects to various data sources using database dialects and APIs, letting it integrate with different data platforms — SQL databases, cloud storage, and data warehouses — without moving the data into Looker it

self.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-03" number={3} question="Can you explain the concept of a LookML model in Looker?" difficulty="medium" topic="LookML">
LookML is Looker's modeling language. It defines the relationships between data tables and creates reusable dimensions and measures. A LookML model is a collection of files describing the structure and logic of your data — the single source of truth that every Explore and dashboard is built on top of.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-04" number={4} question="What is a dimension in Looker?" difficulty="easy" topic="LookML">
A dimension represents a field or attribute in your data. It adds descriptive, qualitative context to your analysis — the counterpart to a measure, which holds the numeric values

you aggregate.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-05" number={5} question="How can you create a calculated field in Looker?" difficulty="medium" topic="LookML">
Calculated fields can be created either in LookML or directly in the Explore interface. LookML-based calculations support more advanced logic and are reusable across every Explore built on that model, while Explore-level calculations are quicker but scoped to a single query.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-06" number={6} question="What is a Looker Explore?" difficulty="easy" topic="Explores">
A Looker Explore is the interface that lets users interactively explore and analyze data through a graphical, point-and-click UI, built on top of the relationships and fields defined in LookML.
</QuestionCar

d>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-07" number={7} question="What is the purpose of a Looker dashboard?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dashboards">
A Looker dashboard is a customizable collection of visualizations and reports that gives a consolidated view of key metrics and data insights, typically built from one or more Explores.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-08" number={8} question="What is the purpose of a Looker filter?" difficulty="easy" topic="Explores">
A Looker filter lets users dynamically limit the data shown in a report or visualization based on specific criteria, without needing to rebuild the underlying query by hand.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-09" number={9} question="What is the difference between Looker's Explore and join types?" dif

ficulty="medium" topic="Explores">
An **Explore** defines a specific, queryable view of your data — the starting point and set of fields available to a user. **Join types** determine how the multiple underlying tables referenced by that Explore are combined (e.g., inner, left outer) to produce the consolidated result set.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-10" number={10} question="Can you explain Looker's data modeling best practices?" difficulty="medium" topic="LookML">
- Use views and Explores deliberately — keep views focused on a single table/concept, and Explores focused on a specific analytical use case.
- Create reusable dimensions and measures rather than duplicating logic across models.
- Organize files and folders in LookML clearly, so models stay navigable as

they grow.
- Apply consistent naming conventions across dimensions, measures, and Explores.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-11" number={11} question="How does Looker handle data modeling for complex data structures?" difficulty="medium" topic="LookML">
LookML's flexibility handles complex data structures by letting you explicitly define relationships, joins, and transformations across files — so even deeply nested or multi-table structures can be modeled as a coherent set of Explores.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-12" number={12} question="What are some advantages of using Looker compared to traditional BI tools?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Looker offers a more agile, self-service approach to data analysis — users can explore data an

d build reports without heavy reliance on IT — while LookML provides centralized, powerful modeling capabilities that keep metric definitions consistent across the organization.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-13" number={13} question="What are some limitations of Looker?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Looker is fundamentally built around batch processing, so real-time capability is limited. It also depends entirely on the underlying data infrastructure (a data warehouse or database) rather than storing data itself, which means Looker's performance and scalability are only as good as what it's connected to.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-14" number={14} question="Can Looker be integrated with other BI tools or data visualization platforms?"

difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystem">
Yes. Looker provides APIs and integrations that let it connect to other BI tools, visualization platforms, or custom applications, rather than functioning only as a closed system.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-15" number={15} question="What are some advanced analytical capabilities offered by Looker?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Advanced calculations, flexible data modeling, advanced filtering, derived tables (including PDTs), and support for custom visualizations for cases the built-in chart library doesn't cover.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-fund-16" number={16} question="Can Looker perform predictive analytics or machine learning?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Not natively — Looker

itself doesn't provide built-in predictive analytics or machine learning capabilities. It can, however, integrate with external tools or platforms that do, surfacing their output through Explores and dashboards.
</QuestionCard>

### LookML, PDTs & Development Workflow

<QuestionList topic="Looker LookML & PDTs" storagePrefix="looker-lookml">

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-01" number={17} question="Can you explain the concept of Looker PDTs (Persistent Derived Tables)?" difficulty="medium" topic="PDTs">
PDTs are precomputed tables that Looker builds back into the connected database to improve query performance. They're especially useful for complex or resource-intensive calculations that would otherwise be recomputed on every query.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-02" number={18} question="What is the purpose of Looker's PDT Events feature?" difficulty="medium" topic="PDTs">
PDT Events lets you schedule PDT builds at specific intervals, or trigger a rebuild based on specific events or up

stream data changes, rather than relying purely on a fixed refresh schedule.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-03" number={19} question="What is the purpose of Looker's PDT Performance Optimization features?" difficulty="hard" topic="PDTs">
These features let you manage PDT builds and refresh schedules more efficiently, so PDTs improve query performance without themselves becoming a source of unnecessary database load.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-04" number={20} question="What is the purpose of Looker's Liquid syntax in LookML?" difficulty="hard" topic="LookML">
Liquid syntax is used inside LookML to dynamically generate SQL, or to control the behavior of dimensions, measures, or filters based on conditions or user inputs — effectively templating

logic that would otherwise require duplicating LookML.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-05" number={21} question="What is the purpose of Looker's Development Mode?" difficulty="medium" topic="Administration">
Development Mode lets developers change LookML models without affecting the production environment, giving them a safe space to test changes before deploying them live.

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-06" number={22} question="How can you create a custom visualization in Looker?" difficulty="medium" topic="Visualization">
Looker supports custom visualizations built with custom JavaScript or HTML — you can build your own from scratch or adapt third-party visualization libraries for cases the built-in chart types don't cover.

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-07" number={23} question="What is the purpose of Looker's SQL Runner?" difficulty="medium" topic="SQL Runner">
SQL Runner provides a SQL interface directly inside Looker, letting users write and execute custom SQL queries against connected data sources without going through LookML or an Explore.

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-08" number={24} question={"What is the purpose of Looker's \"Always Use SQL Runner\" option?"} difficulty="medium" topic="SQL Runner">
This option lets users bypass LookML entirely and directly write/execute custom SQL through the SQL Runner interface — useful for ad-hoc investigation, at the cost of losing LookML's reusable modeling layer for that query.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-09" nu

mber={25} question="Can you explain Looker's dynamic time frame filters?" difficulty="medium" topic="Explores">
Dynamic time frame filters let users select relative, time-based periods — such as "last month" or "last year" — that are evaluated dynamically based on the current date, rather than a fixed date range.

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-10" number={26} question="How does Looker handle data versioning and change management for LookML models?" difficulty="medium" topic="Version Control">
Looker integrates with Git (or other version control systems) so LookML models can be version-controlled like any other codebase. This lets teams track changes, compare versions, revert to a previous version of a model, and manage changes through a standard review process rather

than editing production models directly.

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-11" number={27} question="What is Looker's Explore API used for?" difficulty="medium" topic="API">
The Explore API lets developers programmatically query and retrieve data from Looker Explores, enabling integration with external applications that need Looker-modeled data without going through the UI.

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-12" number={28} question="What is Looker's Explore Embed feature used for?" difficulty="medium" topic="Embedding">
Explore Embed lets developers embed Looker's Explore functionality directly into external applications, giving end users a full data-exploration experience inside a product they're already using rather than a separate Looker login.
</

QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-lookml-13" number={29} question="What are the advantages of using Looker's embedded analytics feature?" difficulty="medium" topic="Embedding">
Embedded analytics lets you embed Looker dashboards and reports directly into external applications, giving users seamless access to data insights inside your own product rather than requiring them to switch to a separate BI tool.

### Performance, Scale & Data Integration

<QuestionList topic="Looker Performance & Integration" storagePrefix="looker-perf">

<QuestionCard id="looker-perf-01" number={30} question="How does Looker handle data caching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
Looker intelligently caches query results to improve performance, and the caching strategy can be customized based on how frequently and how much the underlying data actually changes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="looker-perf-02" number={31} question="What are some ways to optimize Looker performance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
- Optimize the underlying SQL queries that LookML generates
- Use caching effectively rather than hitting the warehouse on every request
- Use PDTs strategically for expensive

or frequently reused calculations
- Reduce the number of queries a dashboard actually issues
- Organize LookML models efficiently, and tune the underlying database's own performance

## Superset: Open-Source BI & Visualization

**Apache Superset is an open-source, Python-built BI platform that pairs a SQL-first exploration workflow (SQL Lab) with a drag-and-drop dashboard builder, connecting to almost any SQLAlchemy-compatible database without licensing cost.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Superset is built on Python and Flask, and stores its own **metadata** (dashboards, charts, connections, users) in a metadata database that's separate from the databases it queries. Every visualization starts as a **slice** — a single chart tied to a dataset — and slices are composed into **dashboards**. Two workflows feed slices: the drag-and-drop **Explore** view for point-and-click chart building, and **SQL Lab**, a full SQL IDE for ad-hoc querying, complete with query history and a saved-query workflow. Because Superset connects via SQLAlchemy, it can talk to most relational databases and several NoSQL/OLAP engines with SQL-like interfaces — including **Druid**, historically the go-to backend for fast, real-time-ish analytics on top of Superset. Security is role-base

d (RBAC), extendable to **row-level security** for restricting which rows a given user's queries can return. As with most BI tools, performance is largely inherited from the underlying database, with Superset's own caching layer sitting on top to avoid re-running identical queries.

<QuestionCard id="superset-perf-01" number={49} question="What are some ways to optimize query performance in Superset?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">

<QuestionCard id="superset-perf-03" number={51} question="What is Superset's data caching mechanism?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">

<QuestionCard id="superset-perf-04" number={52} question="What is Superset's approach to data caching and cache invalidation?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">

ormance to identify and resolve bottlenecks.

## Tableau: Enterprise BI & Visualization

**Tableau is a drag-and-drop business intelligence platform built around fast, associative in-memory querying — the interview bar is less about syntax and more about knowing when to use a calculated field vs. an LOD expression, a join vs. a blend, and a live connection vs. an extract.**

## Key Concepts

Tableau organizes every data source into **measures** (numeric values to aggregate) and **dimensions** (qualitative attributes to slice by), and every field as **continuous** (plotted on an axis) or **discrete** (plotted as a header). Getting data in happens two ways: a **live connection** queries the source directly for up-to-date results, while an **extract** snapshots the data into Tableau's own fast columnar engine (`.hyper`/`.tde`) for speed and offline use. Combining multiple tables is either a **join** (same data source) or a **blend** (across data sources, via a common field). On top of that foundation sit three tiers of calculation — basic calculated fields, **Level of Detail (LOD)** expressions for granularity that doesn't match the view, and **table calculatio

ns** that operate only on what's already rendered — plus **sets**, **groups**, and **parameters** for reshaping how data is filtered and categorized. Interviewers use these building blocks to probe whether you understand *why* a number in a viz looks wrong, not just how to build the viz.

<QuestionCard id="tableau-fund-01" number={1} question="What is data visualization in Tableau?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">

hardware-driven architecture limitations; Tableau has no such dependency.

<QuestionCard id="tableau-fund-03" number={3} question="What are the different Tableau products?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">

Server** — shares dashboards published from Desktop across an organization. An enterprise feature installed on Windows or Linux.

<QuestionCard id="tableau-fund-04" number={4} question="What are shelves in Tableau?" difficulty="easy" topic="Workspace">

tionCard>
