## How do I try Impala out?
To look at the core features and functionality on Impala, the easiest way to try out Impala is to download the Cloudera QuickStart VM and start the Impala service through Cloudera Manager, then use impala-shell in a terminal window or the Impala Query UI in the Hue web interface.
To do performance testing and try out the management features for Impala on a cluster, you need to move beyond the QuickStart VM with its virtualized single-node environment. Ideally, download the Cloudera Manager software to set up the cluster, then install the Impala software through Cloudera Manager.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Does Cloudera offer a Vm for demonstrating Impala?
Cloudera offers a demonstration VM called the QuickStart VM, available in VMWare, VirtualBox, and KVM formats. For more information, see the Cloudera QuickStart VM. After booting the QuickStart VM, many services are turned off by default; in the Cloudera Manager UI that appears automatically, turn on Impala and any other components that you want to try out.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How much Memory is required?
Although Impala is not an in-memory database, when dealing with large tables and large result sets, you should expect to dedicate a substantial portion of physical memory for the impalad daemon. Recommended physical memory for an Impala node is 128 GB or higher. If practical, devote approximately 80% of physical memory to Impala.
The amount of memory required for an Impala operation depends on several factors:
The file format of the table. Different file formats represent the same data in more or fewer data files. The compression and encoding for each file format might require a different amount of temporary memory to decompress the data for analysis.
Whether the operation is a SELECT or an INSERT. For example, Parquet tables require relatively little me

title: Apache Impala
content:
mory to query, because Impala reads and decompresses data in 8 MB chunks. Inserting into a Parquet table is a more memory-intensive operation because the data for each data file (potentially hundreds of megabytes, depending on the value of the PARQUET_FILE_SIZE query option) is stored in memory until encoded, compressed, and written to disk.
Whether the table is partitioned or not, and whether a query against a partitioned table can take advantage of partition pruning.
Whether the final result set is sorted by the ORDER BY clause. Each Impala node scans and filters a portion of the total data, and applies the LIMIT to its own portion of the result set. In Impala 1.4.0 and higher, if the sort operation requires more memory than is available on any particular host, Impala uses a temporary

title: Apache Impala
content:
disk work area to perform the sort. The intermediate result sets are all sent back to the coordinator node, which does the final sorting and then applies the LIMIT clause to the final result set.
For example, if you execute the query:
select * from giant_table order by some_column limit 1000;
and your cluster has 50 nodes, then each of those 50 nodes will transmit a maximum of 1000 rows back to the coordinator node. The coordinator node needs enough memory to sort (LIMIT * cluster_size) rows, although in the end the final result set is at most LIMIT rows, 1000 in this case.
Likewise, if you execute the query:
select * from giant_table where test_val > 100 order by some_column;
then each node filters out a set of rows matching the WHERE conditions, sorts the results (with no size limi

title: Apache Impala
content:
t), and sends the sorted intermediate rows back to the coordinator node. The coordinator node might need substantial memory to sort the final result set, and so might use a temporary disk work area for that final phase of the query.
Whether the query contains any join clauses, GROUP BY clauses, analytic functions, or DISTINCT operators. These operations all require some in-memory work areas that vary depending on the volume and distribution of data. In Impala 2.0 and later, these kinds of operations utilize temporary disk work areas if memory usage grows too large to handle.
The size of the result set. When intermediate results are being passed around between nodes, the amount of data depends on the number of columns returned by the query. For example, it is more memory-efficient to quer

title: Apache Impala
content:
y only the columns that are actually needed in the result set rather than always issuing SELECT *.
The mechanism by which work is divided for a join query. You use the COMPUTE STATS statement, and query hints in the most difficult cases, to help Impala pick the most efficient execution plan.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What are the main features of Impala?
A large set of SQL statements, including SELECT and INSERT, with joins, Subqueries in Impala SELECT Statements, and Impala Analytic Functions. Highly compatible with HiveQL, and also including some vendor extensions. For more information.
Distributed, high-performance queries.
Using Cloudera Manager, you can deploy and manage your Impala services. Cloudera Manager is the best way to get started with Impala on your cluster.
Using Hue for queries.
Appending and inserting data into tables through the INSERT statement.
ODBC: Impala is certified to run against MicroStrategy and Tableau, with restrictions. For more information, see Configuring Impala to Work with ODBC.
Querying data stored in HDFS and HBase in a single query.
In Impala 2.2.0 and h

title: Apache Impala
content:
igher, querying data stored in the Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3).
Concurrent client requests. Each Impala daemon can handle multiple concurrent client requests. The effects on performance depend on your particular hardware and workload.
Kerberos authentication. For more information.
Partitions. With Impala SQL, you can create partitioned tables with the CREATE TABLE statement, and add and drop partitions with the ALTER TABLE statement. Impala also takes advantage of the partitioning present in Hive tables.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What features from relational databases or hive are not available in Impala?
Querying streaming data.
Deleting individual rows. You delete data in bulk by overwriting an entire table or partition, or by dropping a table.
Indexing (not currently). LZO-compressed text files can be indexed outside of Impala, as described in Using LZO-Compressed Text Files.
Full text search on text fields. The Cloudera Search product is appropriate for this use case.
Custom Hive Serializer/Deserializer classes (SerDes). Impala supports a set of common native file formats that have built-in SerDes in CDH.
Checkpointing within a query. That is, Impala does not save intermediate results to disk during long-running queries. Currently, Impala cancels a running query if any host on which that query is execu

title: Apache Impala
content:
ting fails. When one or more hosts are down, Impala reroutes future queries to only use the available hosts, and Impala detects when the hosts come back up and begins using them again. Because a query can be submitted through any Impala node, there is no single point of failure. In the future, we will consider adding additional work allocation features to Impala, so that a running query would complete even in the presence of host failures.
Encryption of data transmitted between Impala daemons.
Hive indexes.
Non-Hadoop data stores, such as relational databases.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Does Impala support Generic Jdbc?
Impala supports the HiveServer2 JDBC driver.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is Avro supported?
Yes, Avro is supported. Impala has always been able to query Avro tables. You can use the Impala LOAD DATAstatement to load existing Avro data files into a table. Starting with Impala 1.4, you can create Avro tables with Impala. Currently, you still use the INSERT statement in Hive to copy data from another table into an Avro table.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How do I Know how many Impala Nodes are in my cluster?
The Impala statestore keeps track of how many impalad nodes are currently available. You can see this information through the statestore web interface. For example, at the URL http://statestore_host:25010/metrics you might see lines like the following:
+ statestore.live-backends:3
+ statestore.live-backends.list:[host1:22000, host1:26000, host2:22000]
The number of impalad nodes is the number of list items referring to port 22000, in this case two. (Typically, this number is one less than the number reported by the statestore.live-backends line.) If an impalad node became unavailable or came back after an outage, the information reported on this page would change appropriately.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Are results returned as they become available or all at once when a query completes?
Impala streams results whenever they are available, when possible. Certain SQL operations (aggregation or ORDER BY) require all of the input to be ready before Impala can return results.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Why does my select statement fail?
When a SELECT statement fails, the cause usually falls into one of the following categories:
A timeout because of a performance, capacity, or network issue affecting one particular node.
Excessive memory use for a join query, resulting in automatic cancellation of the query.
A low-level issue affecting how native code is generated on each node to handle particular WHERE clauses in the query. For example, a machine instruction could be generated that is not supported by the processor of a certain node. If the error message in the log suggests the cause was an illegal instruction, consider turning off native code generation temporarily, and trying the query again.
Malformed input data, such as a text data file with an enormously long line, or with a

title: Apache Impala
content:
delimiter that does not match the character specified in the FIELDS TERMINATED BY clause of the CREATE TABLE statement.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Why does my insert statement fail?
When an INSERT statement fails, it is usually the result of exceeding some limit within a Hadoop component, typically HDFS.

An INSERT into a partitioned table can be a strenuous operation due to the possibility of opening many files and associated threads simultaneously in HDFS. Impala 1.1.1 includes some improvements to distribute the work more efficiently, so that the values for each partition are written by a single node, rather than as a separate data file from each node.
Certain expressions in the SELECT part of the INSERT statement can complicate the execution planning and result in an inefficient INSERT operation. Try to make the column data types of the source and destination tables match up, for example by doing ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE CO

title: Apache Impala
content:
LUMNS on the source table if necessary. Try to avoid CASE expressions in the SELECT portion, because they make the result values harder to predict than transferring a column unchanged or passing the column through a built-in function.
Be prepared to raise some limits in the HDFS configuration settings, either temporarily during the INSERTor permanently if you frequently run such INSERT statements as part of your ETL pipeline.
The resource usage of an INSERT statement can vary depending on the file format of the destination table. Inserting into a Parquet table is memory-intensive, because the data for each partition is buffered in memory until it reaches 1 gigabyte, at which point the data file is written to disk. Impala can distribute the work for an INSERT more efficiently when statist

title: Apache Impala
content:
ics are available for the source table that is queried during the INSERT statement.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Does Impala performance improve as it is deployed to more hosts in a cluster in much the same way that Hadoop performance does?
Yes. Impala scales with the number of hosts. It is important to install Impala on all the DataNodes in the cluster, because otherwise some nodes must do remote reads to retrieve data not available for local reads. Data locality is an important architectural aspect for Impala performance.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is the Hdfs Block Size reduced to achieve faster query results?
No. Impala does not make any changes to the HDFS or HBase data sets.
The default Parquet block size is relatively large (256 MB in Impala 2.0 and later; 1 GB in earlier releases). You can control the block size when creating Parquet files using the PARQUET_FILE_SIZE query option.

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Does Impala use caching?
Impala does not cache table data. It does cache some table and file metadata. Although queries might run faster on subsequent iterations because the data set was cached in the OS buffer cache, Impala does not explicitly control this.
Impala takes advantage of the HDFS caching feature in CDH 5. You can designate which tables or partitions are cached through the CACHED and UNCACHED clauses of the CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE statements. Impala can also take advantage of data that is pinned in the HDFS cache through the hdfscacheadmin command.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What are the good use cases for Impala as opposed to Hive or Mapreduce?
Impala is well-suited to executing SQL queries for interactive exploratory analytics on large data sets. Hive and MapReduce are appropriate for very long running, batch-oriented tasks such as ETL.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is Mapreduce required for impala and will Impala continue to work as expected if Mapreduce is stopped?
Impala does not use MapReduce at all.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Can Impala be used for complex event processing?
For example, in an industrial environment, many agents may generate large amounts of data. Can Impala be used to analyze this data, checking for notable changes in the environment?
Complex Event Processing (CEP) is usually performed by dedicated stream-processing systems. Impala is not a stream-processing system, as it most closely resembles a relational database.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is Impala intended to handle Real Time Queries in Low latency Applications or is it for ad Hoc Queries for the purpose of data exploration?
Ad-hoc queries are the primary use case for Impala. We anticipate it being used in many other situations where low-latency is required. Whether Impala is appropriate for any particular use-case depends on the workload, data size and query volume.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How does Impala compare to Hive and Pig?
Impala is different from Hive and Pig because it uses its own daemons that are spread across the cluster for queries. Because Impala does not rely on MapReduce, it avoids the startup overhead of MapReduce jobs, allowing Impala to return results in real time.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Can I do transforms or add New functionality?
Impala adds support for UDFs in Impala 1.2. You can write your own functions in C++, or reuse existing Java-based Hive UDFs. The UDF support includes scalar functions and user-defined aggregate functions (UDAs). User-defined table functions (UDTFs) are not currently supported.
Impala does not currently support an extensible serialization-deserialization framework (SerDes), and so adding extra functionality to Impala is not as straightforward as for Hive or Pig.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Can any Impala Query also be executed in Hive?
Yes. There are some minor differences in how some queries are handled, but Impala queries can also be completed in Hive. Impala SQL is a subset of HiveQL, with some functional limitations such as transforms.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Can I use Impala to Query data already loaded into Hive and Hbase?
There are no additional steps to allow Impala to query tables managed by Hive, whether they are stored in HDFS or HBase. Make sure that Impala is configured to access the Hive metastore correctly and you should be ready to go. Keep in mind that impalad, by default, runs as the impala user, so you might need to adjust some file permissions depending on how strict your permissions are currently.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is Hive an Impala requirement?
The Hive metastore service is a requirement. Impala shares the same metastore database as Hive, allowing Impala and Hive to access the same tables transparently.
Hive itself is optional, and does not need to be installed on the same nodes as Impala. Currently, Impala supports a wider variety of read (query) operations than write (insert) operations; you use Hive to insert data into tables that use certain file formats.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is Impala production ready?
Impala has finished its beta release cycle, and the 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2 GA releases are production ready. The 1.1.x series includes additional security features for authorization, an important requirement for production use in many organizations. The 1.2.x series includes important performance features, particularly for large join queries. Some Cloudera customers are already using Impala for large workloads.

The Impala 1.3.0 and higher releases are bundled with corresponding levels of CDH 5. The number of new features grows with each release.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How do I configure Hadoop High Availability for Impala?
You can set up a proxy server to relay requests back and forth to the Impala servers, for load balancing and high availability.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What happens if there is an Error in Impala?
There is not a single point of failure in Impala. All Impala daemons are fully able to handle incoming queries. If a machine fails however, all queries with fragments running on that machine will fail. Because queries are expected to return quickly, you can just rerun the query if there is a failure.
The longer answer: Impala must be able to connect to the Hive metastore. Impala aggressively caches metadata so the metastore host should have minimal load. Impala relies on the HDFS NameNode, and, in CDH4, you can configure HA for HDFS. Impala also has centralized services, known as the statestore andcatalog services, that run on one host only. Impala continues to execute queries if the statestore host is down, but it will not get state update

title: Apache Impala
content:
s. For example, if a host is added to the cluster while the statestore host is down, the existing instances of impalad running on the other hosts will not find out about this new host. Once the statestore process is restarted, all the information it serves is automatically reconstructed from all running Impala daemons.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What is the Maximum number of Rows in a Table?
There is no defined maximum. Some customers have used Impala to query a table with over a trillion rows.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## On which hosts does Impala run?
Cloudera strongly recommends running the impalad daemon on each DataNode for good performance. Although this topology is not a hard requirement, if there are data blocks with no Impala daemons running on any of the hosts containing replicas of those blocks, queries involving that data could be very inefficient. In that case, the data must be transmitted from one host to another for processing by "remote reads", a condition Impala normally tries to avoid.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How are Joins performed in Impala?
By default, Impala automatically determines the most efficient order in which to join tables using a cost-based method, based on their overall size and number of rows. (This is a new feature in Impala 1.2.2 and higher.) The COMPUTE STATS statement gathers information about each table that is crucial for efficient join performance. Impala chooses between two techniques for join queries, known as "broadcast joins" and "partitioned joins".

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How does Impala process Join Queries for large tables?
Impala utilizes multiple strategies to allow joins between tables and result sets of various sizes. When joining a large table with a small one, the data from the small table is transmitted to each node for intermediate processing. When joining two large tables, the data from one of the tables is divided into pieces, and each node processes only selected pieces.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What is Impala's aggregation strategy?
Impala currently only supports in-memory hash aggregation. In Impala 2.0 and higher, if the memory requirements for a join or aggregation operation exceed the memory limit for a particular host, Impala uses a temporary work area on disk to help the query complete successfully.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How is Impala Metadata managed?
Impala uses two pieces of metadata: the catalog information from the Hive metastore and the file metadata from the NameNode. Currently, this metadata is lazily populated and cached when an impalad needs it to plan a query.
The REFRESH statement updates the metadata for a particular table after loading new data through Hive. The INVALIDATE METADATA Statement statement refreshes all metadata, so that Impala recognizes new tables or other DDL and DML changes performed through Hive.
In Impala 1.2 and higher, a dedicated catalogd daemon broadcasts metadata changes due to Impala DDL or DML statements to all nodes, reducing or eliminating the need to use the REFRESH and INVALIDATE METADATAstatements.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What load do concurrent queries produce on the Name Node?
The load Impala generates is very similar to MapReduce. Impala contacts the NameNode during the planning phase to get the file metadata (this is only run on the host the query was sent to). Every impaladwill read files as part of normal processing of the query.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## How does Impala achieve its performance improvements?
These are the main factors in the performance of Impala versus that of other Hadoop components and related technologies.
Impala avoids MapReduce. While MapReduce is a great general parallel processing model with many benefits, it is not designed to execute SQL. Impala avoids the inefficiencies of MapReduce in these ways:
Impala does not materialize intermediate results to disk. SQL queries often map to multiple MapReduce jobs with all intermediate data sets written to disk.
Impala avoids MapReduce start-up time. For interactive queries, the MapReduce start-up time becomes very noticeable. Impala runs as a service and essentially has no start-up time.
Impala can more naturally disperse query plans instead of having to fit them in

title: Apache Impala
content:
to a pipeline of map and reduce jobs. This enables Impala to parallelize multiple stages of a query and avoid overheads such as sort and shuffle when unnecessary.
Impala uses a more efficient execution engine by taking advantage of modern hardware and technologies:
+ Impala generates runtime code. Impala uses LLVM to generate assembly code for the query that is being run. Individual queries do not have to pay the overhead of running on a system that needs to be able to execute arbitrary queries.
+ Impala uses available hardware instructions when possible. Impala uses the supplemental SSE3 (SSSE3) instructions which can offer tremendous speedups in some cases. (Impala 2.0 and 2.1 required the SSE4.1 instruction set; Impala 2.2 and higher relax the restriction again so only SSSE3 is requi

title: Apache Impala
content:
red.)
+ Impala uses better I/O scheduling. Impala is aware of the disk location of blocks and is able to schedule the order to process blocks to keep all disks busy.
+ Impala is designed for performance. A lot of time has been spent in designing Impala with sound performance-oriented fundamentals, such as tight inner loops, inlined function calls, minimal branching, better use of cache, and minimal memory usage.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What happens when the data set exceeds available memory?
Currently, if the memory required to process intermediate results on a node exceeds the amount available to Impala on that node, the query is cancelled. You can adjust the memory available to Impala on each node, and you can fine-tune the join strategy to reduce the memory required for the biggest queries. We do plan on supporting external joins and sorting in the future.
Keep in mind though that the memory usage is not directly based on the input data set size. For aggregations, the memory usage is the number of rows after grouping. For joins, the memory usage is the combined size of the tables excluding the biggest table, and Impala can use join strategies that divide up large joined tables among the various nodes rather than

title: Apache Impala
content:
transmitting the entire table to each node.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What are the most Memory intensive operations?
If a query fails with an error indicating "memory limit exceeded", you might suspect a memory leak. The problem could actually be a query that is structured in a way that causes Impala to allocate more memory than you expect, exceeded the memory allocated for Impala on a particular node. Some examples of query or table structures that are especially memory-intensive are:
INSERT statements using dynamic partitioning, into a table with many different partitions. (Particularly for tables using Parquet format, where the data for each partition is held in memory until it reaches the full block size in size before it is written to disk.) Consider breaking up such operations into several different INSERT statements, for example to load data one

title: Apache Impala
content:
year at a time rather than for all years at once.
GROUP BY on a unique or high-cardinality column. Impala allocates some handler structures for each different value in a GROUP BY query. Having millions of different GROUP BY values could exceed the memory limit.
Queries involving very wide tables, with thousands of columns, particularly with many STRING columns. Because Impala allows a STRING value to be up to 32 KB, the intermediate results during such queries could require substantial memory allocation.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## When does Impala hold on to or return memory?
Impala allocates memory using tcmalloc, a memory allocator that is optimized for high concurrency. Once Impala allocates memory, it keeps that memory reserved to use for future queries. Thus, it is normal for Impala to show high memory usage when idle. If Impala detects that it is about to exceed its memory limit (defined by the -mem_limit startup option or the MEM_LIMIT query option), it deallocates memory not needed by the current queries.
When issuing queries through the JDBC or ODBC interfaces, make sure to call the appropriate close method afterwards. Otherwise, some memory associated with the query is not freed.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Is there an update statement?
Impala does not currently have an UPDATE statement, which would typically be used to change a single row, a small group of rows, or a specific column. The HDFS-based files used by typical Impala queries are optimized for bulk operations across many megabytes of data at a time, making traditional UPDATEoperations inefficient or impractical.
You can use the following techniques to achieve the same goals as the familiar UPDATE statement, in a way that preserves efficient file layouts for subsequent queries:
Replace the entire contents of a table or partition with updated data that you have already staged in a different location, either using INSERT OVERWRITE, LOAD DATA, or manual HDFS file operations followed by a REFRESH statement for the table. Optionally

title: Apache Impala
content:
, you can use built-in functions and expressions in the INSERTstatement to transform the copied data in the same way you would normally do in an UPDATE statement, for example to turn a mixed-case string into all uppercase or all lowercase.
To update a single row, use an HBase table, and issue an INSERT ... VALUES statement using the same key as the original row. Because HBase handles duplicate keys by only returning the latest row with a particular key value, the newly inserted row effectively hides the previous one.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Can Impala do User defined functions?
Impala 1.2 and higher does support UDFs and UDAs. You can either write native Impala UDFs and UDAs in C++, or reuse UDFs (but not UDAs) originally written in Java for use with Hive.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Why do I have to use refresh and invalidate Metadata and what do they do?
In Impala 1.2 and higher, there is much less need to use the REFRESH and INVALIDATE METADATA statements:
The new impala-catalog service, represented by the catalogd daemon, broadcasts the results of Impala DDL statements to all Impala nodes. Thus, if you do a CREATE TABLE statement in Impala while connected to one node, you do not need to do INVALIDATE METADATA before issuing queries through a different node.
The catalog service only recognizes changes made through Impala, so you must still issue a REFRESH statement if you load data through Hive or by manipulating files in HDFS, and you must issue an INVALIDATE METADATA statement if you create a table, alter a table, add or drop partitions, or do other DDL stat

title: Apache Impala
content:
ements in Hive.
Because the catalog service broadcasts the results of REFRESH and INVALIDATE METADATA statements to all nodes, in the cases where you do still need to issue those statements, you can do that on a single node rather than on every node, and the changes will be automatically recognized across the cluster, making it more convenient to load balance by issuing queries through arbitrary Impala nodes rather than always using the same coordinator node.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Why is space not freed up when I issue drop table?
Impala deletes data files when you issue a DROP TABLE on an internal table, but not an external one. By default, the CREATE TABLE statement creates internal tables, where the files are managed by Impala. An external table is created with a CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement, where the files reside in a location outside the control of Impala. Issue a DESCRIBE FORMATTED statement to check whether a table is internal or external. The keyword MANAGED_TABLE indicates an internal table, from which Impala can delete the data files. The keyword EXTERNAL_TABLE indicates an external table, where Impala will leave the data files untouched when you drop the table.
Even when you drop an internal table and the files are removed from their original loc

title: Apache Impala
content:
ation, you might not get the hard drive space back immediately. By default, files that are deleted in HDFS go into a special trashcan directory, from which they are purged after a period of time (by default, 6 hours). For background information on the trashcan mechanism.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
Apache Impala
content:
## How do I load a big Csv file into a partitioned table?
To load a data file into a partitioned table, when the data file includes fields like year, month, and so on that correspond to the partition key columns, use a two-stage process. First, use the LOAD DATA or CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement to bring the data into an unpartitioned text table. Then use an INSERT ... SELECT statement to copy the data from the unpartitioned table to a partitioned one. Include a PARTITION clause in the INSERTstatement to specify the partition key columns.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## Can I Do Insert Select Into a partitioned table?
When you use the INSERT ... SELECT * syntax to copy data into a partitioned table, the columns corresponding to the partition key columns must appear last in the columns returned by the SELECT *. You can create the table with the partition key columns defined last. Or, you can use the CREATE VIEW statement to create a view that reorders the columns: put the partition key columns last, then do the INSERT ... SELECT * from the view.

[Table of Contents](#apache-impala)

title: Apache Impala
content:
## What kinds of Impala Queries or data are best suited for Hbase?
HBase tables are ideal for queries where normally you would use a key-value store. That is, where you retrieve a single row or a few rows, by testing a special unique key column using the = or IN operators.
HBase tables are not suitable for queries that produce large result sets with thousands of rows. HBase tables are also not suitable for queries that perform full table scans because the WHERE clause does not request specific values from the unique key column.
Use HBase tables for data that is inserted one row or a few rows at a time, such as by the INSERT ... VALUESsyntax. Loading data piecemeal like this into an HDFS-backed table produces many tiny files, which is a very inefficient layout for HDFS data files.
If th

title: Apache Impala
content:
e lack of an UPDATE statement in Impala is a problem for you, you can simulate single-row updates by doing an INSERT ... VALUES statement using an existing value for the key column. The old row value is hidden; only the new row value is seen by queries.
HBase tables are often wide (containing many columns) and sparse (with most column values NULL). For example, you might record hundreds of different data points for each user of an online service, such as whether the user had registered for an online game or enabled particular account features. With Impala and HBase, you could look up all the information for a specific customer efficiently in a single query. For any given customer, most of these columns might be NULL, because a typical customer might not make use of most features of an onl

title: Apache Impala
content: ine service.

title: Data Warehouses
content:
---
title: Data Warehouses
description: Data warehouse platforms and analytics engines (BigQuery, Redshift, Impala, Greenplum)
---

title: Data Warehouses
content:
# Data Warehouses

This section covers data warehouse platforms and analytical query engines designed for OLAP workloads.

title: Data Warehouses
content:
## Data Warehouse Technologies

- **Snowflake**: Cloud-native, fully-managed data warehouse with elastic scalability and data sharing
- **Databricks**: Unified analytics platform combining data warehousing, engineering, and ML on Apache Spark
- **BigQuery**: Google's serverless, fully-managed data warehouse
- **Redshift**: AWS's columnar data warehouse
- **Impala**: In-memory SQL query engine for Hadoop
- **Greenplum**: Distributed SQL database optimized for analytics

These platforms are designed for analytical queries over large datasets, OLAP operations, and business intelligence use cases. Modern platforms like Snowflake and Databricks offer cloud-native architectures with advanced features like data sharing, lakehouse capabilities, and serverless operations.

## Redshift: AWS's Cluster-Based Cloud Data Warehouse

**Amazon Redshift is AWS's cluster-based, columnar data warehouse — its interview questions center on how distribution and sort keys shape data movement and query performance, alongside deep integration with the rest of the AWS ecosystem.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Redshift runs as an MPP (massively parallel processing) **cluster**: a **leader node** plans and coordinates queries while **compute nodes**, split into **slices**, store data and execute work in parallel. Two settings drive most performance conversations: the **distribution style/key**, which controls how rows are spread across slices (minimizing data movement during joins), and the **sort key**, which controls on-disk row order within each node (enabling range-restricted scans via zone maps). Data typically enters through the **COPY** command, which loads in parallel from S3 (or DynamoDB/EMR/JDBC), and leaves through **UNLOAD**; both have many tuning options (manifest files, compression, error handling). **VACUUM** reclaims space and re-sorts rows after deletes, while

**ANALYZE** refreshes the statistics the query optimizer relies on. **Redshift Spectrum** extends queries directly onto data sitting in S3 without loading it, and **WLM (Workload Management)** governs concurrency and resource allocation across query queues. Redshift is built for OLAP, not OLTP — updates/deletes work but aren't its strength, and durability comes from automated snapshots to S3.

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A query against a large fact table has gotten slow — how do you approach it?"** Read the `EXPLAIN` plan for redistribution versus broadcast in joins, check whether the sort and distribution keys still match the query pattern, and confirm statistics are fresh (`ANALYZE`) and dead rows are reclaimed (`VACUUM`).
- **"Design a distribution and sort key strategy for a star schema fact table."** Distribute on the key most frequently joined against a large dimension (or use `ALL` for small dimensions), sort on the most common range filter such as a date column, and discuss the skew-versus-join-locality trade-off.

r fault tolerance, staging-table-plus-atomic-swap patterns, and compression encoding.

## Snowflake: Cloud Data Warehouse Architecture

**Snowflake is a cloud-native data warehouse whose defining trait is the separation of storage, compute, and services into independently scalable layers — the source of most of its performance, concurrency, and cost-management interview questions.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Snowflake's architecture splits into three layers: **cloud storage** (columnar data on S3/Blob/GCS), **compute** (elastic virtual warehouses that read that data), and **services** (SQL compilation, metadata, and access control). Because compute and storage scale independently, multiple warehouses can query the same data concurrently without contention — the basis for Snowflake's "unlimited concurrency" claims. Performance features build on this split: **result caching** and **metadata caching** avoid recomputation entirely, while **clustering keys** control the physical layout of micro-partitions so filtered queries scan less data. Operationally, **auto-suspend/auto-scaling** control cost, and **time travel**, **fail-safe**, and **zero-copy cloning** provide low-cost rec

overy and environment duplication because they operate on metadata pointers rather than copying data. Security follows a standard **RBAC** model (roles → privileges → objects) layered with encryption at rest/in transit, dynamic data masking, and row/column-level access policies.

### Performance & Optimization

<QuestionList topic="Snowflake Performance" storagePrefix="snowflake-performance">

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-01" number={19} question="What is query performance monitoring in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
Query performance monitoring involves analyzing query statistics, execution plans, and metrics through the Query Profile and web UI (or `QUERY_HISTORY`/`ACCOUNT_USAGE` views), letting you see where time was spent — scanning, joining, spilling to disk, or waiting in a queue.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-02" number={20} question="How do you optimize Snowflake queries?" difficulty="medium" topic="Optimization">
Optimization techniques include using clustering keys on large, frequently filtered tables, materiali

zed views for expensive repeated aggregations, relying on query result caching for identical repeated queries, and right-sizing warehouses so queries aren't starved for compute or spilling to local/remote disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-03" number={21} question="What are clustering keys in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Clustering">
Clustering keys define the sort order and physical layout of data across a table's micro-partitions, improving query performance for filtered queries. They're most useful on very large tables where the natural insertion order doesn't align with common filter columns.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-04" number={22} question="What is the purpose of clustering in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Clustering">
Cl

ustering optimizes data layout for faster filtering and scanning, reducing the amount of data read during query execution through better "pruning" — Snowflake can skip entire micro-partitions that fall outside a query's filter range instead of scanning them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-05" number={23} question="What is Snowflake result caching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">
Result caching stores query results, returning cached results instantly for identical queries executed within a time window (up to 24 hours), without re-running any compute — provided the underlying data hasn't changed and the query text matches exactly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-06" number={24} question="What are the benefits of result caching?" difficulty="easy" topic

="Caching">
Benefits include faster query response times, reduced computation costs (no warehouse credits consumed for a cache hit), and improved user experience for dashboards or reports that re-run the same queries repeatedly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-07" number={25} question="What is query caching in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Caching">
"Query caching" is often used as an umbrella term combining result caching, metadata caching, and local disk (warehouse) caching — together these layers accelerate repeated or related query execution at different levels of the stack.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-08" number={26} question="How does Snowflake handle metadata?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metadata">
Snowflake maintains metadata in the s

ervices layer, tracking table structure, micro-partition statistics (min/max values, row counts), and data distribution — this metadata is what the query optimizer uses to prune partitions and generate execution plans without scanning the raw data first.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-perf-09" number={27} question="What is Snowflake metadata caching?" difficulty="medium" topic="Metadata">
Metadata caching stores information about table structure and statistics in the services layer, enabling faster query planning and optimization — some simple queries (like `COUNT(*)` on an unfiltered table) can even be answered from metadata alone, without touching a warehouse.

<QuestionList topic="Snowflake Security" storagePrefix="snowflake-security">

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-01" number={28} question="How do you implement security in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Security is implemented through authentication (password, SSO, key-pair, MFA), authorization (RBAC), encryption (at rest and in transit), network policies (IP allow-listing), and audit logging via `ACCOUNT_USAGE` and `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` views.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-02" number={29} question="What is role-based access control in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="RBAC">
RBAC controls user access to databases, schemas, tables, and views through roles with specific privileges. Users are assigned roles, roles are grant

ed privileges on objects, and roles can be layered hierarchically so higher-level roles inherit privileges from lower ones.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-03" number={30} question="What are Snowflake roles?" difficulty="easy" topic="RBAC">
Roles are collections of privileges that can be assigned to users, controlling what actions users can perform on which objects. Snowflake ships with system-defined roles (like `ACCOUNTADMIN`, `SYSADMIN`, `SECURITYADMIN`) and supports custom roles for finer-grained access.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-04" number={31} question="What is the principle of least privilege in Snowflake?" difficulty="easy" topic="RBAC">
This principle grants users only the minimum necessary permissions to perform their job functions, enhancing

security by limiting the blast radius of a compromised account or a mistaken query.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-05" number={32} question="How do you encrypt data in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Encryption">
Snowflake provides encryption at rest using AES-256 and encryption in transit using TLS 1.2, applied automatically to all data — there's no opt-out, and no additional configuration is required for baseline encryption.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-06" number={33} question="What is tri-secret encryption?" difficulty="hard" topic="Encryption">
Tri-secret encryption combines Snowflake's platform-managed key, a customer-managed key held in the customer's own key management service, and Snowflake's service key. Because the customer-managed key

is one of the required inputs, revoking it immediately renders the data unreadable — giving customers an independent kill switch over their own data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-07" number={34} question="What are the differences between column and row-level security?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Column-level security restricts access to specific columns (typically via masking policies), while row-level security restricts access to specific rows based on conditions (via row access policies) — for example, letting each sales rep see only rows for their own region.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-08" number={35} question="What is dynamic data masking?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Dynamic data masking automatically masks sensitive data b

ased on the querying user's role, displaying masked values (e.g., a redacted SSN) without modifying the underlying stored data — the same column returns different values to different roles.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-09" number={36} question="How do you handle compliance and auditing in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Compliance">
Compliance is managed through query history, access history, and account usage data, and integration with security information and event management (SIEM) systems — Snowflake also holds certifications (SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, etc.) that support regulated workloads.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-10" number={37} question="What are Snowflake data shares?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Sharing">
Snowflake Secure Data Sha

ring enables secure, real-time data sharing with other Snowflake accounts without copying or moving data — the consumer queries a live share of the provider's data directly, governed by the provider's grants.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-11" number={38} question="What are the benefits of data sharing?" difficulty="easy" topic="Data Sharing">
Benefits include real-time access to shared data (no batch export/import lag), reduced data movement and duplication, improved cross-organization collaboration, and simplified governance since the provider controls access centrally.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-12" number={39} question="How does Snowflake handle zero-copy cloning?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Sharing">
Zero-copy cloning creates instant table, sch

ema, or database clones that share the original object's underlying micro-partitions until modifications occur (copy-on-write), which reduces storage costs and makes cloning production data for dev/test environments essentially free at creation time.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-13" number={40} question="What is time travel in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Recovery">
Time travel allows querying and restoring data from any point in the past (a configurable retention period, up to 90 days on Enterprise edition, 1 day by default) using historical versions of a table — useful for undoing accidental updates/deletes or auditing past state.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="snow-sec-14" number={41} question="What is fail-safe in Snowflake?" difficulty="medium"

topic="Data Recovery">
Fail-safe provides a non-configurable 7-day recovery window *after* time travel expires, ensuring protection against accidental or malicious data deletion. Unlike time travel, fail-safe recovery requires contacting Snowflake support — it's a last-resort safety net, not a self-service feature.
</QuestionCard>

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A dashboard query that used to run in seconds now takes minutes — how do you diagnose it?"** Walk through Query Profile to see where time is spent, check whether the table has grown enough that a clustering key would help pruning, confirm the warehouse isn't undersized or queuing, and rule out whether result caching stopped applying because the query text or underlying data changed.
- **"Design a cost-control strategy for a Snowflake account with many ad-hoc analysts."** Cover warehouse-per-team isolation, aggressive auto-suspend, resource monitors/budgets, and steering analysts toward smaller warehouses with auto-scaling for burst concurrency instead of one large always-on warehouse.
- **"How would you share a filtered, PII-free view of a table with

an external partner?"** Discuss building a secure view with masking/row-access policies applied, then exposing that view (not the base table) through a Secure Data Share.
- **"Someone accidentally dropped a table three days ago — how do you get it back?"** Explain `UNDROP TABLE` via time travel if within the retention window, versus needing to engage Snowflake support for fail-safe recovery if the time travel window has already passed.

## Bigtable: Google's Wide-Column NoSQL Database

**Google Cloud Bigtable is a fully managed, wide-column NoSQL database built for massive, low-latency workloads — its interview questions center on how row-key design drives performance, since Bigtable provides no secondary indexes, no automatic query optimization, and no joins to fall back on.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Bigtable's data model is a sparse, distributed, **multi-dimensional sorted map**: every cell is addressed by a **row key**, a **column key** (grouped into column families), and a **timestamp** for versioning. Because rows are stored in row-key sort order and Bigtable has **no secondary indexes** and **no automatic query optimization**, the row key is the single most consequential design decision — it determines both read efficiency (range scans work only along the key) and write distribution (poorly chosen keys, especially monotonically increasing ones, create **hotspots**). Architecturally, a table is split into **tablets**, each served by exactly one **tablet server**, with a **master server** handling tablet assignment and load balancing while actual bytes live on **C

olossus**, Google's distributed file system. Writes land in an in-memory **memstore** before flushing to immutable sorted files, and **compaction** periodically merges those files while **Bloom filters** skip unnecessary disk reads. Bigtable offers **no ACID transactions** beyond atomic single-row read-modify-write operations, replicates across clusters with **eventual consistency** and last-writer-wins conflict resolution, and delegates access control to **Cloud IAM**.

## Cassandra: Distributed Wide-Column NoSQL Database

**Apache Cassandra is a masterless, peer-to-peer wide-column database built for write-heavy workloads at massive scale — its interview questions center on how the write path, tunable consistency, and replication strategy trade off availability, consistency, and performance.**

## Table of Contents

- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)

- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

## Key Concepts

Cassandra has no leader or master — every node is a peer in a **ring**, communicating via gossip, which is what removes the single point of failure. Data is organized as **keyspace → column family (table) → row → column**, addressed by a **partition key** (determines which node owns the data) and optional **clustering columns** (order rows within a partition), and queried with **CQL**, a SQL-like language. Writes follow a fixed path: append to the **commit log** (crash recovery), write to the in-memory **memtable**, then periodically flush to an immutable **SSTable** on disk; **compaction** later merges SSTables, and **Bloom filters** avoid unnecessary disk reads. Deletes don't remove data immediately — they write a **tombstone** that's cleared during compaction. Cassand

ra's signature feature is **tunable consistency**: per-query read/write consistency levels (`ONE`, `QUORUM`, `ALL`, `LOCAL_*`) let you trade off latency against the strong-consistency condition `R + W > N`. This makes Cassandra an **AP** system under the CAP theorem — it favors availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency, and it deliberately has no joins or ACID transactions, pushing denormalization-heavy, query-pattern-first modeling onto the schema design.

<QuestionCard id="cass-consist-01" number={29} question="Explain the concept of tunable consistency in Cassandra?" difficulty="hard" topic="Consistency">
Tunable Consistency is a phenomenal characteristic that makes Cassandra a favored database choice of Developers, Analysts and Big data Architects. Consistency refers to the up-to-date and synchronized data rows on all their replicas. Cassandra's Tunable Consistency allows users to select the consistency level best suited for their use cases. It supports two consistencies -Eventual and Consistency and Strong Consistency.
The former guarantees consistency when no new updates are made on a gi

ven data item, all accesses return the last updated value eventually. Systems with eventual consistency are known to have achieved replica convergence.
For Strong consistency, Cassandra supports the following condition:
R + W > N, where
N – Number of replicas
W – Number of nodes that need to agree for a successful write
R – Number of nodes that need to agree for a successful read

<QuestionCard id="cass-consist-02" number={30} question="Explain Cap Theorem?" difficulty="hard" topic="Consistency">

rem states that in distributed systems like Cassandra, users can enjoy only two out of these three characteristics.
One of them needs to be sacrificed. Consistency guarantees the return of most recent write for the client, Availability returns a rational response within minimum time and in Partition Tolerance, the system will continue its operations when network partitions occur. The two options available are AP and CP.

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a Cassandra table for a messaging app's conversation history."** Set the partition key to `conversation_id`, use message timestamp as a clustering column for ordering, denormalize sender/recipient details onto the row, and flag the risk of unbounded partition growth for very long-lived conversations.
- **"Reads are returning stale data across data centers — why?"** Walk through the consistency level in use (e.g. `LOCAL_ONE`), hinted handoff and repair, and the `R + W > N` math needed for strong consistency versus the eventual-consistency trade-off the app may already be accepting.
- **"A single partition has become a write hotspot — how do you fix it?"** Discuss redesigning the partition key for higher cardinality, bucketing a naturally hot ke

y with a synthetic suffix, and why this is a schema-design problem, not an operational one.
- **"Explain the trade-off Cassandra makes on the CAP theorem and why."** Cover why Cassandra is an AP system by default, how tunable consistency lets you dial individual queries toward C when needed, and how that compares to a CP system's guarantees.

## DynamoDB: Managed NoSQL Database

**DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database — its entire design (keys, indexes, capacity, consistency) is built around one constraint: you must know your access patterns before you model your data, not after.**

## Key Concepts

Every DynamoDB table is built around a **primary key** — either a simple partition key, or a composite key combining a **partition key** (which determines physical data distribution via hashing) with a **sort key** (which orders items within a partition and enables range queries). This key design is the single most consequential modeling decision in DynamoDB, because unlike a relational database you can't easily bolt on new access patterns later — you address that with **secondary indexes**: Local Secondary Indexes (alternate sort keys within the same partition) and Global Secondary Indexes (alternate partition/sort keys across the whole table, with their own capacity). Reads come in two flavors, **`Query`** (efficient, targets a specific partition via its key) and **`Sc

an`** (reads every item, inefficient at scale), and in two consistency levels, **eventually consistent** (cheaper, may briefly return stale data) and **strongly consistent** (costs more, always current). Capacity is either **provisioned** (reserved throughput, cost-predictable) or **on-demand** (pay-per-request, better for spiky/unpredictable workloads), and both are vulnerable to **hot partitions** if the partition key doesn't distribute traffic evenly.

### Tables, Keys & Capacity Model

<QuestionList topic="DynamoDB Data Model" storagePrefix="dynamodb-data-model">

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-01" number={1} question="What is DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL database service provided by AWS that handles large-scale, high-performance distributed workloads.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-02" number={2} question="What are the key characteristics of DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Serverless, fully managed, highly scalable, low latency, built-in replication across availability zones, automatic backup, and pay-per-request pricing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-03" number={3} question="What is the difference between DynamoDB

and relational databases?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
DynamoDB is NoSQL — flexible schema, horizontal scaling by design — while relational databases use a fixed schema and traditionally scale vertically. DynamoDB also requires you to design around known access patterns upfront, rather than querying flexibly with joins after the fact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-04" number={4} question="What is a DynamoDB table?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
A DynamoDB table is a collection of items (records) with attributes (columns), identified by a unique primary key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-05" number={5} question="What is a partition key in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
The partition key (hash key) determines which physic

al partition stores an item, based on a hash of the key's value. It's the primary lever for how evenly data and traffic spread across DynamoDB's underlying storage.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-06" number={6} question="What is a sort key in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
The sort key (range key) orders items within a partition, allowing range queries (e.g., "all orders for this customer between two dates") on items that share the same partition key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-07" number={7} question="What is the difference between partition key and sort key?" difficulty="easy" topic="Keys">
The partition key distributes data across partitions; the sort key orders data within a single partition. Together they form a composite key that supp

orts both distribution and rich per-partition querying.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-08" number={8} question="What is a composite key in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Keys">
A composite key combines a partition key and a sort key, enabling efficient queries on both dimensions — items are distributed by partition key, then queryable and orderable by sort key within that partition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-09" number={9} question="What is throughput in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Capacity">
Throughput measures a table's read/write capacity — how many read and write operations per second the table can handle, expressed in read and write capacity units.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-10" number={10} question="What is a r

ead capacity unit in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Capacity">
One RCU (read capacity unit) equals one strongly consistent read per second, or two eventually consistent reads per second, for items up to 4KB. Larger items consume proportionally more RCUs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-11" number={11} question="What is a write capacity unit in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Capacity">
One WCU (write capacity unit) equals one write per second for items up to 1KB. Larger items consume proportionally more WCUs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-12" number={12} question="What is on-demand billing in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Capacity">
A pay-per-request pricing model: you pay for actual reads/writes performed, without provisioning capacity

upfront — well suited to unpredictable or spiky traffic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-13" number={13} question="What is provisioned billing in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Capacity">
You reserve read/write capacity upfront and pay a fixed rate for it. Better for predictable, steady workloads where you can forecast throughput and want lower, stable costs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-14" number={14} question="How do you handle hot partitions in DynamoDB?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
Use better partition key design (higher-cardinality, evenly-distributed keys, possibly with a random or calculated suffix to spread "hot" items), implement DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as an in-memory cache to absorb read pressure, or switch to on-demand bil

ling so the table can adapt to spikes automatically.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-core-15" number={15} question="What is auto scaling in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Capacity">
Auto scaling automatically adjusts provisioned capacity up or down based on actual traffic patterns, within limits you configure — it keeps provisioned mode responsive to changing load without manual intervention.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### Indexes, Queries & Advanced Features

<QuestionList topic="DynamoDB Queries" storagePrefix="dynamodb-queries">

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-01" number={16} question="What are secondary indexes in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexes">
Secondary indexes let you query on non-key attributes, providing flexible access patterns beyond what the table's primary key alone supports — DynamoDB offers two kinds: Local Secondary Indexes and Global Secondary Indexes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-02" number={17} question="What is a Global Secondary Index?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexes">
A GSI lets you query on a different partition key (and optional sort key) than the base table, across the entire table, with its own provisioned throughput independent of the b

ase table's capacity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-03" number={18} question="What is a Local Secondary Index?" difficulty="medium" topic="Indexes">
An LSI lets you query using an alternate sort key while keeping the same partition key as the base table, sharing that partition's throughput. It's limited to 10GB of data per partition key value.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-04" number={19} question="What is eventual consistency in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Consistency">
Eventually consistent reads return the most recent write in milliseconds in the common case, but might briefly return stale data if a read hits a replica that hasn't yet received the latest write. It's the default and cheaper read type.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="d

db-query-05" number={20} question="What is strong consistency in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Consistency">
Strongly consistent reads always return the most recent successful write, but consume twice the read capacity of an eventually consistent read and aren't supported on Global Secondary Indexes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-06" number={21} question="How do you query DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Querying">
Use the `Query` API to retrieve items matching a specific partition key value, with optional sort key conditions to narrow the range — this is the efficient, key-driven way to read from DynamoDB.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-07" number={22} question="What is a scan operation in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Querying">

`Scan` reads every item in a table (or index), which is useful for full-table operations but inefficient and expensive at scale since it consumes capacity for every item read, not just matches.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-08" number={23} question="What is the difference between query and scan?" difficulty="medium" topic="Querying">
`Query` uses key conditions to target a specific partition (efficient); `Scan` reads every item in the table or index (inefficient but flexible when you don't know the key upfront).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-09" number={24} question="What is projection in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="Querying">
Projection specifies which attributes to return in query or scan results, reducing data transfer and, for indexes, cont

rolling which attributes are copied into the index in the first place.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-10" number={25} question="What is filtering in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Querying">
A filter expression applies conditions to items *after* DynamoDB retrieves them (post key-condition evaluation), reducing the result set size — but it doesn't reduce the read capacity consumed, since filtering happens after the read.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-11" number={26} question="How do you handle transactions in DynamoDB?" difficulty="hard" topic="Transactions">
Use `TransactWriteItems` for multiple atomic writes across one or more tables, or `TransactGetItems` for atomic reads — both succeed or fail as a unit, giving you ACID guarantees for the spe

cific items involved.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-12" number={27} question="What is batch processing in DynamoDB?" difficulty="medium" topic="Batch Operations">
`BatchGetItem` reads multiple items (potentially across multiple tables) in one request, and `BatchWriteItem` writes or deletes multiple items in one request — both are more efficient than issuing many individual requests, though neither is atomic across items the way transactions are.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-13" number={28} question="What is TTL in DynamoDB?" difficulty="easy" topic="TTL">
TTL (Time To Live) automatically deletes items after a specified expiration timestamp attribute is reached, useful for managing data expiration (session data, temporary caches) without writing cleanu

p jobs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-14" number={29} question="What is DynamoDB Streams?" difficulty="medium" topic="Streams">
Streams capture item-level modifications (inserts, updates, deletes) as an ordered, time-limited log, enabling real-time processing with AWS Lambda or other consumers — commonly used for change data capture, replication, or triggering downstream workflows.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="ddb-query-15" number={30} question="How do you design DynamoDB tables?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Modeling">
Plan access patterns upfront (this is the step relational modeling doesn't force you to do), choose partition keys that distribute traffic evenly, use secondary indexes for alternate access patterns you didn't design the base table's key around

, and optimize the overall data model — including denormalizing and using single-table design where appropriate — for the specific queries the application needs.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a DynamoDB table for an e-commerce order history feature."** Walk through identifying access patterns first (get all orders for a customer, get a specific order by ID), then choosing `customer_id` as the partition key and `order_date#order_id` as a composite sort key to support both patterns, and where a GSI would be needed for a third pattern like "look up an order by ID alone."
- **"One partition is getting throttled while the rest of the table is idle — what's happening and how do you fix it?"** This is a hot partition. Diagnose via CloudWatch partition-level metrics, then discuss redesigning the partition key for higher cardinality, adding a random/calculated suffix to spread a naturally hot key, or introducing DAX as a caching layer.
- **

"When would you reach for a GSI versus an LSI?"** Cover that LSIs must be created at table creation time and share the base table's partition and throughput, while GSIs can be added later, use their own partition key, and have independent capacity — making GSIs the more common choice for genuinely new access patterns.
- **"How would you keep a search index or analytics store in sync with a DynamoDB table in near-real time?"** Talk through DynamoDB Streams feeding a Lambda function that writes to OpenSearch, Kinesis, or a downstream data pipeline.

---

## Further Reading

- [MongoDB](/level-3-technologies/databases/mongodb/) and [Cassandra](/level-3-technologies/databases/cassandra/) — other NoSQL databases with different key, consistency, and modeling trade-offs
- [Bigtable](/level-3-technologies/databases/bigtable/) — Google Cloud's wide-column counterpart to DynamoDB
- [Data Modeling](/level-2-core-concepts/data-modeling/) — the access-pattern-first modeling approach DynamoDB design questions build on

## What are the differences between RDBMS and HBase data model?
The main differences between RDBMS and HBase data model are as follows:
Schema: In RDBMS, there is a schema of tables, columns etc. In HBASE, there is no schema.
Normalization: RDBMS data model is normalized as per the rule of Relation DB normalization.
HBase data model does not require any normalization.
Partition: In RDBMS we can choose to do partitioning. In HBase, partitioning happens automatically.

[Table of Contents](#Hbase)

## Explain what is Hbase?
Hbase is a column-oriented database management system which runs on top of HDFS (Hadoop Distribute File System). Hbase is not a relational data store, and it does not support structured query language like SQL.
In Hbase, a master node regulates the cluster and region servers to store portions of the tables and operates the work on the data.

## Explain what is WAL and Hlog in Hbase?
WAL (Write Ahead Log) is similar to MySQL BIN log; it records all the changes occur in data. It is a standard sequence file by Hadoop and it stores HLogkey’s.  These keys consist of a sequential number as well as actual data and are used to replay not yet persisted data after a server crash. So, in cash of server failure WAL work as a life-line and retrieves the lost data’s.

## Explain what is the row key?
Row key is defined by the application. As the combined key is pre-fixed by the rowkey, it enables the application to define the desired sort order. It also allows logical grouping of cells and make sure that all cells with the same rowkey are co-located on the same server.

[Table of Contents](#Hbase)

title: Hbase
content:
## Explain deletion in Hbase? Mention what are the three types of tombstone markers in Hbase?
When you delete the cell in Hbase, the data is not actually deleted but a tombstone marker is set, making the deleted cells invisible.  Hbase deleted are actually removed during compactions.
Three types of tombstone markers are there:
Version delete marker: For deletion, it marks a single version of a column
Column delete marker: For deletion, it marks all the versions of a column
Family delete marker: For deletion, it marks of all column for a column family

[Table of Contents](#Hbase)

title: Hbase
content:
## Explain how does Hbase actually delete a row?
In Hbase, whatever you write will be stored from RAM to disk, these disk writes are immutable barring compaction. During deletion process in Hbase, major compaction process delete marker while minor compactions don’t. In normal deletes, it results in a delete tombstone marker- these delete data they represent are removed during compaction.
Also, if you delete data and add more data, but with an earlier timestamp than the tombstone timestamp, further Gets may be masked by the delete/tombstone marker and hence you will not receive the inserted value until after the major compaction.

[Table of Contents](#Hbase)

title: Hbase
content:
## Explain what happens if you alter the block size of a column family on an already occupied database?
When you alter the block size of the column family, the new data occupies the new block size while the old data remains within the old block size. During data compaction, old data will take the new block size.  New files as they are flushed, have a new block size whereas existing data will continue to be read correctly. All data should be transformed to the new block size, after the next major compaction.

[Table of Contents](#Hbase)

In Hbase, whatever you write will be stored from RAM to disk, these disk writes are immutable barring compaction. During deletion process in Hbase, major compaction process delete marker while minor compactions don’t. In normal deletes, it results in a delete tombstone marker- these delete data they represent are removed during compaction.
Also, if you delete data and add more data, but with an earlier timestamp than the tombstone timestamp, further Gets may be masked by the delete/tombstone marker and hence you will not receive the inserted value until after the major compaction.

During data compaction, old data will take the new block size. New files as they are flushed, have a new block size whereas existing data will continue to be read correctly. All data should be transformed to the new block size, after the next major compaction.

In Major compaction, all the HFiles of a column are emerged and a single HFiles is created. The delted HFiles are discarded and it is generally triggered manually.

Generate Hbase data file(StoreFile) using a custom mapreduce job) from the data source. The StoreFile is created in Hbase internal format which can be efficiently loaded.
