## Flume: Distributed Log Collection for Hadoop

**Apache Flume is a distributed service for collecting, aggregating, and moving large volumes of log data into Hadoop, built around a simple agent pipeline of sources, channels, and sinks.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

A Flume **Agent** is a JVM process hosting the three core components of every flow: a **Source** (receives events from an external system), a **Channel** (a temporary store that holds events until a sink consumes them), and a **Sink** (removes events from the channel and forwards them to a destination like HDFS or another agent). The **Channel** you pick is a reliability/throughput trade-off — MEMORY is fastest but can lose data, FILE is the most durable because it persists to disk before acknowledging, and JDBC stores events in an embedded Derby database. **Channel Selectors** (replicating or multiplexing) decide whether an event goes to one channel or is fanned out to several, and **Interceptors** sit between source/channel or channel/sink to filter or enrich events in

flight. Reliability comes from channel-based **transactions**: an event only moves to the next hop once both the sending and receiving agent commit their transaction, giving Flume end-to-end guaranteed delivery. Multi-hop topologies are wired together with the **Avro RPC** mechanism, and agent behavior is entirely driven by local configuration files defining each agent's sources, channels, and sinks.

---
## Interview Questions

### Core Architecture & Components

<QuestionList topic="Flume Core Architecture" storagePrefix="flume-core">

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-01" number={1} question="What is Apache Flume?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Apache Flume is a distributed, reliable, and available service for efficiently collecting, aggregating, and moving large amounts of log data from many different sources to a centralized data store — most commonly Hadoop. It has a simple, flexible architecture based on streaming data flows, is robust and fault-tolerant with tunable reliability mechanisms and failover/recovery mechanisms, and uses a simple extensible data model that supports online analytic applications.

Flume is fundamentally a framework for populating Hadoop with data: agents are deployed th

roughout an organization's IT infrastructure — inside web servers, application servers, and mobile devices, for example — to collect data and integrate it into Hadoop.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-02" number={2} question="What is an Agent?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
An Agent is a process that hosts Flume components such as sources, channels, and sinks, and thus has the ability to receive, store, and forward events to their destination.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-03" number={3} question="What is a Channel?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
A Channel stores events. Events are delivered to the channel via sources operating within the agent, and an event stays in the channel until a sink removes it for further transport.
</Quest

ionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-04" number={4} question="What are Flume's core components?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
Source, Channel, and Sink are the core components in Apache Flume. When a Flume source receives an event from an external source, it stores the event in one or multiple channels. The channel temporarily stores and holds the event until it's consumed by the sink — acting as Flume's repository. The sink then removes the event from the channel and puts it into an external repository like HDFS, or moves it on to the next Flume hop.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-05" number={5} question="What is a Flume Event?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
A Flume Event is a unit of data with a set of string attributes. An external source,

like a web server, sends events to the source. Internally, Flume has built-in functionality to understand the source's format — each log file is typically considered an event. Each event has a header and a value section: the header holds header information, and the value is the appropriate content assigned to that header.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-06" number={6} question="Why Flume?" difficulty="medium" topic="Use Cases">
Flume isn't limited to collecting logs from distributed systems — it's capable of other use cases too, such as:
- collecting readings from an array of sensors
- collecting impressions from custom apps for an ad network
- collecting readings from network devices in order to monitor their performance

Flume is designed to preserve reliability, s

calability, manageability, and extensibility while serving a maximum number of clients with higher quality of service (QoS).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-07" number={7} question="Why are we using Flume?" difficulty="easy" topic="Use Cases">
Hadoop developers most often use this tool to get data from social media sites. It was developed by Cloudera for aggregating and moving very large amounts of data. Its primary use is to gather log files from different sources and asynchronously persist them into a Hadoop cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-core-08" number={8} question="Name two features of Flume." difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Flume collects data efficiently, and aggregates and moves large amounts of log data from many different sources i

nto a centralized data store. It's also not restricted to log data aggregation — it can transport massive quantities of event data including, but not limited to, network traffic data, social-media-generated data, email messages, and pretty much any other data source.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### Channels, Reliability & Failure Handling

<QuestionList topic="Flume Reliability" storagePrefix="flume-reliability">

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-01" number={9} question="Which is the reliable channel in Flume to ensure there is no data loss?" difficulty="medium" topic="Channels">
The FILE channel is the most reliable channel among the three (JDBC, FILE, and MEMORY), because it writes events to disk before acknowledging them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-02" number={10} question="Explain the different channel types in Flume, and which channel type is faster?" difficulty="medium" topic="Channels">
The three built-in channel types available in Flume are:
- **MEMORY Channel** — events are read from the source into memory and passed to the sink
-

**JDBC Channel** — stores events in an embedded Derby database
- **FILE Channel** — writes the contents to a file on the file system after reading the event from a source; the file is deleted only after the contents are successfully delivered to the sink

MEMORY Channel is the fastest of the three, but carries the risk of data loss. The channel you choose depends entirely on the nature of the big data application and the value of each event.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-03" number={11} question="Does Flume provide 100% reliability to the data flow?" difficulty="medium" topic="Reliability">
Yes — Apache Flume provides end-to-end reliability because of its transactional approach to data flow.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-04" number={1

2} question="Explain reliability and failure handling in Apache Flume." difficulty="hard" topic="Reliability">
Flume NG uses channel-based transactions to guarantee reliable message delivery. When a message moves from one agent to another, two transactions are started: one on the agent that delivers the event, and one on the agent that receives it. For the sending agent to commit its transaction, it must receive a success indication from the receiving agent. The receiving agent only returns a success indication once its own transaction commits properly first. This guarantees delivery semantics between every hop the flow makes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-reliability-05" number={13} question="Explain the replication and multiplexing selectors in Flume." difficulty="hard" to

pic="Channels">
Channel Selectors are used to handle multiple channels. Based on the Flume header value, an event can be written to just a single channel or to multiple channels. If a channel selector isn't specified for a source, the default is the Replicating selector, which writes the same event to all the channels in the source's channel list. The Multiplexing channel selector is used when the application needs to send different events to different channels.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### Sinks, Integrations & Data Flow

<QuestionList topic="Flume Sinks and Integrations" storagePrefix="flume-sinks">

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-01" number={14} question="How can Flume be used with HBase?" difficulty="hard" topic="Sinks">
Apache Flume can be used with HBase using one of two HBase sinks:
- **HBaseSink** (`org.apache.flume.sink.hbase.HBaseSink`) supports secure HBase clusters and also the newer HBase IPC introduced in HBase 0.96.
- **AsyncHBaseSink** (`org.apache.flume.sink.hbase.AsyncHBaseSink`) has better performance than HBaseSink, since it can make non-blocking calls to HBase.

**HBaseSink** converts a Flume Event into HBase Increments or Puts: a serializer implements `HBaseEventSerializer`, which is instantiated when the sink starts. For every event, the sin

k calls the serializer's `initialize` method, which translates the Flume Event into the HBase increments and puts sent to the HBase cluster.

**AsyncHBaseSink** implements `AsyncHBaseEventSerializer`. Its `initialize` method is called only once, when the sink starts. The sink invokes `setEvent` and then calls `getIncrements` and `getActions`, similar to HBaseSink. When the sink stops, the serializer's `cleanUp` method is called.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-02" number={15} question="Differentiate between FileSink and FileRollSink." difficulty="medium" topic="Sinks">
The major difference is where the events end up: HDFS FileSink writes events into the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), whereas FileRollSink stores events into the local file system.
</QuestionCard

>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-03" number={16} question="Does Apache Flume provide support for third-party plugins?" difficulty="easy" topic="Extensibility">
Yes — most data analysts rely on Apache Flume's plug-in-based architecture, since it can load data from external sources and transfer it to external destinations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-04" number={17} question="Can Flume distribute data to multiple destinations?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Flow">
Yes. It supports multiplexing flows — an event can flow from one source to multiple channels and multiple destinations. This is achieved by defining a flow multiplexer.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-05" number={18} question="How can a multi-hop agent be set up in Flume?" difficulty="m

edium" topic="Data Flow">
The Avro RPC Bridge mechanism is used to set up a multi-hop agent in Apache Flume.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-06" number={19} question="Can you explain configuration files in Flume?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
The agent's configuration is stored in a local configuration file. It comprises each agent's source, sink, and channel information.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-07" number={20} question="What are Interceptors?" difficulty="medium" topic="Data Flow">
Interceptors are used to filter events between a source and channel, or between a channel and sink. These interceptors can filter out unnecessary or targeted log entries. You can chain as many interceptors as your requirements need.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-sinks-08" number={21} question="Is it possible to leverage real-time analysis on the big data collected by Flume directly?" difficulty="medium" topic="Integrations">
Yes — data from Flume can be extracted, transformed, and loaded in real time into Apache Solr servers using the `MorphlineSolrSink`.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### Flume in the Hadoop Ecosystem

<QuestionList topic="Flume Ecosystem" storagePrefix="flume-ecosystem">

<QuestionCard id="flume-ecosystem-01" number={22} question="What is Flume-NG?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
Flume-NG is a real-time loader for streaming data into Hadoop. It stores data in HDFS and HBase. It's the successor to the original Flume and the version you'll want to get started with, since it improves substantially on the original.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-ecosystem-02" number={23} question="What are the complicated steps in Flume configuration?" difficulty="medium" topic="Configuration">
Flume processes streaming data, so once started there is no stop/end to the process — it asynchronously flows data from source to HDFS via an agent. First,

the agent needs to know how its individual components are connected to load data, so configuration is what triggers loading of streaming data. For example, `consumerKey`, `consumerSecret`, `accessToken`, and `accessTokenSecret` are the key factors needed to download data from Twitter.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-ecosystem-03" number={24} question="What are the data extraction tools in Hadoop?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
Sqoop can be used to transfer data between RDBMS and HDFS. Flume can be used to extract streaming data from social media, web logs, and similar sources, and store it on HDFS.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flume-ecosystem-04" number={25} question="What are the similarities and differences between Apache Flume and Apache Kafka?" difficulty="

medium" topic="Ecosystem">
Flume pushes messages to their destination via its Sinks. With Kafka, you instead need to consume messages from the Kafka Broker using a Kafka Consumer API — Kafka is pull-based rather than push-based. Both move large volumes of event data, but Flume is purpose-built for ingesting data into Hadoop-ecosystem sinks, while Kafka is a general-purpose distributed log that many different consumers can read from independently.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a Flume agent that ships web server logs into HDFS without losing data during a downstream outage."** Talk through choosing the FILE channel over MEMORY for durability, how channel-based transactions guarantee each hop only advances after a commit, and where backpressure builds up if HDFS becomes slow.
- **"You need the same event stream to go to both HDFS for archival and Solr for real-time search."** Explain the Replicating channel selector for fan-out, versus Multiplexing when different event types need to go to different channels, and mention `MorphlineSolrSink` for the real-time path.
- **"How would you decide between Flume and Kafka for a new ingestion pipeline?"** Walk through the push vs. pull distinction, Flume's built-in Hadoop-ecosy

stem sinks vs. Kafka's general-purpose consumer model, and when you might use both together (Flume as a Kafka producer, for example).

---

- [Kafka](/level-3-technologies/streaming/kafka/) — the distributed log Flume is most often compared against

## NiFi: Flow-Based Dataflow Automation

**Apache NiFi automates the movement and light transformation of data between systems through a visual, flow-based programming model built around FlowFiles, processors, and connections.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Everything in NiFi revolves around the **FlowFile** — a unit of data made up of **content** (the actual bytes, stored separately in a content repository and only referenced by the FlowFile) and **attributes** (key/value metadata describing it). **Processors** are the workhorses that create, route, transform, and move FlowFiles; when a processor finishes with a FlowFile it emits a **relationship** (success, failure, or a custom outcome) that determines where the FlowFile goes next. Connections between processors have configurable **backpressure** limits (by count or size) so a fast producer can't overwhelm a slow consumer. Operationally, NiFi supports **templates** for reusable flows, **bulletins** for surfacing warnings/errors in the UI, a **variable registry** for exter

nalizing configuration, and a **zero-master clustering** model coordinated by ZooKeeper (a Cluster Coordinator and a Primary Node are elected, and failover is automatic).

---

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="NiFi" storagePrefix="nifi">

<QuestionCard id="nifi-01" number={1} question="What is Apache NiFi?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
NiFi is helpful in creating DataFlows. It means you can transfer data from one system to another system, as well as process the data in between.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-02" number={2} question="What is a NiFi FlowFile?" difficulty="easy" topic="FlowFiles">
A FlowFile is a message, event, or piece of user data that is pushed or created in NiFi. A FlowFile has two main parts attached to it: its content (the actual payload — a stream of bytes) and its attributes (key/value pairs attached to the content, essentially metadata for the content).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-03"

number={3} question="What is a Relationship in a NiFi DataFlow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Processors">
When a processor finishes processing a FlowFile, it can result in a Failure, a Success, or another relationship. Based on this relationship, you can route data to a downstream/next processor or otherwise mediate it accordingly.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-04" number={4} question="What is a Reporting Task?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
A Reporting Task is a NiFi extension point capable of reporting and analyzing NiFi's internal metrics, in order to provide that information to external resources or report status information as bulletins that appear directly in the NiFi User Interface.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-05" number={5} question="What is a

NiFi Processor?" difficulty="easy" topic="Processors">
The Processor is the main component in NiFi that actually works on the FlowFile content, helping create, send, receive, transform, route, split, merge, and otherwise process FlowFiles.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-06" number={6} question="Is there a programming language that Apache NiFi supports?" difficulty="medium" topic="Extensibility">
NiFi is implemented in the Java programming language and allows extensions (processors, controller services, and reporting tasks) to be implemented in Java. In addition, NiFi supports processors that execute scripts written in Groovy, Jython, and several other popular scripting languages.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-07" number={7} question="How do you define the NiFi Co

ntent Repository?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Contents are not stored in the FlowFile itself. They are stored in the content repository and referenced by the FlowFile. This allows the contents of FlowFiles to be stored independently and efficiently, based on the underlying storage mechanism.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-08" number={8} question="What is Backpressure in the NiFi system?" difficulty="medium" topic="Flow Control">
Sometimes a producer system is faster than the consumer system, so messages are consumed more slowly than they're produced. All the messages (FlowFiles) that aren't yet processed remain in the connection's buffer. You can limit the connection's backpressure size either by number of FlowFiles or by data size. Once that limit is reached,

the connection applies backpressure to the producer processor so it stops running — no more FlowFiles are generated until the backpressure is reduced.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-09" number={9} question="What is a template in NiFi?" difficulty="easy" topic="Templates">
A template is a re-usable workflow that you can import and export within the same or different NiFi instances. It can save a lot of time versus recreating a flow again and again each time. A template is created as an XML file.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-10" number={10} question="What is bulleting and how does it help in NiFi?" difficulty="medium" topic="Monitoring">
Rather than checking logs for anything interesting, it's much more convenient to have notifications pop up directly on screen. I

f a Processor logs anything as a WARNING or ERROR, a "Bulletin Indicator" shows up in the top-right-hand corner of the Processor. This indicator looks like a sticky note and is shown for five minutes after the event occurs. Hovering over the bulletin shows what happened, so the user doesn't have to sift through log messages to find it. In a cluster, the bulletin also indicates which node emitted it. You can also change the log level at which bulletins occur in the Settings tab of a Processor's Configure dialog.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-11" number={11} question="Do attributes get added to content (the actual data) when data is pulled by NiFi?" difficulty="medium" topic="FlowFiles">
You can certainly add attributes to your FlowFiles at any time — that's the whole point of

separating metadata from the actual data. Essentially, one FlowFile represents an object or message moving through NiFi. Each FlowFile contains a piece of content (the actual bytes); you can extract attributes from the content and store them in memory, then operate against those attributes without touching the content. This saves a lot of I/O overhead, making the whole flow management process extremely efficient.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-12" number={12} question="What happens if you have stored a password in a dataflow and create a template out of it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
Password is a sensitive property. So while exporting the DataFlow as a template, the password is dropped — as soon as you import the template into the same or a different NiFi system,

the password will need to be re-entered.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-13" number={13} question="How does NiFi support huge volumes of payload in a DataFlow?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Huge volumes of data can transit through a DataFlow because, as data moves through NiFi, only a pointer to the data is passed around (referred to as a FlowFile). The content of the FlowFile is only accessed as needed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-14" number={14} question="What is a NiFi custom properties registry?" difficulty="hard" topic="Configuration">
To load custom key/value pairs, you can use a custom properties registry, configured in `nifi.properties`:

```properties
nifi.variable.registry.properties=/conf/nifi_registry
```

You put key/value pairs i

n that file and can then reference them in your NiFi processors using expression language, for example `${OS}`, if you've configured that property in the registry file.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="nifi-15" number={15} question="Does NiFi work as a Master-Slave architecture?" difficulty="hard" topic="Clustering">
No — from NiFi 1.0 onward, a zero-master philosophy is used, and every node in a NiFi cluster is the same. The NiFi cluster is managed by ZooKeeper: Apache ZooKeeper elects a single node as the Cluster Coordinator, and failover is handled automatically by ZooKeeper. All cluster nodes report heartbeat and status information to the Cluster Coordinator, which is responsible for disconnecting and connecting nodes. Additionally, every cluster has one Primary Node, also electe

d by ZooKeeper.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a NiFi flow that ingests files from an SFTP server, validates them, and loads them into a warehouse."** Talk through the processor chain, how relationships (success/failure) route FlowFiles, and where you'd apply backpressure to protect a slower downstream system.
- **"A NiFi flow is silently falling behind — how do you find out why?"** Discuss checking connection queues for backpressure being applied, bulletins for WARN/ERROR events on specific processors, and reviewing reporting tasks for internal metrics.
- **"How would you move a tested dataflow from a dev NiFi cluster to production without leaking credentials?"** Explain templates as the export/import mechanism, and why sensitive properties like passwords are dropped on export and must be

reconfigured in the target environment.

---

## Further Reading

- [CDC](/level-3-technologies/ingestion/cdc/) — a complementary ingestion pattern for capturing database changes that NiFi flows often consume
- [Flume](/level-3-technologies/ingestion/flume/) — a narrower, log-focused alternative to NiFi's general-purpose dataflow model
- [Kafka](/level-3-technologies/streaming/kafka/) — a common source/sink for NiFi processors in streaming architectures

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Airflow" storagePrefix="airflow">

<QuestionCard id="af-01" number={1} question="What is Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Apache Airflow is an open-source workflow management platform. It began in October 2014 at Airbnb as a solution for managing the company's increasingly complex workflows. Airbnb's creation of Airflow enabled them to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor their workflows via the built-in Airflow user interface. Airflow is a data transformation pipeline ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) workflow orchestration tool.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-02" number={2} question="What issues does Airflow resolve compared to cron?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Cron is an old technique for t

- **Scalability** — cron requires external tooling to log, track, and manage tasks, while the Airflow UI tracks and monitors workflow execution out of the box.
- **Dependencies** — creating and maintaining a relationship between tasks in cron is a challenge, whereas it's as simple as writing Python code in Airflow.
- **Reproducibility** — cron jobs aren't reproducible unless configured externally; Airflow maintains an audit trail of every task run.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-03" number={3} question="Explain how a workflow is designed in Airflow." difficulty="easy" topic="DAGs">
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is used to design an Airflow workflow. That is to say, when creating a workflow, you consider ho

The overall logic of your workflow is based on the shape of the graph. An Airflow DAG can have multiple branches, and you can choose which ones to follow and which to skip during workflow execution.

Airflow can be completely stopped, and running workflows will then resume by restarting the last unfinished task. It's important to remember that Airflow tasks can be run more than once when designing them — each task should be **idempotent**, capable of being performed multiple times without causing unintended consequences.
</QuestionCard>

There are four major components to Airflow:

- **Webserver** — the Airflow UI built on Flask, which provides an overview of the overall health of various DAGs and helps visualize their components and states. It also lets you manage users, roles, and configuration.
- **Scheduler** — every few seconds, the scheduler walks over the DAGs and schedules tasks for execution.
- **Executor** — an internal component used by the scheduler. Executors are what actually execute the tasks, while the scheduler orchestrates them. Airflow has different executor types, including `SequentialExecutor`, `LocalExecutor`, `CeleryExecutor`, and `KubernetesExecutor` — teams generally pick whichever is best suited to their use case.
- **Worker** — workers run the tasks that the execut

- **Metadata Database** — Airflow supports a range of metadata storage databases. This database holds information about DAGs, their runs, and other Airflow configuration such as users, roles, and connections. The webserver reads DAG state and run history from this database, and the scheduler is what keeps it updated.

- **KubernetesExecutor** — runs each task in its own Kubernetes pod. Unlike Celery, it spins up worker pods on demand, which allows for more efficient use of resources.

People generally choose the executor that's best for their use case.

A **connection** stores the credentials and connection details for an external system (host, login, password, extra config) in Airflow's metadata database, referenced by a `conn_id` string rather than hardcoded values. A **hook** is the Python interface that uses a connection to actually talk to that system — `PostgresHook`, `S3Hook`, `SlackHook` — so operators are typically thin wrappers that call a hook under the hood.

from airflow.models import BaseOperator

<QuestionCard id="af-23" number={23} question="What is a sensor in Airflow, and how does it differ from a regular task?" difficulty="medium" topic="Sensors">
A sensor is a special operator that waits for a condition to become true — a file to land in S3, a partition to appear in a table, another DAG to finish — before letting downstream tasks run. Unlike a regular task that does work and finishes, a sensor's job *is* the waiting; it repeatedly checks (`poke`s) the condition on an interval until it succeeds or times out.

```python
from airflow.sensors.filesystem import FileSensor

wait_for_file = FileSensor(task_id="wait_

<QuestionCard id="af-24" number={24} question="What's the difference between poke mode and reschedule mode for a sensor?" difficulty="hard" topic="Sensors">
In **poke mode** (the default), a sensor occupies a worker slot for its entire wait, repeatedly checking on `poke_interval` — fine for short waits, wasteful for long ones since that slot can't run anything else. In **reschedule mode** (`mode="reschedule"`), the sensor gives up its worker slot between checks and reschedules itself, freeing that slot for other tasks while it waits — much better for sensors that might wait for hours.
</QuestionCard>

A deferrable operator (Airflow 2.2+) suspends itself entirely and hands the waiting off to a separate lightweight **triggerer** process, freeing its worker slot completely rather than just periodically — unlike reschedule mode, which still consumes scheduler/worker resources on each check. This lets a single triggerer process efficiently manage thousands of concurrent waits (for S3 files, external task completion, etc.) that would otherwise each tie up a full worker slot.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-32" number={32} question="How do you set task dependencies in Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Dependencies">
```python
extract >> transform >> load          # extract, then transform, then load
extract >> [transform_a, transform_b] # both run after extract, in parallel
[transform_a, transform_b] >> load    # load waits for both
```

`>>` sets "runs after" (downstream), `<<` sets "runs before" (upstream) — both are shorthand for `.set_downstream()`/`.set_upstream()`. Dependencies can fan out to a list (parallel branches) or fan back in (a task wai

<QuestionCard id="af-33" number={33} question="How does branching work with BranchPythonOperator?" difficulty="medium" topic="Branching">
```python
from airflow.operators.python import BranchPythonOperator

def choose_path(**context):
    return "path_a" if some_condition else "path_b"   # must return a task_id

branch = BranchPythonOperator(task_id="branch", python_callable=choose_path)
branch >> [path_a, path_b]
```

The branching function returns the `task_id` (or list of ids) that should run next; every other downstream task in that branch point is automatically skipped, not just left unscheduled. This is how a DAG expresses "run path A or path B, never both" based on a runtime condition.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-36" number={36} question="What's the difference between execution_date and data_interval in Airflow scheduling?" difficulty="hard" topic="Scheduling">
The older `execution_date` was confusingly named — a DAG scheduled `@daily` for "Jan 2" actually runs *after* Jan 2 ends (processing Jan 2's data), not at the start of Jan 2, which tripped up nearly everyone. Airflow 2.2+ replaced this with explicit `data_interval_start`/`data_interval_end`, naming the time range the run is actually processing, with `logical_date` as the modern (still slightly con

title: Pulls the return_value XCom from "pushing_task"
content:
fusing but clearer) equivalent of the old term.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-37" number={37} question="What's the difference between catchup and backfill?" difficulty="medium" topic="Backfills">
**`catchup`** (a DAG-level setting) controls whether Airflow automatically creates runs for every interval between a DAG's `start_date` and now the first time it's turned on (`catchup=True`) or only starts from the current interval going forward (`catchup=False`, usually what you want). **Backfill** is a manual, on-demand action (`airflow dags backfill`) to (re)run a DAG for a specific past date range — for example, after fixing a bug, to regenerate historical outputs that were wrong.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-38" number={38} question="What is an SLA in Airflow, and what

title: Pulls the return_value XCom from "pushing_task"
content:
happens when one is missed?" difficulty="medium" topic="SLAs">
An SLA is a maximum expected duration for a task, set via `sla=timedelta(hours=2)`. If a task is still running (or hasn't started) past that threshold relative to the DAG's expected schedule, Airflow logs an SLA miss and can trigger a notification callback — but critically, it does **not** stop or fail the task; it's purely an alerting mechanism, not an enforcement one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-39" number={39} question="What are pools and priority weights used for?" difficulty="hard" topic="Resource Management">
A **pool** caps how many tasks can run concurrently against a shared, limited resource (a database that can only handle 5 concurrent connections, an API with a rate limit) — tasks assigned to that poo

l queue once its slot limit is reached, regardless of how much broader worker capacity is free. **`priority_weight`** breaks ties among tasks queued for the same pool or worker slots, so higher-priority work (e.g., a time-sensitive report) jumps ahead of lower-priority backlog work competing for the same constrained resource.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-40" number={40} question="How do you unit test an Airflow DAG?" difficulty="medium" topic="Testing">
```python
def test_dag_has_no_import_errors():
    from airflow.models import DagBag
    dagbag = DagBag()
    assert len(dagbag.import_errors) == 0

def test_transform_task_logic():
    # test the underlying Python function directly — no need to run it through Airflow at all

Two layers are worth testing: DAG-integrity tests (does it parse without errors,

does the expected task count/structure match) using `DagBag`, and unit tests of the actual business logic inside each task's callable — which, if written well, don't need Airflow at all to test, since they're just plain functions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-41" number={41} question="How do you set up alerting when a task fails?" difficulty="easy" topic="Monitoring">
```python
def notify_slack(context):
    send_slack_message(f"Task {context['task_instance'].task_id} failed")

default_args = {"on_failure_callback": notify_slack}
```

`on_failure_callback` (and `on_success_callback`, `sla_miss_callback`) fire automatically on the relevant event, letting you push a notification to Slack, PagerDuty, or email without polling anything. Set sensible defaults at the DAG leve

<QuestionCard id="af-42" number={42} question="Why does DAG file parsing performance matter, and what's a common mistake that hurts it?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
The scheduler re-parses every DAG file on a regular interval (to pick up code changes) — if a DAG file runs slow or expensive code at **import time** (a database query, an API call, a large computation outside of any task), that cost is paid on every single parse cycle, not once per run, and can meaningfully slow down the whole scheduler across all DAGs. The fix is keeping DAG files themselves lightweight — only DAG/task *definitions* at the top level, with any real work happening inside a task's callable, which only exec

title: Pulls the return_value XCom from "pushing_task"
content:
utes when the task actually runs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-43" number={43} question="How does Airflow compare to Dagster or Prefect?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystem">
Airflow is the most established and widely adopted, with the largest ecosystem of providers/integrations, but its DAG model is comparatively low-level about data (tasks pass small XComs, not first-class typed data assets). **Dagster** is built around "software-defined assets" — it tracks data products themselves, not just task execution, with stronger typing and local testability out of the box. **Prefect** emphasizes a more Pythonic, dynamic flow definition with less rigid DAG structure and easier local development. In practice, Airflow's maturity and ecosystem size are still the main reason it remains

title: Pulls the return_value XCom from "pushing_task"
content:
the default choice for many teams.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="af-44" number={44} question="What can you do with the Airflow REST API or CLI that you can't easily do from the UI?" difficulty="easy" topic="Operations">
Both let you script and automate operations that would otherwise require manual clicks: triggering a DAG run with specific config from an external system (`airflow dags trigger` or `POST /dags/{dag_id}/dagRuns`), running backfills, managing connections/variables as part of infrastructure-as-code, and integrating DAG triggers into CI/CD pipelines — anything you want driven programmatically rather than by a person in the browser.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: Orchestration
description: Workflow and infrastructure orchestration
---

## Orchestration: Workflow & Infrastructure Management

Orchestration tools manage complex workflows and infrastructure across data pipelines.

## Tools Covered

- **Airflow**: Apache Airflow workflow orchestration
- **Kubernetes**: Container orchestration platform

## Kubernetes: Container Orchestration Platform

**Kubernetes is the container orchestration platform that schedules, scales, and heals containerized workloads across a cluster of nodes — and for data engineers it's most often the substrate that runs Airflow's `KubernetesExecutor`, Spark-on-Kubernetes, or other per-task isolated workloads.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Kubernetes schedules **pods** (one or more containers) onto **nodes**, using **requests** and **limits** to control resource usage and the scheduler's placement decisions. **Services** and **Ingress** solve networking: a Service gives a stable address for a set of pods (via a label selector), while Ingress handles L7 HTTP routing and TLS termination from outside the cluster into services. **Namespaces** partition a cluster for multi-team or multi-environment isolation, and **RBAC**, network policies, and admission control are the main security levers. Day-2 operations lean on constructs like **PodDisruptionBudgets** (safe draining), **init containers** (pre-work before the main container starts), **node affinity/nodeSelector** (pod placement), and **Operators** (custom c

ontrollers that encode operational knowledge for stateful applications). Monitoring and logging typically layer Prometheus and an EFK/ELK-style pipeline on top of the cluster.

---

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Kubernetes" storagePrefix="kubernetes">

<QuestionCard id="k8s-01" number={1} question="How do you perform maintenance activity on a K8s node?" difficulty="medium" topic="Cluster Ops">
Whenever security patches are available, the Kubernetes administrator has to apply them to the running containers to prevent vulnerabilities — an unavoidable part of administration. Two commands are used to safely drain a K8s node:

```bash
kubectl cordon <node-name>
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets
```

`cordon` moves the node into maintenance mode (marks it unschedulable), and `drain` then evicts the pods from the node. Once `drain` succeeds, you can perform maintenance.

Note: if you only need to inspect nodes first, use `kubectl get

nodes` to list all nodes, then `kubectl drain <node-name>` to drain a particular one.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-02" number={2} question="How do you control the resource usage of a pod?" difficulty="medium" topic="Resource Management">
Resource usage of a pod is controlled with `requests` and `limits`:

- **Request** — the amount of resources requested for a container. If a container exceeds its request, it can be throttled back down to that request.
- **Limit** — an upper cap on the resources a single container can use. If it tries to exceed this limit, it can be terminated if Kubernetes decides another container needs those resources. If you're sensitive to pod restarts, it makes sense to keep the sum of all container resource limits at or below your cluster's total re

source capacity.

Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: example1
      image: example/example1
      resources:
        requests:
          memory: "256Mi"
          cpu: "250m"
        limits:
          memory: "512Mi"
          cpu: "500m"
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-03" number={3} question="What are the various K8s services running on nodes, and what is the role of each?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
A K8s cluster mainly consists of two types of nodes: executor (worker) nodes and the master (control plane).

**Executor node services:**
- **kube-proxy** — runs on every node and handles communication of pods within the cluster and to the outside network, maintaining network p

rotocols as pods communicate.
- **kubelet** — a running service on each node that keeps the node in sync with its configuration (YAML/JSON). Note: kubelet only manages containers created by Kubernetes.

**Master (control plane) services:**
- **kube-apiserver** — the master API service that acts as the entry point to the K8s cluster.
- **kube-scheduler** — schedules pods according to available resources on executor nodes.
- **kube-controller-manager** — a control loop that watches the shared state of the cluster through the API server and makes changes attempting to move the current state toward the desired state.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-04" number={4} question="What is a PDB (Pod Disruption Budget)?" difficulty="medium" topic="Availability">
A Kubernetes administra

tor can create a `PodDisruptionBudget` for high availability of an application. It ensures that the minimum number of running pods is respected, as defined by the `minAvailable` field. This is useful during a drain: the drain will halt until the PDB is respected, ensuring the application's high availability. The following spec shows `minAvailable: 2`, meaning at least 2 pods must remain available even during a voluntary disruption:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: zk-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: zookeeper
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-05" number={5} question="What's an init container, and when can it be used?" difficulty="easy" topic="Init Containers">
Init containers set the

stage for you before the actual pod's main container(s) start running. Common uses:

- Wait for some condition before starting the app container, with a command like `sleep 60`.
- Clone a git repository into a volume so the main container can use it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-06" number={6} question="What is the role of a load balancer in Kubernetes?" difficulty="easy" topic="Networking">
Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers, which helps ensure the application stays available to users. In Kubernetes, all incoming traffic lands on a single IP address on the load balancer — a way to expose your service outside the cluster — which then routes traffic to a particular pod (via a Service) using an algorithm like round-robin. If a pod goe

s down, the load balancer is notified so traffic isn't routed to that unavailable pod. Load balancers in Kubernetes are therefore responsible for distributing incoming traffic across the pods behind a service.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-07" number={7} question="What can be done to increase Kubernetes security?" difficulty="medium" topic="Security">
- By default, any pod can communicate with any other pod — set up **network policies** to limit this communication between pods.
- Use **RBAC** (role-based access control) to narrow down permissions.
- Use **namespaces** to establish security boundaries.
- Set **admission control policies** to avoid running privileged containers.
- Turn on **audit logging**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-08" number={8} question="H

ow do you monitor a Kubernetes cluster?" difficulty="easy" topic="Monitoring">
Prometheus is commonly used for Kubernetes monitoring. The Prometheus ecosystem consists of multiple components:

- The Prometheus server, which scrapes and stores time-series data.
- Client libraries for instrumenting application code.
- A push gateway for supporting short-lived jobs.
- Special-purpose exporters for services like StatsD, HAProxy, Graphite, etc.
- An alertmanager to handle alerts across various support tools.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-09" number={9} question="How do you get centralized logs from pods?" difficulty="medium" topic="Logging">
This depends on the application and several other factors. Common logging patterns include:

- Node-level logging agent.
- Streaming

sidecar container.
- Sidecar container with a dedicated logging agent.
- Exporting logs directly from the application.

One common setup: `journalbeat` and `filebeat` run as a DaemonSet, dumping collected logs to a Kafka topic, which is eventually written into the ELK stack. The same result can be achieved with an EFK stack and `fluent-bit`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-10" number={10} question="How would you turn the following Service into an externally accessible one, and what would the Ingress equivalent look like?" difficulty="hard" topic="Services">
Starting Service (internal only, no external access):

```yaml
spec:
  selector:
    app: some-app
  ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080
```

**Option 1 — expose via a LoadBalan

cer Service.** Add `type: LoadBalancer` and a `nodePort`:

```yaml
spec:
  selector:
    app: some-app
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 32412
```

**Option 2 — expose via Ingress.** One of several ways to write it:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: someapp-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: my.host
      http:
        paths:
          - backend:
              serviceName: someapp-internal-service
              servicePort: 8080
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-11" number={11} question="How do you configure TLS with Ingress?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ingress">
Add `tls` and `secretName` entries to the Ingress spec:

```yaml
spec:

tls:
    - hosts:
        - some_app.com
      secretName: someapp-secret-tls
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-12" number={12} question="Why use namespaces? What is the problem with using only the default namespace?" difficulty="medium" topic="Namespaces">
Using only the default namespace makes it hard, over time, to get an overview of all the applications you manage in your cluster. Namespaces make it easier to organize applications into groups that make sense — for example, a namespace for all monitoring applications and a namespace for all security applications.

Namespaces are also useful for managing Blue/Green environments, where each namespace can hold a different version of an app while still sharing resources in other namespaces (logging, monitoring, etc.).

Another use case is a single cluster shared by multiple teams. Without namespaces, teams can end up stepping on each other — for example, if two teams create an app with the same name, one overrides the other, since there can't be two apps with the same name in the same namespace.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-13" number={13} question="In the following ConfigMap, which service and namespace is being referred to?" difficulty="medium" topic="Namespaces">
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: some-configmap
data:
  some_url: silicon.chip
```

This value follows the in-cluster DNS pattern `<service>.<namespace>`, so it's referencing the service **"silicon"** in the namespace called **"chip"**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-14" number={14} q

uestion="What is an Operator?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operators">
Operators are software extensions to Kubernetes that make use of custom resources to manage applications and their components. Operators follow Kubernetes principles, notably the control loop.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-15" number={15} question="Why do we need Operators?" difficulty="medium" topic="Operators">
Managing applications in Kubernetes isn't as straightforward for stateful applications as it is for stateless ones, where reaching the desired state and performing upgrades is handled the same way for every replica. In stateful applications, upgrading each replica might require different handling since each replica can be in a different state — traditionally requiring a human operator. A Kubernetes

Operator is meant to assist with this, encoding that operational knowledge into software. This also helps automate a standard process across multiple Kubernetes clusters.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-16" number={16} question="What is GKE?" difficulty="easy" topic="Cloud">
GKE is Google Kubernetes Engine, a managed service for managing and orchestrating Docker containers. With the help of Google Cloud, it also handles orchestrating the underlying container cluster infrastructure for you.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-17" number={17} question="What is an Ingress default backend?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ingress">
It specifies what to do with an incoming request to the Kubernetes cluster that isn't mapped to any backend — i.e., what happens when no rule matches

the incoming HTTP request. If a default backend service isn't defined, it's recommended to define one so users see a meaningful message instead of an unclear error.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-18" number={18} question="How do you run Kubernetes locally?" difficulty="easy" topic="Local Dev">
Kubernetes can be set up locally using Minikube. It runs a single-node cluster in a VM on your computer, making it a good way for users who are just starting to learn Kubernetes.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-19" number={19} question="What is Kubernetes load balancing?" difficulty="easy" topic="Load Balancing">
Load balancing is one of the most common and standard ways of exposing services. There are two types in K8s:

- **Internal load balancer** — automatically balances l

oad and allocates pods for internal, in-cluster traffic.
- **External load balancer** — directs traffic from external sources to backend pods.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-20" number={20} question="What does the following Deployment configuration snippet mean?" difficulty="medium" topic="Secrets">
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
    - name: my-app
      env:
        - name: USER_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: some-secret
              key: password
```

The `USER_PASSWORD` environment variable will store the value from the `password` key in the Secret called `some-secret`. In other words, you're referencing a value from a Kubernetes Secret rather than hardcoding it.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-21" number={21}

question="What is the difference between Docker Swarm and Kubernetes?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
- The installation procedure for Kubernetes is more complicated, but once installed, the cluster is robust. Docker Swarm's installation is much simpler, but the resulting cluster isn't as robust.
- Kubernetes can handle auto-scaling of pods based on incoming load; Docker Swarm cannot.
- Kubernetes is a full-fledged framework — since it maintains cluster state more consistently, its autoscaling reacts less quickly than Docker Swarm's.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-22" number={22} question="How do you troubleshoot a pod that isn't getting scheduled?" difficulty="medium" topic="Troubleshooting">
The K8s scheduler is responsible for placing pods onto nodes. Many facto

rs can lead to an unschedulable pod, the most common being running out of resources. Use `kubectl describe <pod> -n <namespace>` to see the reason the pod isn't starting, and keep an eye on `kubectl get events` to see all events coming from the cluster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-23" number={23} question="How do you run a pod on a particular node?" difficulty="medium" topic="Scheduling">
Several methods are available:

- **`nodeName`** — specify the name of a node directly in the pod spec; it will try to run the pod on that specific node.
- **`nodeSelector`** — assign a specific label to a node with special resources, and use the same label in the pod spec so the pod only runs on nodes with that label.
- **Node affinity** — `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecutio

n` and `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` express hard and soft requirements for running a pod on specific nodes, based on node labels. This is intended to eventually replace `nodeSelector`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-24" number={24} question="What are the different ways to provide external network connectivity to K8s?" difficulty="medium" topic="Networking">
By default, a pod can reach the external network, but the reverse requires some setup. Options for connecting to a pod from outside the cluster:

- **NodePort** — exposes one port on each node to communicate with the service.
- **Load balancers** — operate at L4 (TCP/IP).
- **Ingress** — operates at L7 (HTTP).
- **kube-proxy** — can expose a service that only has a cluster IP on the local system's p

ort:

```bash
kubectl proxy --port=8080
```

Then access the service via:

```
http://localhost:8080/api/v1/namespaces/<namespace>/services/<service-name>:<port>/proxy/
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="k8s-25" number={25} question="How would you forward a request from container port 8080, to service port 8080, to ingress port 8080, to the browser on port 80?" difficulty="hard" topic="Networking">
The Ingress exposes port 80 externally for the browser to access, and connects to a Service that listens on 8080. The Ingress listens on port 80 by default. An "Ingress controller" is a pod that receives external traffic, handles the Ingress, and is configured by an Ingress resource — for this to work you need to configure the Ingress controller's selector; if no Ingress contro

ller selector matches, no controller will manage the Ingress.

A simple Ingress config looks like:

```yaml
spec:
  rules:
    - host: abc.org
      http:
        paths:
          - backend:
              serviceName: abc-service
              servicePort: 8080
```

And the corresponding Service:

```yaml
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: abc-service
spec:
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080       # port the service listens on
      targetPort: 8080 # port forwarded to the container
```
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A pod won't start — walk me through how you'd debug it."** Talk through `kubectl describe pod` for events (scheduling failures, resource pressure, image pull errors) and `kubectl get events` for cluster-wide context, then narrow down to resource requests/limits or node affinity constraints.
- **"How would you expose a service running in your cluster to the internet, with TLS?"** Compare NodePort, LoadBalancer, and Ingress, then walk through adding a `tls` block with a `secretName` referencing a TLS secret on the Ingress resource.
- **"We're running Airflow's KubernetesExecutor and getting a flood of small pods — how do you keep that under control?"** Discuss resource requests/limits per task pod, namespaces for isolation, PodDisruptionBudgets during

node maintenance, and centralized logging so per-task pod logs remain accessible after the pod is gone.

---

## Further Reading

- [Airflow](/level-3-technologies/orchestration/airflow/) — the orchestration layer that commonly runs tasks as Kubernetes pods
- [Data Engineering Roadmap](/roadmaps/data-engineering/) — where orchestration and infrastructure fit into the broader curriculum

## Apache Flink: Stream Processing Framework

**Flink is a distributed engine built around one idea — that batch is just a special, bounded case of streaming — which is what lets a single runtime handle real-time event processing and large-scale batch jobs with the same execution model.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

Every Flink program follows the same shape — **Source → Transformation → Sink** — executed as a distributed dataflow graph coordinated by a **JobManager** and run by **TaskManagers**, each offering a fixed number of **task slots** that bound how much work it can execute in parallel. Flink distinguishes three notions of time — **event time** (when something actually happened), **ingestion time**, and **processing time** — and uses **watermarks** to reason about how far event time has progressed despite out-of-order arrival, which is what makes **windowing** (tumbling, sliding, session) correct over unbounded streams. For reliability, Flink periodically snapshots operator **state** — held in a pluggable state backend (in-memory, filesystem, or RocksDB) — into **checkpoints

**, using a barrier-based algorithm so a failed job can recover from a consistent point without losing or duplicating results. That checkpointing mechanism, combined with a two-phase-commit protocol at the sinks, is the basis of Flink's end-to-end exactly-once guarantee.

---
## Interview Questions

### Fundamentals, Architecture & Deployment

What Flink is, how it compares to Spark and Hadoop, and the shapes it can be deployed in.

<QuestionList topic="Fundamentals, Architecture & Deployment" storagePrefix="flink-fund">

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-01" number={1} question="Can you briefly introduce Apache Flink?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Flink is a real-time computing framework, and like Spark it's a unified batch-and-stream processing engine. It provides both bounded (batch) and unbounded (streaming) stream computation, treating streaming as the general case and batch as the special case with a defined boundary. Its main external APIs are the DataSet API, DataStream API, and Table API, alongside libraries for graph computing (Gelly) and machine learning (Flink

ML). It offers language interfaces for Java, Scala, and Python.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-02" number={2} question="What is Apache Flink?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Apache Flink is an open-source, unified stream- and batch-processing framework created by the Apache Software Foundation. It's built around a distributed streaming dataflow engine written in Java and Scala, and it runs every dataflow program in a data-parallel, pipelined fashion.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-03" number={3} question="What are the differences between Flink and Spark Streaming?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
- **Design philosophy** — Flink treats batch processing as a special case of streaming; Spark treats streaming as a special case of batch (mi

cro-batching).
- **Architecture** — Spark has Driver, Master, Worker, and Executor. Flink has JobManager, TaskManager, Task, SubTask, and Slot.
- **Streaming depth** — Flink's streaming support is considerably richer: it supports three notions of time (event, ingestion, processing) versus Spark's more limited model, and offers more window types.
- **Out-of-order handling** — Flink handles out-of-order data better via watermarks: a window is triggered once the watermark (current time minus the configured out-of-order allowance) passes the window's end.
- **Fault tolerance** — Flink supports two-phase-commit transactions, so a program crash doesn't cause data to be reprocessed. Spark also has checkpoints, but they only guarantee data isn't lost — not that it won't be reprocessed/duplicat

ed.

On the deeper "why," Flink and Spark are both trying to be a similar "open source technology stack" — batch, streaming, graph computation, interactive query, and machine learning, all in-memory. The key architectural difference is that Spark's compute model is built on the RDD: it treats streaming as a special batch case, and its `DStream` abstraction is really just a sequence of RDDs underneath. Flink instead treats batch as a special streaming case, but internally still runs two distinct engines abstracted as the `DataSet` and `DataStream` APIs. Flink also tends to perform better on streaming latency — it does true continuous stream computation rather than Spark's micro-batch ("quasi-streaming") approach — and its batch performance improves relative to Spark as iteration counts in

crease, though Spark has historically had the more mature batch engine.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-04" number={4} question="Explain Apache Flink's architecture." difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Apache Flink is based on the **Kappa architecture**, which uses a single stream processor: everything is treated as a stream, and the streaming engine processes data in real time, with batch data modeled as a special, bounded form of streaming data.

This contrasts with the **Lambda architecture** that most big data frameworks are built on, which uses separate processors — and separate codebases — for batch and streaming views, requiring those views to be merged to answer a query. Maintaining and combining separate codebases is a real operational cost; Kappa avoids

it by having only one real-time view and one processing engine, eliminating the need to merge codebases at query time. That said, Kappa isn't unconditionally "better" than Lambda — which architecture is optimal depends on the use case.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-05" number={5} question="What are the Flink component stacks?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Flink's stack spans several layers:

- **Deployment** — Local, Cluster, or Cloud, and standalone/YARN-managed cluster modes.
- **Runtime** — the layer performing Flink's basic distributed services.
- **Core APIs** — the DataStream API (streaming) and DataSet API (batch) sit above the runtime.
- **High-level libraries** — Table API (SQL-like relational queries), CEP (complex event processing), FlinkML

(machine learning), and Gelly (graph processing).
- **Storage/connectors** — at the storage level Flink supports file systems like HDFS and the local filesystem, and databases like HBase and MongoDB.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-06" number={6} question="What are the features of Apache Flink?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- Uses a common runtime for both streaming and batch applications.
- Can run both batch and stream programs on the same engine.
- Provides multiple APIs (DataSet, DataStream, Table).
- Very high processing speed with low latency.
- Integrates easily with big data tools like Hadoop and MapReduce.
- Highly scalable.
- Fault tolerant, via state snapshots and checkpointing.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-07" number={7}

question="What are the features of the Apache Flink execution engine?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
At its core, Flink is a robust, distributed dataflow engine that executes programs as a stream, using cyclic dataflow execution. It provides cost-based optimization for both batch and streaming programs, aiming for optimal execution plans, and it's built to operate within distributed memory rather than shuffling everything through disk.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-08" number={8} question="Does Flink need to depend on Hadoop?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
No — Flink can run completely independently of Hadoop, without relying on any of its components. That said, as a foundational piece of the big data ecosystem, Hadoop is hard to fully avoid in pract

ice: Flink supports YARN for resource scheduling, HBase for real-time data storage and dimension-table access, and HDFS for state storage and offline computation, among other integrations.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-09" number={9} question="Can Apache Flink be considered an alternative to Hadoop? If so, why?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
Yes, with caveats. Flink offers more features and flexibility than Hadoop's classic MapReduce because it uses a cyclic dataflow programming model rather than MapReduce's two-stage, disk-bound model. Flink programs can run in memory and aren't tied exclusively to Hadoop's filesystem — they work with other filesystems too. Flink also provides a unified framework where a single data flow can combine batch, streaming, machine

learning, and SQL queries, which classic Hadoop MapReduce doesn't offer on its own.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-10" number={10} question="What are the use cases of Apache Flink?" difficulty="easy" topic="Use Cases">
Real-world industries using Apache Flink include:

- **Financial Services** — real-time fraud detection with mobile notifications.
- **Healthcare** — collecting data from devices like MRI machines and IV pumps for real-time issue detection and analysis.
- **Ad Tech** — determining real-time customer preferences.
- **Oil & Gas** — real-time monitoring of pumping operations and issue detection.
- **Telecommunications** — real-time billing/payment views, per-user antenna location optimization, and mobile offers.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="fli

nk-fund-11" number={11} question="What are the most common types of applications that use Apache Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Use Cases">
- **Event-driven applications** — fraud detection, anomaly detection, rule-based alerting, and similar patterns.
- **Data analytics applications** — quality checks for telecom data, mobile application product analysis, and similar reporting use cases.
- **Data pipeline applications** — for example, building search indexes for e-commerce.

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-12" number={12} question="What are the different ways to deploy and use Apache Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-13" number={13} question="How would you size a Flink cluster for production?" difficulty="medium" topic="Deployment">

YARN itself supports multiple deployment modes — running each job as its own isolated YARN application ("per-job" mode) versus applying for a large, shared pool of resources up front and submitting many jobs into it ("session" mode). Per-job mode is the more common choice, since it isolates resource usage and failures between jobs.

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-14" number={14} questio

n="What are the roles in a Flink cluster, and what are their functions?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Flink programs are driven by three roles at runtime:

- **JobManager** — the cluster's coordinator/manager. It receives submitted Flink jobs, coordinates checkpoints, recovers from failures, and manages the TaskManagers.
- **TaskManager** — responsible for the resources on the node it runs on (memory, disk, network), and reports those resources to the JobManager when it starts.
- **Client** — created when a user submits a Flink program; it preprocesses the submitted program and then submits it to the cluster for execution.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-15" number={15} question="Explain the Apache Flink job execution architecture." difficulty="medium" to

pic="Architecture">
- **Program** — the code that gets executed on the Flink cluster.
- **Client** — takes the submitted program's code and builds a job dataflow graph from it, which is passed to the JobManager. It's also responsible for retrieving job data back from the cluster.
- **JobManager** — takes the Job Dataflow Graph from the Client and generates the execution graph, assigns the job's tasks to TaskManagers across the cluster, and monitors execution.
- **TaskManager** — executes all tasks assigned to it by the JobManager, running them in its slots at the specified parallelism, and reports task status back to the JobManager.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-16" number={16} question="What is the responsibility of the JobManager in an Apache Flink cluster?" diffic

ulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
The JobManager manages and coordinates the distributed processing of a program: it assigns tasks to TaskManagers, handles failure recovery, and performs checkpointing. Internally it's composed of three components — the ResourceManager, the Dispatcher, and the JobMaster.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-17" number={17} question="What is the responsibility of the TaskManager in an Apache Flink cluster?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
The TaskManager executes the dataflow tasks assigned to it and returns results to the JobManager. It runs each task inside a slot, so the number of slots a TaskManager offers determines how many tasks it can execute concurrently.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-fund-18" number={18} ques

tion="Can Flink replace Spark's batch processing capabilities?" difficulty="hard" topic="Comparison">
Flink's long-term goal is to fully unify batch and streaming, since a bounded dataset can be understood as just a finite stream. Flink has invested heavily here — especially since Flink 1.9, which added deep Hive integration, letting Flink SQL read Hive's metadata and datasets and process them with Flink SQL logic. That said, at present Flink's raw batch-processing performance still generally trails Spark's, which has the more mature and heavily optimized batch engine. Flink remains the stronger choice specifically when real-time/streaming processing is the priority.
</QuestionCard>

### Programming Model, APIs & Tooling

Parallelism, slots, the DataSet/DataStream/Table APIs, and the SQL and CLI tooling around them.

<QuestionList topic="Programming Model, APIs & Tooling" storagePrefix="flink-api">

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-01" number={20} question="What is the Flink programming model?" difficulty="easy" topic="Programming Model">
At its simplest, every Flink program follows the shape **Source → Transformation → Sink**. Flink exposes this through two complementary programming models: the **DataStream** model for real-time stream processing, and the **DataSet** model for batch processing — both sitting above Flink's other architectural layers (runtime, and the higher-level Table/CEP/ML/graph libraries).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-02" numbe

r={21} question="What is a TaskSlot in Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
A TaskManager is a single JVM process — the actual worker node that executes your program. To achieve resource isolation and parallel execution, Flink introduces the concept of a **TaskSlot**, which controls how many tasks a given TaskManager can accept. For example, a source operator with a parallelism of 3 uses 3 slots. Operators that share the same degree of parallelism and don't require a shuffle between them (i.e. their output doesn't need to be redistributed) can be chained together into the same slot — a scheduling optimization that avoids unnecessary network/serialization overhead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-03" number={22} question="What is parallelism in Flink, and how d

o you set it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
Parallelism is the number of parallel instances Flink runs for a given operator. For example, a Kafka source's parallelism defaults to the number of partitions in the topic it reads from. The degree of parallelism you choose for an operator determines how many task slots it needs — that's the core lever for scaling out computation. In general, parallelism should be set according to data volume: it's usually best to keep source and map operators un-shuffled (since they're rarely the bottleneck), while operators later in the pipeline — once the data has been "widened" by joins or enrichment — often need a higher degree of parallelism.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-04" number={23} question="What is the relationship be

tween a Flink slot and parallelism?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
A **slot** is a TaskManager-level concept — it determines how many slots a given TaskManager offers, which caps how much parallelism it can support. **Parallelism** is a program/execution-level concept — how many parallel instances the developer's job actually uses. In short, the TaskManager is the *provider* of slots, and the running program is the *consumer* of them.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-05" number={24} question="What are the commonly used operators in Flink?" difficulty="easy" topic="Programming Model">
- `Map`
- `Filter`
- `KeyBy`
- `Window`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-06" number={25} question="What is the DataSet API in Apache Flink?" difficulty="medium" t

opic="APIs">
The DataSet API is used for batch operations over data, available in Java, Scala, and Python. It performs transformations on datasets such as filtering, mapping, aggregating, joining, and grouping — internally, batch processing is treated as a special case of stream processing over a bounded source. Datasets are created from sources like files or local collections, and results are written out through sinks; execution can run in a local JVM or across a cluster of machines.

```java
DataSet<Tuple2<String, Integer>> wordCounts = text
    .flatMap(new LineSplitter())
    .groupBy(0)
    .sum(1);
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-07" number={26} question="What is the DataStream API in Apache Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="APIs">
The DataStream API han

dles data as a continuous stream, supporting operations like filtering, routing, windowing, and aggregation. It can read from different source types — message queues, files, socket streams — and write results to different sinks, such as a command-line terminal. It's supported by both Java and Scala.

```java
DataStream<Tuple2<String, Integer>> dataStream = env
    .socketTextStream("localhost", 9091)
    .flatMap(new Splitter())
    .keyBy(0)
    .timeWindow(Time.seconds(7))
    .sum(1);
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-08" number={27} question="What is the Apache Flink Table API?" difficulty="medium" topic="APIs">
The Table API is a relational API with an expression language similar to SQL, capable of both batch and stream processing. It's interoperable with t

he Dataset and Datastream APIs — tables can be created from an internal DataSet/DataStream or from an external data source. It supports operations like join, select, aggregate, and filter, and crucially, query semantics are the same regardless of whether the input is batch or streaming.

```scala
val tableEnvironment = TableEnvironment.getTableEnvironment(env)
// register a Table
tableEnvironment.registerTable("TestTable1", ...)
// create a new Table from a Table API query
val newTable2 = tableEnvironment.scan("TestTable1").select(...)
```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-api-10" number={29} question="What is Apache FlinkML?" difficulty="medium" topic="Libraries">
