### State, Time, Windowing & Watermarks

Event time vs. processing time, watermarks, window types, and how Flink models and stores state.

<QuestionList topic="State, Time, Windowing & Watermarks" storagePrefix="flink-state">

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-01" number={38} question="What is the difference between stream processing and batch processing?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
In batch processing, the data is a bounded set with a defined start and end point, so processing only begins once the entire dataset has been ingested. In stream processing, the data is unbounded — there's no defined end — so processing is continuous, handling events as they arrive rather than waiting for a complete dataset.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-02" number={39} quest

ion="What are unbounded streams in Apache Flink?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streams">
Any kind of data can be produced as a stream of events, and Flink can process that stream as unbounded or bounded. **Unbounded** streams have a beginning but no defined end — they don't terminate, and continue supplying data as it's produced. Because the input is unbounded and never "complete," unbounded streams must be processed continuously, handling events as soon as they're consumed rather than waiting for everything to arrive. Processing unbounded data also sometimes requires consuming events in a specific order — such as the order they arrive in — in order to reason about the completeness of results.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-03" number={40} question="What are bounded streams

in Apache Flink, and what is bounded vs. unbounded data?" difficulty="easy" topic="Streams">
**Bounded** streams have both a beginning and an end point. They can be processed by consuming all of the data before performing any computation, and — since a bounded dataset can always be sorted — ordered ingestion isn't required to process them correctly. Processing bounded streams this way is also called **batch processing**.

Put together: bounded data has a start and an end, so computation only starts once all the data has arrived; unbounded data has a start but no end, so processing is continuous and never waits for "all" the data, since there is no "all."
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-04" number={41} question="What kinds of time exist in Flink?" difficulty="medium" t

opic="Time Semantics">
- **Event time** — the time an event actually occurred, typically embedded in the event itself.
- **Ingestion time** — the time the event entered Flink.
- **Processing time** — the time the event reaches and is handled by a given operator.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-05" number={42} question="What is a watermark in Flink?" difficulty="hard" topic="Time Semantics">
A watermark is Flink's mechanism for handling out-of-order data when working with event time. Since real-world sources like Kafka partitions can deliver events out of order across partitions (even if each partition is internally ordered), Flink triggers a window based on the *minimum* watermark across all relevant partitions — every partition has to reach the trigger point before t

he window fires. Concretely, a window is triggered once the maximum observed event time minus the watermark's allowed lateness exceeds the window's end time.

For example, with a window size of 5 seconds and a watermark (allowed out-of-order lag) of 2 seconds, the effective trigger delay is 7 seconds: if the first window covers event time `[0, 5000)`ms, it won't actually fire until the watermark passes `6999`ms; the next window, covering `[5000, 10000)`ms, fires once the watermark passes `13999`ms (i.e. once `10999`ms of event time is confirmed to have fully arrived across all partitions).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-06" number={43} question="What windows does Flink support?" difficulty="medium" topic="Windowing">
Flink supports dividing a stream into windows based

on time or count (a session window is also, conceptually, time-based):

- **Tumbling Count Window** — fires once a fixed count of elements is reached; windows don't overlap.
- **Sliding Time Window** — fires once a period of time is reached, and windows *can* overlap — commonly used for "recent N minutes" style metrics.
- **Tumbling Time Window** — fires once a period of time is reached, with no overlap between windows — effectively a micro-batch.
- **Sliding Count Window** — fires once a count is reached, with overlap between windows.
- **Session Window** — has no fixed size; boundaries are determined by a gap parameter the user supplies, and windows don't overlap. Commonly used for something like grouping a user's activity between login and logout.
</QuestionCard>

```
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-08" number={45} question="What are Flink's state storage backends?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Flink often needs to store intermediate state during a computation to avoid data loss and support recovery from failure. The choice of state backend affects how the JobManager and each subtask interact when persisting state. Flink provides three:

- `MemoryStateBackend`
- `FsStateBackend`
- `RocksDBStateBackend`
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-09" number={46} question="What can you do with state in Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
State in Flink is mainly used two ways:

- **Checkpoint-based data recovery** — restoring a job to a consistent point after a failure.
- **Logical computation** — using state to hold intermediate results needed by the application's own business logic (e.g. running aggregates, deduplication).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-10" number={47} question="How does keyedProcessFunction work in Flink?" difficulty="hard" topic="State">
`KeyedProcessFunction` supports registering an `onTimer` callback. Whether it fires depends on which time characteristic is in use: with event time, Flink checks whether the current watermark has passed the registered trigger time before firing; if not, the timer waits. For a source like Kafka, since partitions can be out of sync, the effective trigger point is governed by the earlies

t (minimum) watermark across all partitions for that key.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-11" number={48} question="What are the building blocks of Apache Flink streaming applications?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fundamentals">
Applications that run on a Flink cluster are defined around three building blocks for stream processing: **Streams**, **State**, and **Time**.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-12" number={49} question="What is Flink's distributed cache?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Flink's distributed cache works similarly to Hadoop's: it reads a file once and places it locally on each TaskManager node, so tasks don't repeatedly re-fetch the same data — reducing unnecessary I/O and improving performance.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard i

d="flink-state-13" number={50} question="What are broadcast variables in Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="State">
Because Flink executes in parallel, a given computation may run across many different task slots, and sometimes every one of those parallel instances needs access to the same data. Broadcast variables solve this: you broadcast a dataset once, and it becomes available as a shared, read-only variable to every parallel task — with only a single copy of that data held on each node, not one copy per task.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-14" number={51} question="A brief introduction to CEP and state programming in Flink." difficulty="hard" topic="CEP">
**Complex Event Processing (CEP)** is Flink's library for detecting patterns across an endless stream of event

s. It lets you match a sequence of simple events against a defined rule (a pattern potentially spanning one or more streams), and outputs the complex events that satisfy that rule.

Alongside CEP, Flink also provides primitives for aggregating data **without** a window:

- `ValueState` — holds a single value.
- `ListState` — holds a list of elements.
- `MapState` — holds a set of key-value pairs.
- `ReducingState` — has the same interface as `ListState` but returns a single value aggregated via a `ReduceFunction`.
- `AggregatingState` — similar to `ReducingState`, but returns a value that may have a different internal type than the elements added to it, via an `AggregateFunction`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-15" number={52} question="When should you use aggreg

ate vs. process?" difficulty="medium" topic="Windowing">
- **`aggregate`** — performs incremental aggregation, updating a running result as each element arrives. Use it for cumulative/rolling computations.
- **`process`** — performs computation over the full, materialized contents of a window at once. Use it when the operation genuinely needs the complete window's data together — for example, sorting elements within the window.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-state-16" number={53} question="How do you handle late-arriving data in Flink?" difficulty="hard" topic="Time Semantics">
Watermarks are fundamentally a delayed-trigger mechanism, and they're what Flink uses (paired with windows) to process out-of-order data. For example, with a maximum allowed out-of-order time of 2 se

conds and a window size of 5 seconds, a window covering event time up to `T` won't fire until the watermark passes `T + 2s` — effectively a 7-second worst-case delay for that window's data. When the source is partitioned (as with Kafka), the watermark that actually drives triggering is the *minimum* watermark across all partitions, since only the slowest partition's progress guarantees that all earlier data has genuinely arrived.

Beyond watermarks, Flink also supports an explicit **allowed lateness** on windows (processing updates for events that arrive after the watermark but within the allowance) and **side outputs** for routing events that arrive too late even for that — so they aren't silently dropped.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

### Fault Tolerance, Checkpointing & Operations

Recovery guarantees, checkpoint tuning, serialization, and handling skew and bad data in production.

<QuestionList topic="Fault Tolerance, Checkpointing & Operations" storagePrefix="flink-ops">

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-01" number={54} question="What happens if a Flink program encounters an abnormal restart?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
Flink offers configurable restart strategies, and as long as checkpointing is enabled, a restarted job can resume with at-least-once (or, with the right components, exactly-once) semantics rather than starting from scratch. A common choice is a fixed-delay restart strategy; restarting doesn't delete existing checkpoints. A typical production setup might cap retries at, say, 4 attem

pts — alerting the team if the job still fails after that — and always resume from the last successful checkpoint on restart.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-02" number={55} question="How does Apache Flink handle fault tolerance?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
For streaming applications, Flink manages fault tolerance by periodically capturing a snapshot of the streaming dataflow's state; if a failure occurs, that snapshot is used to recover. For batch processing, Flink instead uses the program's sequence of transformations to recompute and recover the necessary data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-03" number={56} question="How does Flink guarantee exactly-once (accurate one-time) processing?" difficulty="hard" topic="Fault Tolerance">
Flink

relies on two complementary mechanisms:

**1. Checkpoint mechanism** — When checkpointing is enabled, Flink injects a *barrier* at the source, and that barrier flows downstream alongside the actual data. When the barrier reaches an operator, that operator snapshots its state as of that point and writes it to the configured state backend. When the barrier reaches a `keyBy` or shuffle operator fed by multiple upstream streams, Flink performs **barrier alignment** — it waits until the barrier has arrived from every upstream input before triggering that operator's checkpoint, then lets the barrier continue downstream. When the barrier reaches the sink, the sink completes its own checkpoint and reports completion back to the JobManager, which finalizes checkpoint *n* only once every operator

has confirmed.

**2. Two-phase commit (2PC)** — Flink exposes `CheckpointedFunction` and `CheckpointListener`. `CheckpointedFunction` provides a `snapshotState()` method, invoked every time a checkpoint is triggered — this is where an operator typically flushes buffered/cached data into state, acting as a pre-commit. `CheckpointListener` provides `notifyCheckpointComplete()`, called only after a checkpoint has been confirmed complete — this is where the actual commit happens. `FlinkKafkaConsumer`/producer use this to commit Kafka offsets only once the corresponding checkpoint is durably complete. If a checkpoint fails partway through, it rolls back with no impact on consistency; if a checkpoint is reported complete but the job then crashes before the listener callback runs, the pending

transaction is committed on restart inside `initializeState()`, based on the checkpoint's persisted state — guaranteeing the commit still happens exactly once.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-04" number={57} question="Is there any possibility of data loss in Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
Flink supports three data consumption semantics:

- **At-Most-Once** — a message is consumed at most once; on failure, data may be lost.
- **At-Least-Once** — a message is consumed at least once; on failure, data may be duplicated.
- **Exactly-Once** — a message is processed exactly once; failures don't cause loss or duplication.

Newer versions of Flink no longer offer At-Most-Once as an option, since Exactly-Once and At-Least-Once cover essentially all produc

tion needs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-05" number={58} question="How do you troubleshoot a Flink checkpoint that keeps timing out?" difficulty="hard" topic="Fault Tolerance">
Work through these in order:

1. Check for network issues between nodes.
2. Check for barrier-related problems (e.g. barriers stuck waiting on a slow upstream operator).
3. Check the Flink web UI for signs of data skew across subtasks.
4. If skew is present, fixing the skew itself is usually what resolves the checkpoint timeout, since one overloaded subtask can hold up barrier alignment for the whole checkpoint.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-06" number={59} question="How do you maintain (retain multiple) checkpoints in Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fault Tolerance">
B

y default, if checkpointing is enabled, Flink only retains the single most recently completed checkpoint, and recovers from that one if the job fails. To retain more than one and be able to choose which to recover from — useful for more flexible recovery — configure the maximum number of retained checkpoints in `conf/flink-conf.yaml` via the `state.checkpoints.num-retained` setting.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-07" number={60} question="How do Spark Streaming and Flink differ in their checkpoint behavior?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
Spark Streaming's checkpoint mechanism can lead to repeated (duplicated) consumption of data on recovery. Flink's checkpoint mechanism, by contrast, guarantees exactly-once processing, and can be incremental for faster checkpoin

ting. Flink supports three checkpoint state backends: in-memory, RocksDB, and HDFS.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-08" number={61} question="What is the difference between Spark and Flink serialization?" difficulty="medium" topic="Comparison">
Spark defaults to Java's built-in serialization, with Kryo available as an optimization on top of it. Flink uses its own, self-implemented serialization mechanism, built around its `TypeInformation` system.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-09" number={62} question="How do you handle data skew in a Flink job?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
First, confirm the skew: the Flink web UI shows the amount of data each subtask processes, and a serious skew looks like most subtasks handling, say, 100 MB while one handl

es only 1 MB (or vice versa). From there, the fix depends on where the skew originates:

- **Skew at the Kafka source** — often caused by upstream key hotspots. Apply load balancing right after ingestion, before any `keyBy`.
- **Skew in an aggregation operator** — apply pre-aggregation (a local/partial aggregate) followed by a global aggregation, so no single key's full volume has to flow through one subtask.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-10" number={63} question="How do you associate a stream with offline (dimension) data — i.e. how do you do dimension table lookups?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
Common approaches, roughly in order of sophistication:

1. **Async I/O** — issue non-blocking lookups against the external store so throughput isn't gated by loo

kup latency.
2. **Broadcast** — broadcast the (typically small, slowly-changing) dimension dataset to every task so lookups are purely local.
3. **Async I/O + cache** — combine async I/O with a local cache to cut down on repeated external lookups.
4. **Periodic refresh via `open()`** — load the dimension data in the operator's `open()` method, then refresh it on a fixed schedule from a background thread, typically by deleting the stale cache entry first and then repopulating it (and writing the update back to the cache) — trading a small window of staleness for simplicity.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-11" number={64} question="How do you handle abnormal (bad) data in Flink?" difficulty="hard" topic="Data Quality">
Abnormal data generally falls into two categories:

- **Outliers** — for example, an implausible customer age value in a maternal/infant e-commerce dataset (a field that matters a great deal for that business, since very few customers over a certain age are buying maternity or infant products). Common patterns include values like "unknown" or clearly-wrong ages. These are typically surfaced to store and regional managers so they're aware of the scale of the problem. Where a value can be corrected, it's fixed in real time using surrounding purchase context (e.g. maternity-wear size, infant formula stage, diaper size can all hint at the likely correct age range). Where real-time correction isn't practical, a lower-priority batch job (e.g. run nightly or weekly) handles the correction instead.
- **Missing fields** — fixed if there's enough c

ontext to safely infer the value, and discarded otherwise. A common example: filtering out records with missing fields entirely in a downstream recommendation pipeline.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-12" number={65} question="What is the difference between Flink's TopN and offline TopN computations?" difficulty="hard" topic="Performance">
TopN is a common requirement in both offline and real-time computing, but streaming TopN is meaningfully harder than its offline counterpart. In offline computing, TopN is computed once over a complete, static dataset. In streaming, data is continuous and never "complete," so Flink has to maintain an in-memory TopN data structure that's continuously updated as each new record arrives — recomputing incrementally rather than from scratch.

</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="flink-ops-13" number={66} question="How do you decide parallelism and allocate resources when submitting a Flink job?" difficulty="medium" topic="Performance">
A common approach is to base the job's parallelism on the partition count of its Kafka source topic — for example, matching a topic with 3 partitions to a parallelism of 3, with each parallel task allocated a defined amount of resources (e.g. a few GB of memory each), sized to the expected per-partition throughput.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a real-time fraud detection pipeline on top of Flink and Kafka."** Talk through event-time processing so out-of-order card-swipe events are handled correctly, watermarks and allowed lateness for late data, `KeyedProcessFunction` or CEP for pattern detection, RocksDB as the state backend for a large key space, and checkpointing for exactly-once alerting.
- **"A Flink job's checkpoints keep timing out in production — how do you debug it?"** Walk through the standard checklist: network issues between TaskManagers, barrier alignment stalls, and — most commonly — data skew visible in the Flink web UI, then discuss fixes like pre-aggregation for a hot key or switching to unaligned checkpoints.
- **"How do you handle late-arriving events in a windowe

d aggregation without silently losing them?"** Explain the layered defense: watermarks with an out-of-order allowance, `allowedLateness` on the window itself for updates after the watermark passes, and a side output as the last resort so nothing is dropped without a trace.
- **"Walk through how you'd get exactly-once delivery from Kafka, through Flink, into a database sink."** Combine Flink's checkpoint barriers with a two-phase-commit sink (`CheckpointedFunction` for pre-commit, `CheckpointListener.notifyCheckpointComplete()` for the actual commit), the same pattern Flink's own Kafka connector uses for offset commits.

---

## Further Reading

- [Kafka](/level-3-technologies/streaming/kafka/) — the streaming source Flink is most commonly paired with in production pipelines
- [Spark](/level-3-technologies/batch-processing/spark/) — the engine Flink is most often compared against for both batch and streaming workloads
- [Data Engineering Roadmap](/roadmaps/data-engineering/) — where Flink fits into the broader curriculum

title: Streaming
description: Real-time data streaming technologies
---

## Streaming: Real-Time Data Processing

Streaming technologies enable real-time or near real-time data ingestion and processing.

## Technologies Covered

- **Kafka**: Distributed event streaming platform
- **Flink**: Stream processing framework

## Apache Kafka: Distributed Event Streaming

**Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log that decouples the systems producing data from the systems consuming it — the backbone most streaming architectures build on for durable, replayable, high-throughput messaging.**

## Table of Contents
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Interview Questions](#interview-questions)
- [Consumer Groups & Rebalancing](#consumer-groups--rebalancing)
- [Ecosystem: Connect, Streams & Schema Registry](#ecosystem-connect-streams--schema-registry)
- [Retention, Compaction & Security](#retention-compaction--security)
- [Common Interview Scenarios](#common-interview-scenarios)
- [Further Reading](#further-reading)

---

## Key Concepts

A **topic** is a named stream of records, split into **partitions** that are distributed and replicated across the **brokers** in a cluster — this is how Kafka scales horizontally and survives broker failures. Every record in a partition gets a monotonically increasing **offset**, and consumers (organized into **consumer groups**) track their own read position by committing offsets rather than the broker tracking per-consumer state. That single mechanism is what lets Kafka support both queue-like delivery (one consumer group splitting partitions among its members) and pub-sub delivery (many independent consumer groups each reading the whole topic) from the same underlying log. **Producers** write records to a partition, either directly or via a partitioning key that hash

es to one. Durability comes from **replication**: each partition has a leader replica that serves all reads/writes and follower replicas that copy it, with the **In-Sync Replica (ISR)** set tracking which followers are caught up enough to safely take over as leader if the current one fails.

---

## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="Kafka" storagePrefix="kafka">

<QuestionCard id="kafka-01" number={1} question="What is Apache Kafka?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Apache Kafka is a distributed publish-subscribe messaging system originally developed at LinkedIn and written in Java and Scala. At its core it's a distributed, partitioned, and replicated commit log service — a durable, append-only sequence of records that producers write to and consumers read from independently.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-02" number={2} question="What is the traditional method of transferring messages, and how does Kafka's consumer group model generalize it?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
Traditional messaging used two separate models:

- **Queuing** —

a pool of consumers reads from the server, and each message goes to exactly one of them (good for scaling out work, but no consumer sees every message).
- **Publish-Subscribe** — messages are broadcast to every consumer (good for fan-out, but you can't easily scale a single logical consumer across multiple processes).

Kafka's **consumer group** abstraction generalizes both: within a group, partitions are divided among members so each message is processed once per group (queue-like), while multiple independent groups can each subscribe to the same topic and get their own full copy of the stream (pub-sub-like).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-03" number={3} question="What are the benefits of Apache Kafka over traditional messaging techniques?" difficulty="medium" topic="Fund

amentals">
- **Scalability** — scales out horizontally by adding brokers to the cluster, handling more partitions and higher throughput without downtime.
- **Performance** — high throughput for both publishing and subscribing, using a disk structure optimized for sequential, batched writes and reads.
- **Durability and reliability** — replicates data across multiple brokers (configurable replication factor) so data survives individual broker failures.
- **Fault tolerance** — the distributed architecture, combined with replication, keeps the system operating even when individual components fail.
- **Real-time processing** — producers and consumers exchange data with minimal latency, supporting real-time analytics and monitoring.
- **Decoupling of data streams** — producers and consume

rs operate independently; neither needs to know about or coordinate with the other.
- **Replayability** — Kafka retains data for a configurable retention period, so applications can replay history or recover from errors by reprocessing.
- **High availability** — the distributed, replicated design keeps the system available even when some brokers or partitions are temporarily unavailable.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-04" number={4} question="What is the meaning of broker in Apache Kafka?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
A broker is a single server in a Kafka cluster that stores and manages data. Each broker holds a set of topic partitions, so Kafka spreads load across the cluster by distributing partitions among brokers. Brokers handle all producer and consumer rea

d/write requests and coordinate data replication to prevent data loss.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-05" number={5} question="What is the maximum size of a message that Kafka can receive?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
It's governed by two configuration parameters — `message.max.bytes` on the broker and `max.message.bytes` on the topic. By default Kafka allows messages up to 1 MB (1,048,576 bytes), but both parameters can be increased if the workload needs larger messages.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-06" number={6} question="What is ZooKeeper's role in Kafka's ecosystem, and can Kafka run without it?" difficulty="medium" topic="Architecture">
ZooKeeper historically managed and coordinated Kafka brokers — leader election for partitions, cluster mem

bership, and configuration management.

As of **KRaft mode** (Kafka Raft metadata mode), Kafka can run without ZooKeeper entirely. KRaft replaces it with a built-in Raft-based consensus mechanism for managing cluster metadata, simplifying the architecture and improving scalability.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-07" number={7} question="How are messages consumed by a consumer in Apache Kafka?" difficulty="easy" topic="Consumers">
Kafka consumers use a **pull-based model**. A consumer subscribes to one or more topics and polls the broker at regular intervals to fetch new messages, reading them in the order they're stored within each partition. Each consumer tracks its own offset per partition — the position of the next message to read — so it can resume exactly where it left

off after a restart or failure.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-08" number={8} question="How can you improve the throughput of a remote consumer?" difficulty="medium" topic="Consumers">
- **Increase bandwidth** — ensure the network connection has enough capacity for the data volume.
- **Optimize serialization** — use efficient formats to shrink the data being transmitted.
- **Concurrency** — process data in parallel where possible.
- **Batch processing** — batch records together to cut down on round trips.
- **Caching** — cache frequently accessed data on the consumer side.
- **Compression** — compress data before transmission.
- **Optimize network routes** — use better network paths or a CDN to cut latency.
- **Tune timeouts and buffers** — adjust network timeout and

buffer size settings for the connection.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-09" number={9} question="How can you achieve exactly-once messaging from Kafka during data production?" difficulty="hard" topic="Producers">
1. **Enable idempotence** — set `enable.idempotence=true` on the producer so retries after network errors don't create duplicates.
2. **Use the transactional API** — set `transactional.id` and wrap writes with `beginTransaction()`, `commitTransaction()`, and `abortTransaction()`. Either every message in the transaction is published, or none are.
3. **Configure supporting settings** — set `acks=all` (or `-1`) so every in-sync replica acknowledges the write, tune `retries`, and set `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1` when using transactions to avoid reordering

on retry.
4. **Keep partitioning consistent** — if message order matters, use a stable partitioning strategy so retries don't shuffle messages across partitions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-10" number={10} question="What is In-Sync Replicas (ISR) in Apache Kafka?" difficulty="medium" topic="Replication">
ISR is the set of replicas for a partition that are fully caught up with the leader. The **leader** replica handles all reads and writes for a partition; **follower** replicas replicate its log, and once a follower has replicated everything up to the leader's last acknowledged message, it's considered in-sync.

The ISR is what makes failover safe — if the leader fails, Kafka elects a new leader only from the ISR, minimizing data loss and downtime.
</QuestionCard>

<Q

uestionCard id="kafka-11" number={11} question="How can you reduce churn (frequent changes) in the ISR?" difficulty="medium" topic="Replication">
- **Optimize network configuration** — stable, sufficiently fast connections between brokers keep followers from falling behind and dropping out of the ISR.
- **Adjust replica lag configuration** — `replica.lag.time.max.ms` controls how far behind a replica can fall before it's considered out of sync; tuning it changes how much slack followers get.
- **Monitor and scale resources** — make sure every broker has enough CPU, memory, and disk I/O for its workload; overloaded brokers fall behind more easily.
- **Use dedicated replication networks** — isolating replication traffic from other network load prevents it from being starved.
</QuestionC

ard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-12" number={12} question="When does a broker leave the ISR?" difficulty="medium" topic="Replication">
- **Falling behind** — if a replica lags the leader beyond the configured thresholds (`replica.lag.time.max.ms` or `replica.lag.max.messages`), it's removed from the ISR.
- **Broker failure** — if a broker crashes or disconnects from the cluster, its replicas drop out of the ISR.
- **Manual intervention** — an administrator can remove a replica manually, though this is uncommon and should be done carefully.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-13" number={13} question="What does it indicate if a replica stays out of the ISR for a long time?" difficulty="medium" topic="Replication">
It means the replica can't keep up with the leader's log updates —

usually due to network issues, hardware problems, or high broker load. While it's out of the ISR, it can't participate in acknowledging writes and can't be elected leader if the current leader fails, so it becomes a risk to partition availability and durability until it catches back up.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-14" number={14} question="What happens if the preferred replica is not in the ISR list?" difficulty="medium" topic="Replication">
If the preferred (originally-assigned leader) replica isn't in the ISR, Kafka either waits for it to catch up (depending on the configured `acks` settings) or continues serving from another broker that is in the ISR — data integrity is preserved by only using fully up-to-date replicas. Consumers configured to read only from the prefer

red replica may see a delay in data availability until it rejoins the ISR.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-15" number={15} question="What is the purpose of replication in Apache Kafka?" difficulty="easy" topic="Replication">
Replication increases data availability and durability. By copying each partition's data across multiple brokers, Kafka ensures that a single broker failure doesn't lose data — it can still be read from the other replicas. This is fundamental to fault tolerance and high availability in production.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-16" number={16} question="Is it possible to get the message offset after producing to a topic?" difficulty="easy" topic="Producers">
Yes. When a producer sends a message, the producer API returns metadata about it, inc

luding the offset it was assigned within the topic partition — useful for tracking exactly where a given message landed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-17" number={17} question="What is the difference between Apache Kafka, Apache Storm, and Apache Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Ecosystem">
All three are distributed systems for processing large volumes of data, but they serve different roles:

- **Kafka** — primarily a distributed messaging/streaming platform focused on high-throughput, fault-tolerant storage and transport of streaming data. Often sits as the buffer between producers and consumers rather than doing the processing itself.
- **Storm** — a real-time computation system built for record-by-record processing with very low latency, well suited to immediate-res

ponse use cases like real-time analytics.
- **Flink** — a stream processing framework that also handles batch processing, known for event-time processing, stateful computation, and running complex computations at in-memory speed across common cluster environments.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-18" number={18} question="What are the main components of Kafka?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
- **Topic** — a stream of messages of the same type
- **Producer** — publishes messages to a topic
- **Broker** — a server that stores published messages
- **Consumer** — subscribes to topics and pulls data from brokers
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-19" number={19} question="What is the role of the offset in Kafka?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
The off

set is a unique, monotonically increasing identifier for each record within a partition — its position in that partition's log. Consumers use offsets to track which records they've already read, enabling fault-tolerant, scalable consumption: a consumer can resume from its committed offset after a restart or failure, so messages are neither lost nor reprocessed unnecessarily.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-20" number={20} question="Can you explain the concept of leader and follower in the Kafka ecosystem?" difficulty="easy" topic="Architecture">
Every partition has one broker acting as its **leader** and zero or more brokers acting as **followers**:

- **Leader** — handles all read and write requests for that partition. Produced messages are written to the leader first, whic

h stores them in order.
- **Follower** — continuously pulls messages from the leader to stay in sync, maintaining an exact copy of its data. If the leader broker fails, one of the in-sync followers is elected as the new leader, keeping the partition available.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-21" number={21} question="How do you define a partitioning key?" difficulty="medium" topic="Producers">
The partitioning key is supplied by the producer to determine which partition a message goes to. By default Kafka uses a hash-based partitioner on the key to pick the partition ID, but a custom `Partitioner` implementation can be supplied for other routing logic.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-22" number={22} question="In the Producer, when does a QueueFullException occur?"

difficulty="medium" topic="Producers">
It occurs when the producer is trying to send messages faster than the broker can handle them. Since the producer doesn't block by default in this scenario, the fix is to add enough brokers/capacity to the cluster to absorb the increased load rather than let the send buffer overflow.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-23" number={23} question="Can you explain the role of the Kafka Producer API?" difficulty="easy" topic="Producers">
The Producer API lets applications send streams of records to one or more Kafka topics, handling the reliable and scalable distribution of that data across the cluster. Kafka historically exposed two producer types — `SyncProducer` and `AsyncProducer` — with the goal of surfacing all producer functionality throu

gh a single, unified client API.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Consumer Groups & Rebalancing

What actually happens when consumers join, leave, or fail within a group.

<QuestionList topic="Consumer Groups & Rebalancing" storagePrefix="kafka-rebalance">

<QuestionCard id="kafka-24" number={24} question="What is consumer group rebalancing, and when does it get triggered?" difficulty="medium" topic="Rebalancing">
Rebalancing is the process of reassigning partitions among the members of a consumer group — triggered when a consumer joins, leaves (including crashing or being killed), or a subscribed topic's partition count changes. During a rebalance, consumption pauses while partitions are redistributed, which is why frequent rebalances (from flaky consumers or slow processing triggering session timeouts) directly hurt throughput.
</QuestionCar

d>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-25" number={25} question="What's the difference between eager and cooperative sticky rebalancing?" difficulty="hard" topic="Rebalancing">
**Eager rebalancing** (the original protocol) revokes *all* partitions from *every* consumer at the start of a rebalance, then reassigns them — even consumers keeping the same partitions briefly stop processing. **Cooperative sticky rebalancing** only reassigns the specific partitions that actually need to move, letting unaffected consumers keep processing uninterrupted — significantly reducing the "stop the world" pause, especially in large consumer groups.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-26" number={26} question="What is static group membership, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="hard" topic="Rebalan

cing">
Setting `group.instance.id` gives a consumer a persistent identity across restarts, so a brief restart or network blip (a rolling deploy, a pod restarting) doesn't trigger a full rebalance — Kafka recognizes the returning consumer and hands it back its previous partitions once it reconnects within `session.timeout.ms`. This avoids the throughput hit of unnecessary rebalances for routine, short-lived disruptions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-27" number={27} question="What's the difference between auto-commit and manual offset commit?" difficulty="medium" topic="Offsets">
With `enable.auto.commit=true` (the default), the client library commits the latest consumed offset on a timer, regardless of whether that record has actually finished processing — simple, but risks

marking a message "done" before it's safely written downstream, losing it on a crash. Manual commit (`commitSync()`/`commitAsync()`) lets you commit only after processing genuinely completes, trading a bit of code complexity for control over exactly when a message counts as consumed.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Ecosystem: Connect, Streams & Schema Registry

The tools built around core Kafka for getting data in/out and enforcing message structure.

<QuestionList topic="Ecosystem" storagePrefix="kafka-ecosystem">

<QuestionCard id="kafka-28" number={28} question="What is Kafka Connect, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Kafka Connect">
Kafka Connect is a framework for moving data between Kafka and external systems (databases, S3, Elasticsearch) using pre-built, configuration-only **connectors**, instead of hand-writing a custom producer or consumer application for every integration. It handles the operational concerns (scaling, offset tracking, fault tolerance, restarts) generically, so adding a new source or destination is usually a config file, not new code.
</

QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-29" number={29} question="What's the difference between a source connector and a sink connector?" difficulty="easy" topic="Kafka Connect">
A **source connector** pulls data from an external system *into* a Kafka topic (a Postgres CDC connector streaming database changes in). A **sink connector** pushes data *out of* a Kafka topic into an external system (an S3 sink connector writing consumed records out as files). Both run inside the same Kafka Connect cluster, just moving data in opposite directions.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-30" number={30} question="What is Kafka Streams, and how does it differ from using an external engine like Flink?" difficulty="medium" topic="Stream Processing">
Kafka Streams is a Java library for building

stream processing applications that read from and write to Kafka topics, running as a normal application process rather than on a separate cluster — no separate job manager or cluster to operate, unlike Flink. The trade-off is scope: Kafka Streams is tightly coupled to Kafka as both source and sink and has a narrower feature set than a general-purpose engine like Flink, which can read from many sources and offers more advanced windowing/state-management capabilities.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-31" number={31} question="What is Schema Registry, and why is it important for Kafka pipelines?" difficulty="medium" topic="Schema Registry">
Schema Registry is a service that stores and versions schemas (typically Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema) for the messages flowing through Ka

fka topics, and validates that producers/consumers use compatible schemas. Without it, a producer can silently start sending a differently-shaped message and every consumer breaks independently and confusingly — with it, an incompatible schema change is rejected at publish time, with the failure surfacing at the actual source of the problem.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-32" number={32} question="What are the schema compatibility modes (backward, forward, full) in Schema Registry?" difficulty="hard" topic="Schema Registry">
**Backward** compatibility means a new schema can read data written with the previous schema (safe to upgrade consumers first). **Forward** compatibility means old schema code can read data written with the new schema (safe to upgrade producers first). **

Full** compatibility requires both directions to hold. Choosing the right mode up front determines which side (producers or consumers) you're free to deploy first without coordinating a synchronized rollout.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Retention, Compaction & Security

How long data actually stays in a topic, and controlling who can read or write it.

<QuestionList topic="Retention, Compaction & Security" storagePrefix="kafka-retention">

<QuestionCard id="kafka-33" number={33} question="What retention policies does Kafka support?" difficulty="easy" topic="Retention">
Retention is controlled per topic, primarily by **time** (`retention.ms` — delete segments older than this) and **size** (`retention.bytes` — delete oldest segments once the partition exceeds this size), whichever limit is hit first. This is separate from log compaction (a different retention *strategy* entirely, not just a different limit) — a topic can use time/size-based deletion, compaction, or both together.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard

id="kafka-34" number={34} question="What is log compaction, and how does it differ from time/size-based retention?" difficulty="hard" topic="Retention">
Log compaction retains only the **most recent** record for each key, discarding older records with the same key regardless of age — rather than deleting whole segments based on a time/size cutoff. It's the mechanism behind Kafka's use as a changelog for things like `__consumer_offsets` or Kafka Streams' state stores, where you only care about a key's current value, not its full history of updates.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-35" number={35} question="What are the trade-offs of increasing a topic's partition count?" difficulty="hard" topic="Partitioning">
More partitions mean more parallelism (more consumers in a group can

be active simultaneously) and higher potential throughput, but also more open file handles and memory overhead per broker, longer leader-election time during failover, and — critically — partition count can only be **increased**, never decreased, and increasing it changes key-to-partition hashing, which can break ordering guarantees for existing keyed data.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-36" number={36} question="How do you secure a Kafka cluster — authentication, authorization, and encryption?" difficulty="hard" topic="Security">
**Authentication** verifies client identity, typically via SASL (SASL/SCRAM, SASL/GSSAPI for Kerberos) or mutual TLS. **Authorization** is handled by ACLs, granting specific principals permission to produce/consume/manage specific topics or consume

r groups, rather than an all-or-nothing cluster credential. **Encryption** uses TLS for data in transit between clients and brokers (and between brokers themselves); disk-level encryption handles data at rest, usually via the underlying filesystem/cloud storage layer rather than Kafka itself.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="kafka-37" number={37} question="What are the different producer acks settings, and what do they trade off?" difficulty="medium" topic="Producers">
- **`acks=0`** — don't wait for any broker acknowledgment; fastest, but messages can be silently lost.
- **`acks=1`** — wait for the leader to write the message; if the leader fails before followers replicate it, it can still be lost.
- **`acks=all`** (or `-1`) — wait for every in-sync replica to acknowledge; stronge

st durability guarantee, at the cost of higher latency.

This is the core throughput-vs-durability dial for a Kafka producer, and `acks=all` combined with a sufficient `min.insync.replicas` is what's required for the strong delivery guarantees discussed elsewhere on this page.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"Design a Kafka pipeline for order events feeding fraud detection, analytics, and notifications."** Talk through topic and partition design, one consumer group per downstream system so each gets its own full copy of the stream, and the tradeoffs of partitioning by `order_id` vs. `customer_id` (ordering guarantees vs. even load distribution).
- **"A consumer group's lag keeps growing — how do you diagnose and fix it?"** Check partition count vs. consumer count (a group can't have more active consumers than partitions), per-message processing time, `poll()`/batch-size tuning, and whether scaling consumers up to the partition count resolves it.
- **"How would you guarantee exactly-once processing from Kafka into a downstream database?"** Idempotent produ

cers plus the transactional API on the write side, paired with idempotent writes downstream (upserts keyed on a dedup key, or storing the last-processed offset transactionally with the write).
- **"How do you handle a broker failure in production without losing data?"** Replication factor, `min.insync.replicas`, `acks=all` on the producer, and leader election constrained to the ISR so a stale replica never becomes leader.
- **"Consumers keep dropping out and rejoining during routine deploys, and throughput tanks every time."** Point to rebalancing as the cause, and static group membership (`group.instance.id`) plus cooperative sticky rebalancing as the fix — recognizing a returning consumer instead of treating every restart as a full membership change.
- **"A producing team wants to add

a field and rename another on a topic several teams consume."** Reach for Schema Registry and compatibility modes — talk through why adding a field is typically backward-compatible (safe) while a rename is usually a breaking change that needs a coordinated rollout or a new topic version.

---

## Further Reading

- [Flink](/level-3-technologies/streaming/flink/) — the stream processing engine most commonly paired with Kafka for stateful, event-time computation
- [Data Engineering Roadmap](/roadmaps/data-engineering/) — where Kafka fits into the broader curriculum
- [Change Data Capture](/level-3-technologies/ingestion/cdc/) — a common source pattern for getting data into Kafka topics in the first place
- [Data Quality](/level-2-core-concepts/data-quality/#interview-questions) — schema drift and contract enforcement, upstream of what Schema Registry solves for Kafka specifically

## Key Concepts

A **dbt model** is just a `SELECT` statement saved as a `.sql` file; dbt compiles it, resolves dependencies via `ref()`, and materializes it in the warehouse as a **view**, **table**, or **incremental** table. Projects are typically layered into **staging** (light cleaning, close to sources), **intermediate** (reusable joins/transforms), and **marts** (business-facing fact/dimension tables) — a structure that keeps models testable and reusable. **Incremental models** avoid full rebuilds by processing only new/changed rows, which requires a well-designed `unique_key` and a deterministic "latest record" rule. dbt's **testing** layer (generic tests like `unique`/`not_null`/`relationships`, plus custom singular tests) and **sources** with freshness checks catch broken data e

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
arly, while **snapshots** capture SCD2-style history from mutable source tables. **Macros** (Jinja functions) remove repetition, and **state selection** lets CI run only the models affected by a change instead of rebuilding the whole DAG. dbt itself only transforms — it's typically one step inside a broader pipeline orchestrated by a tool like Airflow.

---

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
## Interview Questions

<QuestionList topic="DBT" storagePrefix="dbt">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-01" number={1} question="What is dbt?" difficulty="easy" topic="Fundamentals">
dbt (data build tool) is a transformation framework where you write transformations as SQL (and Jinja-templated SQL), and dbt builds a DAG of models and runs them in the right order. It is commonly used to transform raw data into cleaned, documented, tested analytics tables in a warehouse/lakehouse.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-02" number={2} question="How is dbt different from Airflow?" difficulty="easy" topic="Orchestration">
Airflow is an orchestration system that schedules and coordinates tasks of any kind. dbt focuses specifically on SQL-based transformations and their dependency graph, plus test

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
ing and documentation. In practice, Airflow often runs dbt as one step of a larger pipeline (ingestion → transform → publish).
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-03" number={3} question="What is a dbt model?" difficulty="easy" topic="Models">
A dbt model is a select query stored as a `.sql` file in the `models/` directory. dbt materializes the model into a relation in your warehouse (view/table/incremental) and manages dependencies between models.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-04" number={4} question="What does ref() do?" difficulty="medium" topic="Models">
`ref('model_name')` declares a dependency on another dbt model. dbt uses it to build the DAG, order execution, and resolve the correct schema/database per environment. It also enables features like automated lineage

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
in dbt docs.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-05" number={5} question="What are the typical layers in a dbt project?" difficulty="medium" topic="Project Structure">
A common pattern is:
- **staging** — light cleaning and renaming, close to sources
- **intermediate** — reusable transformations and joins
- **marts** — business-facing fact/dimension tables and metrics-ready datasets

This makes models easier to test, reuse, and maintain.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-06" number={6} question="What is a materialization in dbt?" difficulty="easy" topic="Materializations">
A materialization defines how dbt builds a model in the warehouse (for example, as a view, table, or incremental table). It controls the build strategy and how changes are applied over time.
</Ques

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
tionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-07" number={7} question="When would you use view vs. table materializations?" difficulty="medium" topic="Materializations">
Views are useful for fast iteration and when compute cost per query is acceptable. Tables are useful when queries are expensive or many downstream queries reuse the same result. The trade-off is storage cost and the need to keep tables updated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-08" number={8} question="What is an incremental model and what problems does it solve?" difficulty="medium" topic="Incremental Models">
An incremental model only processes new or changed data instead of rebuilding the entire table each run. It reduces runtime and cost for large datasets. It requires correct keys and logic to avoid duplicates and miss

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
ed updates.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-09" number={9} question="How do you design a reliable unique_key?" difficulty="hard" topic="Incremental Models">
The `unique_key` should uniquely identify a record in the target table, usually a stable business key or a surrogate key derived from stable columns. If the source can update records, you also need a deterministic "latest record" rule (for example, using an `updated_at` column) so merges are correct.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-10" number={10} question="What are dbt tests and what types exist?" difficulty="medium" topic="Testing">
dbt supports:
- **generic tests** (built-in or custom): `unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values`, `relationships`
- **singular tests**: custom SQL queries that should return zero fa

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
iling rows

Tests run as queries in the warehouse and fail the run if assertions are violated.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-11" number={11} question="What are sources in dbt and how do you test them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Testing">
Sources declare upstream tables and their metadata in `sources.yml`. You can test sources with freshness checks and column-level tests (like `not_null`) to detect broken ingestion or schema drift early.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-12" number={12} question="What are snapshots in dbt and when would you use them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Snapshots">
Snapshots capture slowly changing dimension history by tracking changes in source records over time. They are useful when you need point-in-time analysis or to implement SCD2-styl

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
e history from mutable source tables.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-13" number={13} question="What are macros in dbt and when should you use them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Macros">
Macros are Jinja functions that generate SQL. Use them to avoid repetition (standardized column selection, reusable filters, dynamic SQL) and to keep business logic consistent across models. Overusing macros for complex logic can hurt readability and debugging.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-14" number={14} question="What is dbt state selection?" difficulty="hard" topic="CI/CD">
State selection runs only models that changed (and their dependents) compared to a previous artifact state. In CI, this reduces runtime by avoiding full rebuilds, while still validating that changes compile, r

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
un, and pass tests for affected parts of the DAG.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-15" number={15} question="How do you approach CI/CD for dbt projects?" difficulty="medium" topic="CI/CD">
A common approach is:
- **in CI**: `dbt deps`, `dbt compile`, run selected models/tests (state-based or tags)
- **in CD**: deploy artifacts and run scheduled jobs in production

You usually also enforce code review, documentation, and data tests for critical marts.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
## Seeds, Sources & Project Configuration

The parts of a dbt project that aren't models — static data, environment config, and runtime parameters.

<QuestionList topic="Seeds, Sources & Config" storagePrefix="dbt-config">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-16" number={16} question="What are seeds in dbt, and when should you use one?" difficulty="easy" topic="Seeds">
A seed is a CSV file in the `seeds/` directory that dbt loads into the warehouse as a table via `dbt seed`. They're meant for small, static, rarely-changing reference data you control directly — a country-code-to-region mapping, a list of holiday dates — not for actual source data, which should come from a real ingestion pipeline instead.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-17" number={17} question="What are environments and

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
targets in dbt (profiles.yml), and why do they matter?" difficulty="medium" topic="Configuration">
A `target` in `profiles.yml` defines a specific connection (dev, staging, prod) — its warehouse, schema, and credentials — and dbt commands run against whichever target is active. This lets the same model code build into a personal dev schema while developing and into the shared production schema when deployed, without changing a single line of SQL.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-18" number={18} question="What are dbt variables, and how do you use them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Configuration">
```yaml

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
# dbt_project.yml
vars:
  start_date: '2024-01-01'
```
```sql
{% if var('is_full_refresh', false) %} ... {% endif %}
```
```bash
dbt run --vars '{"start_date": "2024-06-01"}'
```
Variables let you parameterize model logic without hardcoding values — a cutoff date, a feature flag, an environment-specific limit — set as defaults in `dbt_project.yml` and optionally overridden per invocation with `--vars`.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-19" number={19} question="What are exposures, and why declare them?" difficulty="medium" topic="Documentation">
An exposure declares a downstream consumer of dbt models — a BI dashboard, an ML pipeline, a reverse-ETL sync — as a first-class object in `dbt docs`, linked to the specific models it depends on. Declaring them means anyone chang

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
ing a model can see, right in the DAG/docs, which dashboards or downstream systems that change might break, instead of finding out from an angry Slack message after the dashboard goes blank.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-20" number={20} question="What is the purpose of dbt_project.yml, and what kinds of settings live there?" difficulty="easy" topic="Configuration">
`dbt_project.yml` is the project-wide configuration file — it sets the project name, declares folder paths (`model-paths`, `seed-paths`), and configures default materializations, tags, and variables per directory (e.g., all models under `models/marts/` default to `materialized: table`). Model-level `.yml` files can still override these project-wide defaults for a specific model.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
## Materializations & Incremental Strategies

Going deeper than view/table/incremental — the fourth materialization type, and how incremental models actually apply changes.

<QuestionList topic="Materializations & Incremental Strategies" storagePrefix="dbt-materializations">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-21" number={21} question="What is an ephemeral materialization, and when would you use one?" difficulty="medium" topic="Materializations">
An ephemeral model isn't built as its own view or table in the warehouse at all — it's inlined as a CTE into every model that references it via `ref()`. Use it for a small, intermediate transformation step that exists purely to keep upstream models readable and DRY, but that nobody needs to query directly or that doesn't justify the overhead of its own

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
database object.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-22" number={22} question="What incremental strategies does dbt support, and how do you choose between them?" difficulty="hard" topic="Incremental Models">
- **`merge`** (most warehouses) — upserts: updates matching rows on `unique_key`, inserts new ones. The most common choice when the warehouse supports it natively.
- **`delete+insert`** — deletes rows matching the incremental batch's keys, then inserts the new batch. Useful when `merge` isn't available or efficient for the target.
- **`append`** — just inserts new rows, no update/delete logic at all. Only correct when source rows are truly immutable and never revised (pure event logs).

The choice mostly comes down to what the target warehouse supports efficiently and whethe

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
r source records can actually change after the fact.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-23" number={23} question="When and why would you run a full refresh on an incremental model?" difficulty="medium" topic="Incremental Models">
```bash
dbt run --full-refresh --select my_incremental_model
```
A full refresh drops and rebuilds the entire table from scratch instead of processing only new/changed rows — needed when the incremental logic itself changes (a new column, a changed `unique_key`), when you suspect the incremental table has drifted from what the logic would now produce, or the first time a model is ever run.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-24" number={24} question="What are dbt model contracts, and what do they enforce?" difficulty="hard" topic="Contracts">
```

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
yaml
models:
  - name: orders
    config:
      contract: {enforced: true}
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        data_type: string
        constraints: [{type: not_null}]
```
A model contract declares the exact column names, types, and constraints a model must produce — dbt validates the built model against this contract and **fails the build** if reality doesn't match, rather than silently letting a schema change flow downstream. It's the mechanism that turns a data contract (see [Data Quality](/level-2-core-concepts/data-quality/#interview-questions)) from a documented agreement into something dbt itself actively enforces.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-25" number={25} question="What are pre-hooks and post-hooks used for?" difficulty="medium" topic="Hooks">
``

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
`yaml
{{ config(
    pre_hook="INSERT INTO audit_log (model, started_at) VALUES ('{{ this }}', current_timestamp)",
    post_hook="GRANT SELECT ON {{ this }} TO ROLE analyst"
) }}
```
`pre_hook`/`post_hook` run arbitrary SQL immediately before or after a model builds — common uses are audit logging, granting permissions on the freshly-built table, or refreshing a downstream materialized view. They're an escape hatch for warehouse operations that don't fit naturally into "define a `SELECT` and let dbt build it."
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
## Jinja & Packages

Templating and reusable code — how dbt generates SQL dynamically and shares logic across projects.

<QuestionList topic="Jinja & Packages" storagePrefix="dbt-jinja">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-26" number={26} question="How do Jinja control structures (if/for) get used inside a dbt model?" difficulty="medium" topic="Jinja">
```sql
SELECT
    order_id,
    {% for status in ["pending", "shipped", "cancelled"] %}
    SUM(CASE WHEN status = '{{ status }}' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS {{ status }}_count{{ "," if not loop.last }}
    {% endfor %}
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_id
```
Jinja `{% %}` blocks run at **compile time**, generating the final SQL text before it's ever sent to the warehouse — a `{% for %}` loop here writes out one `SUM(CASE...)` column per status witho

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
ut hand-typing each one, and `{% if %}` can conditionally include entire blocks of SQL based on a variable or target.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-27" number={27} question="What is dbt_utils, and what's an example of a macro from it you'd actually use?" difficulty="medium" topic="Packages">
`dbt_utils` is the most widely-used community package, providing macros for things nearly every project needs but dbt Core doesn't ship natively — `dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key()` (hash multiple columns into one surrogate key), `dbt_utils.date_spine()` (generate a row per date in a range, useful for a date dimension), and generic tests like `dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns`. Reaching for it first avoids reinventing well-tested utility macros from scratch.
</QuestionCard>

<Q

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
uestionCard id="dbt-28" number={28} question="How would you write a custom generic test?" difficulty="hard" topic="Testing">
```sql
-- macros/test_is_positive.sql
{% test is_positive(model, column_name) %}
SELECT *
FROM {{ model }}
WHERE {{ column_name }} <= 0
{% endtest %}
```
```yaml
columns:
  - name: amount
    tests: [is_positive]
```
A custom generic test is a macro following the `test_<name>` naming convention that returns a query — like any dbt test, it fails if that query returns any rows. Writing your own is worthwhile once the same non-standard business rule (positive amounts, valid enum-like values not covered by `accepted_values`) needs to be checked across many models.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-29" number={29} question="How do you manage third-pa

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
rty dbt packages in a project?" difficulty="easy" topic="Packages">
```yaml

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
# packages.yml
packages:
  - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
    version: [">=1.0.0", "<2.0.0"]
```
Declare packages in `packages.yml` with a version range, then run `dbt deps` to install them into `dbt_packages/` — this keeps the dependency list explicit and version-pinned (usually committed alongside a lockfile) rather than implicitly relying on whatever happens to already be installed.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

---

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
## Documentation, Governance & Ecosystem

Generating docs, controlling test severity, access control, and where dbt is headed beyond SQL models.

<QuestionList topic="Documentation & Ecosystem" storagePrefix="dbt-ecosystem">

<QuestionCard id="dbt-30" number={30} question="How does dbt documentation generation work, and what does it produce?" difficulty="easy" topic="Documentation">
`dbt docs generate` introspects the project (model SQL, `.yml` descriptions, test definitions, and the warehouse's actual column metadata) and produces a static site with searchable model/column descriptions and an interactive DAG lineage graph — served locally with `dbt docs serve` or hosted for the whole team. Documentation quality is only as good as the `description:` fields authors actually fill in i

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
n each model's `.yml` file.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-31" number={31} question="What's the difference between warn and error severity on a dbt test?" difficulty="easy" topic="Testing">
```yaml
tests:
  - not_null:
      config: {severity: warn}
```
An `error`-severity test (the default) fails the entire `dbt build`/`dbt test` run when it fails. A `warn`-severity test logs a warning but lets the run continue — useful for checks that are informative but not yet reliable enough (or not yet important enough) to block a deploy, without losing visibility into the issue entirely.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-32" number={32} question="What are grants in dbt, and why configure them in code rather than manually?" difficulty="medium" topic="Governance">
```yaml
mo

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
dels:
  - name: revenue_mart
    config:
      grants:
        select: ["role:analyst", "role:bi_tool"]
```
The `grants` config applies warehouse permissions (who can `SELECT` on a model) as part of the build itself, rather than someone remembering to run a `GRANT` statement manually after every deploy. Defining access in code means it's version-controlled, reviewed like any other change, and automatically reapplied if a table gets rebuilt from scratch.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-33" number={33} question="What's the difference between dbt Core and dbt Cloud?" difficulty="easy" topic="Ecosystem">
**dbt Core** is the open-source CLI — you run it yourself, on your own infrastructure or orchestrator (often triggered by Airflow). **dbt Cloud** is the managed SaaS product b

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
uilt on top of it, adding a scheduler, hosted docs, an IDE, and the Semantic Layer, aimed at teams that don't want to build and operate that infrastructure themselves. The underlying model/test/macro code is the same either way — the difference is entirely in how and where it's run and managed.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-34" number={34} question="What are dbt Python models, and when would you reach for one over SQL?" difficulty="hard" topic="Python Models">
On warehouses that support it (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery), a dbt model can be a `.py` file returning a DataFrame instead of a `.sql` file — it still participates in the same `ref()`/DAG/testing system as SQL models. Reach for one when the transformation genuinely needs something SQL is awkward at — a statistical/ML

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
computation, a complex text-parsing step, calling a Python library — not as a general substitute for logic that's perfectly expressible in SQL, which stays simpler and more portable across warehouses.
</QuestionCard>

<QuestionCard id="dbt-35" number={35} question="What is the dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow, and what problem does it solve?" difficulty="hard" topic="Semantic Layer">
The Semantic Layer lets you define metrics (revenue, active users) once in code, with their aggregation logic and dimensions, and have every BI tool and query pull a **consistent** value for that metric instead of each tool/analyst re-implementing the same calculation slightly differently. MetricFlow is the engine that compiles a metric query into the correct SQL against the underlying marts — it directly

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
targets the classic "why do these two dashboards show different revenue" problem by making the metric definition the single source of truth.
</QuestionCard>

</QuestionList>

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
## Common Interview Scenarios

- **"A dbt model takes 40 minutes to build every night and it's only getting slower."** Talk through switching it from a table to an incremental materialization, choosing a reliable `unique_key`, and using state selection so CI doesn't rebuild the whole DAG on every PR.
- **"How would you catch a broken upstream schema before it reaches your marts?"** Discuss declaring the table as a dbt source, adding freshness checks and column tests (`not_null`, `relationships`), and failing the run loudly rather than silently propagating bad data downstream.
- **"You need point-in-time history for a dimension that only exists as a mutable table in the source system."** Explain dbt snapshots as the SCD2 mechanism, and how they differ from just re-running a model that a

title: dbt_project.yml
content:
lways reflects "now."
- **"Two BI dashboards show different revenue numbers, built from the same marts."** Point to the Semantic Layer/MetricFlow as the structural fix — a single defined metric every tool queries — rather than a one-off SQL reconciliation, and mention model contracts as the related mechanism for catching a schema mismatch before it causes the same kind of silent drift.
- **"A model change needs to not break a downstream dashboard nobody on the data team directly owns."** Talk through exposures (declaring that dependency explicitly in docs) combined with state-based CI selection, so anyone changing the upstream model sees the affected downstream consumer before merging, not after it breaks.
